questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female comes to Gynecology OPD for pre-conceptual counseling, with 2 prior second trimester abortions. What is the next investigation you will advise?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pelvic sonography

The most common cause of second trimester abortions are uterocervical structural anomalies and the next investigaton advised in this patient would be pelvic sonography to look for these anomalies.

Although, Hysterosalpingography (Option B) can be used in the patient during the interconceptional period to diagnose internal anatomical abnormalities of the uterus and cervix, it is an invasive procedure and hence is reserved for use only after nonivasive procedures such as sonography is done. Hysterosalpingography (HSG) has limited use in diagnosing the external uterine contour and it is contraindicated in pregnancy.

Pelvic sonography is a non-invasive investigation that can be used to detect certain anatomical anomalies leading to abortions. A 3D sonography will provide better images of uterine and cervical contour than a 2D sonography. This investigation can also be done in pregnant female.

Karyotyping (Option D) is done to rule out any suspicion of chromosomal abnormalities which, more commonly cause first trimester abortions.

Some Causes of Midtrimester(second trimester) abortions

Fetal Anomalies- Structural,Chromosomal

Maternal Disorders-Autoimmune, Infections, Metabolic disorders

Placental Causes-Abruption, previa Vasculopathy,Chorioamnionitis

Uterine Defects-Congenital anomalies, submucosal Leiomyomas, cervical incompetance

NOTE: If a suspicion of cervical incompetence (H/O 1 painless second trimester loss) is present, a TVS is performed in a pregnant female between 18-24weeks and the cervical length and the cervical shape is determined.

• Normal cervical length-3-4cm ; In cervical incompetence ≤2.5cm
• Normal cervix shape-Tshape; In cervical incompetence U shape

In the presence of ≥ 2 painless second trimester abortions, a history based diagnosis of cervical incompetence is made and the pregnant female can undergo prophylactic cervical cerclage with progesterone supplementation.
questions.learning: Pelvic sonography — The most common cause of second trimester abortions are uterocervical structural anomalies and the next investigaton advised in this patient would be pelvic sonography to look for these anomalies.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with developmental delay, recurrent seizures, and history of thromboembolic episodes. On examination, he has marfanoid habitus, osteoporosis, and downward dislocation of the lens. Which of the following vitamin supplementation is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B6

The clinical picture describes homocystinuria (most commonly due to cystathionine β-synthase deficiency), an amino acid metabolism disorder.

• Intellectual disability (mental retardation)
• Seizures
• Thromboembolic tendency
• Osteoporosis / marfanoid habitus
• Ectopia lentis (downward displacement of lens)

Biochemical basis:

• Defect in conversion of homocysteine → cystathionine
• Leads to ↑ homocysteine and ↑ methionine

Treatment:

• Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is a cofactor for cystathionine β-synthase
• Some patients are B6-responsive, leading to ↓ homocysteine levels

Why not others:

• Vitamin B12: Involved in remethylation of homocysteine → methionine (different pathway)
• Thiamine (B1): Carbohydrate metabolism
• Vitamin B2: FAD-dependent reactions

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Classical galactosemia is due to a deficiency of which enzyme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase

Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency leads to classical galactosemia. It is an autosomal recessive disorder.

Clinical features :

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver causes liver damage & leads to hepatomegaly, vomiting, convulsions.

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate depletes the liver of inorganic phosphate leading to diminished ATP synthesis which affects gluconeogenesis resulting in hypoglycemia.

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the nerves causes intellectual disability.

* Accumulation of galactitol in the lens causes oil-drop cataract.

Urinary reducing sugar (Benedict's test) and Mucic acid test is positive.

Treatment is galactose-free diet.
questions.learning: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency leads to classical galactosemia. It is an autosomal recessive disorder.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the molecular biology technique shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CRISPR-Cas system

The image depicts the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing system, in which a guide RNA (gRNA) directs the Cas9 endonuclease to a specific DNA sequence adjacent to a PAM (Protospacer Adjacent Motif). Cas9 introduces a site-specific double-stranded DNA break, allowing targeted gene knockout, correction, or insertion through DNA repair mechanisms.

• The presence of Cas9, gRNA, PAM sequence, and DNA cleavage are hallmark features of the CRISPR-Cas9 system.

Why not the other options?

• B. Microarray analysis: Used to analyze gene expression or detect DNA variants; does not cut DNA.
• C. RNA interference (RNAi): Silences gene expression by degrading mRNA using siRNA/miRNA; no DNA editing.
• D. Zinc finger motif: A DNA-binding protein domain; zinc finger nucleases are gene-editing tools but do not use gRNA or PAM sequences.
questions.learning: CRISPR-Cas system — The image depicts the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing system, in which a guide RNA (gRNA) directs the Cas9 endonuclease to a specific DNA sequence adjacent to a PAM (Protospacer Adjacent Motif).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the National Deworming Day?
questions.explanation: In India, National Deworming Day (NDD) is a nationwide initiative observed every year on 10th February. The program aims to deworm all children and adolescents aged 1–19 years to prevent Soil-Transmitted Helminths (STH) infections. A "mop-up" round is typically conducted on 15th February for those who missed the initial dose. While a second biannual round often occurs in August (Option B), 10th February is the officially designated primary National Deworming Day. Options C (10th March) and D (11th January) are not associated with this public health campaign. During NDD, single doses of Albendazole (400 mg) are administered in schools and Anganwadi centers. This initiative is crucial for reducing childhood anemia and improving overall nutritional status and educational outcomes. Therefore, 10th February is the specific date for this high-priority health intervention
questions.learning: In India, National Deworming Day (NDD) is a nationwide initiative observed every year on 10th February. The program aims to deworm all children and adolescents aged 1–19 years to prevent Soil-Transmitted Helminths (STH) infections.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient presents with persistent itching, redness, and scaling of the skin. Skin scraping is performed for microscopic examination, revealing a pathogen with a characteristic pencil-shaped morphology. Which pathogen is most likely responsible for the patient’s dermatological symptoms?
questions.explanation: Dermatophytosis, or fungal skin infection, is diagnosed by the microscopic appearance of macroconidia in skin scrapings. Trichophyton species are characterized by their "pencil-shaped" or cigar-shaped, thin-walled, multi-septate macroconidia. They are the most common genus of dermatophytes causing infections of the skin, hair, and nails (tinea). Microsporum (Option B) produces spindle-shaped macroconidia with thick, rough walls, which look very different from the smooth "pencil" shape of Trichophyton. Epidermophyton (Option C) produces club-shaped or "snowshoe-shaped" macroconidia, often occurring in clusters of two or three. The patient's symptoms of itching, redness, and scaling are the standard clinical manifestations of tinea. Since the microscopic evidence specifically identifies a pencil-shaped morphology, Trichophyton is the correct genus. Identifying these microscopic features is essential for differentiating between the three main genera of dermatophytes that cause clinically similar skin lesions
questions.learning: Dermatophytosis, or fungal skin infection, is diagnosed by the microscopic appearance of macroconidia in skin scrapings. Trichophyton species are characterized by their "pencil-shaped" or cigar-shaped, thin-walled, multi-septate macroconidia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What are the primary referral centers in India's healthcare system?
options: Primary health centres and district hospitals
Community health centres and medical colleges
Sub-district hospitals and community health centres
questions.explanation: India’s healthcare system is organized into a three-tier structure: primary, secondary, and tertiary care. Primary referral centres refer to facilities where patients are first referred from lower-level institutions (like sub-centres or primary health centres) for more specialized care. Community Health Centres (CHCs) function as the first referral units (FRUs) in rural areas. They provide specialist services such as medicine, surgery, pediatrics, and obstetrics. When cases require even more advanced care, patients are referred further to tertiary care centres, such as medical colleges, which are equipped with highly specialized services, advanced diagnostics, and teaching facilities. Other options are incorrect: (A) Primary health centres and district hospitals PHCs are first-contact facilities, not referral centres (B) Medical colleges and district hospitals district hospitals are referral centres, but PHCs are missing (D) Sub-district hospitals and CHCs these are secondary-level facilities but do not represent the full referral hierarchy

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Substances and the type of transport across a membrane are given below, choose the correct combination:

1. Oxygen: Simple diffusion
2. Glucose: Facilitated diffusion
3. Sodium: Voltage-gated channel
4. Sodium: Secondary active transport
5. Calcium: Active transport
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 are correct

All the given combinations 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 are correct.

1) Oxygen is a non-polar molecule and hence can diffuse across the lipid membrane of the cells.

2) Facilitated diffusion - Transporting the molecule from one side of the cell membrane to the other is done with the help of transport proteins called carriers. Molecules move from areas of high concentration to areas of low concentration. No energy input is required when carrier proteins move substances in the direction of their gradients. Glucose transport by the glucose transporter is an example, which moves glucose down its concentration gradient from the ECF to the cytoplasm of the cell.

3) Voltage-gated channels are simple ion channels acting as transport proteins, gated by membrane potential alterations. Sodium transported via voltage-gated channels is an example.

4) Transporting more than one substance together using a single transport protein against the gradient is known as secondary active transport. An example is SGLT 1, the cotransporter of sodium and glucose from the intestinal lumen into mucosal cells.

5)Active transport - Transporting of substances against the gradients, and requires energy. Ca2+ ATPase that pumps out calcium out of the cells is an example.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 are correct All the given combinations 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 are correct. 1) Oxygen is a non-polar molecule and hence can diffuse across the lipid membrane of the cells.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The image below shows simple muscle twitch along with the time trace, recorded in a frog gastrocnemius muscle. Calculate the minimum tetanizing frequency. (The time tracer was made with a 100Hz tuning fork).
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 20 per second

The tetanizing frequency of the muscle, based on the given diagram, is 20 per second.

Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period. It is the frequency at which individual muscle fibres twitch that fuse and cause sustained muscle contraction, where the contraction period is the time taken from latent period to maximum force of contraction.

In this case, the time tracer was taken using a 100Hz tuning fork. Which means the tracer recorded 100 waves per second.
Therefore, the duration of each wave in time tracer = 0.01 seconds.

In the image given in the question, between the point B (end of latent period) to point C (maximum force of contraction), there are about 5 waves.
Hence, the duration of contraction = 5 x 0.01 = 0.05 seconds.

Substituting the value in the formula, we get:
Tetanizing frequency = 1/0.05 sec = 100/5 = 20/sec.

Tetanization:

The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches. The adding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall muscle contraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways:

• by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously, which is multiple ﬁber summations.
• by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead to tetanization.

When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level, the successive contractions eventually fuse together, and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous, this is called tetanization. Beyond this point, a further increase in the frequency, will not result in increased force of contraction.

Tetanization occurs in two ways:

• Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli.
• Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summated stimuli.
questions.learning: 20 per second The tetanizing frequency of the muscle, based on the given diagram, is 20 per second. Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following does not require 5' capping?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. tRNA of Alanine

5′ capping (addition of 7-methylguanosine) occurs on RNA polymerase II transcripts, mainly mRNA and some small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) like U1, U2, U4, U5, to:

• Protect RNA from degradation
• Facilitate nuclear export
• Promote translation initiation

tRNAs are transcribed by RNA polymerase III and instead undergo processing and modification at their ends, not 5′ capping. Similarly, siRNAs are processed from double-stranded RNA and do not require 5′ caps. Histone mRNAs are an exception; they have a special 3′ stem-loop instead of a poly-A tail, but still receive a 5′ cap.

Why other options are incorrect:

B. U6 snRNA: Does not get a 7-methylguanosine cap, but it is transcribed by RNA polymerase III; still small nuclear RNA function.

C. mRNA for histone/any protein, including ApoB-100: 5′ capping occurs even for histone mRNAs..

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are absolute contraindications of Combined Oral Contraceptive (COCs)? 1. Arterial or venous thrombosis history 2. Severe hypertension 3. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia 4. Diabetes with vascular complications Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Combined Oral Contraceptives (COCs) contain estrogen and progestin. Because estrogen increases the risk of thromboembolism and cardiovascular events, COCs are contraindicated in women with conditions that predispose to vascular complications.

• 1. Arterial or venous thrombosis history ✅

• Absolute contraindication.
• Estrogen increases the risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE), stroke, and myocardial infarction.

• 2. Severe hypertension ✅

• Absolute contraindication (BP ≥160/100 mmHg).
• COCs further increase the risk of stroke and cardiovascular events.

• 3. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia ❌

• Not an absolute contraindication.
• Hormonal contraception, including COCs, may be used once appropriate management has begun and pregnancy has been excluded.

• 4. Diabetes with vascular complications ✅

• Absolute contraindication.
• Estrogen increases the risk of vascular events in women with diabetic nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy, or other vascular disease.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Combined Oral Contraceptives (COCs) contain estrogen and progestin. Because estrogen increases the risk of thromboembolism and cardiovascular events, COCs are contraindicated in women with conditions that predispose to vascular complications. • 1.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve passes through the foramen marked in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inferior alveolar nerve

The marked structure is mandibular foramen and inferior alveolar nerve passes through it.

The inferior alveolar nerve (IAN), a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3), it descends behind the lateral pterygoid, at the lower border of the muscle, the nerve passes between the sphenomandibular ligament and the mandibular ramus and enters the mandibular canal via the mandibular foramen
The mandibular foramen is located above the mandibular angle, the opening through which the IAN and the vessels of the mandible pass.
The IAN continues its course through the mandibular canal and then branches off to supply the lower teeth, gums, and lower lip.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: An 8 months old baby on examination shows signs of Vitamin A deficiency. What is the dose of Vitamin A to be administered to the baby?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 100, 000 IU orally

The vitamin A dose for an 8 months old baby with clinical signs of deficiency is 100,000 IU orally.

Treatment of children with Vit A deficiency:

* 100,000 IU orally or 50,000 IU IM for a child < 12 months and

* 200,000 IU of vitamin A orally or 100,000 IU by intramuscular injection for a child above 12 months.

The same dose of Vitamin A is repeated the next day and on the 14th day.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A teenage patient presented with a history of dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain. On ultrasonography, a transverse vaginal septum was seen. What is the most common complication that can be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endometriosis

The most common complication that can be seen in this patient is endometriosis.

Transverse vaginal septum leads to obstructed flow of menstrual blood. This may lead to retrograde menstruation, which increases the likelihood of the development of endometriosis, according to Sampson's theory of endometriosis.

Transverse vaginal septum occurs as a result of the failure of Müllerian duct fusion or failure of vaginal plate canalization. It may be obstructive or non-obstructive. The commonest site of a transverse septum is the junction between the upper and middle third of the vagina.

Patients with an obstructive or imperforate vaginal septum present with symptoms similar to the imperforate hymen. Symptoms include amenorrhoea, cyclical abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, and a palpable pelvic mass. The vagina may appear shortened and the cervix may not be identifiable. Secondary sexual characteristics appear normal. The diagnosis can be confirmed with ultrasound or MRI.

There is an increased risk of endometriosis. Other complications such as pyomucocolpos, pyometra, and pyosalpinges can also develop in infants with obstructive vaginal septums.

Treatment is by manual dilatation of the perforation or surgical excision of the septum.

Other options:

Option B: Tubo-ovarian abscess develops in pelvic inflammatory disease.

Option C: Dermoid cysts are cystic ovarian tumors that are often associated with mucinous cystadenomas.

Option D: Theca lutein cysts are found in association with hydatidiform moles, choriocarcinoma, and gonadotropin or clomiphene citrate therapy. They regress with the management of the mole and choriocarcinoma and discontinuation of gonadotropin therapy.
questions.learning: Endometriosis — The most common complication that can be seen in this patient is endometriosis. Transverse vaginal septum leads to obstructed flow of menstrual blood.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In which condition is the reservoir sign seen along with mastoid tenderness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute mastoiditis

Reservoir sign along with the tenderness of the mastoid is seen in acute mastoiditis.

Reservoir sign is seen in acute mastoiditis/coalescent Mastoiditis where mastoid acts as a reservoir of pus and pus reappear in EAC immediately after cleaning.

Mastoiditis is a complication of otitis media.

Other signs of acute mastoiditis:

The light-house effect is seen is acute mastoiditis. It is described as a pulsatile mucopurulent or purulent discharge, coming through a central pin-hole perforation of pars tensa. It suggests a reservoir of infection in the mastoid and middle ear.

Note: In CSF rhinorrhea, the fluid which had collected in the sinuses, particularly sphenoid, empties into the nose is also called reservoir sign.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Fetal anaemia is monitored by?
questions.explanation: The monitoring of fetal anemia, particularly in cases of Rh isoimmunization, is primarily done using Middle Cerebral Artery Peak Systolic Velocity (MCA-PSV) Doppler ultrasound. This non-invasive tool is based on the principle that anemic fetuses increase their cardiac output and decrease blood viscosity, leading to a measurable increase in the velocity of blood flow in the cerebral arteries. An MCA-PSV value greater than 1.5 Multiples of the Median (MoM) for gestational age predicts moderate to severe anemia with high sensitivity. While maternal blood tests (Option B) like the Indirect Coombs Test help identify the risk of sensitization, they cannot measure the current degree of fetal anemia. Fetal blood sampling (Option C) and amniocentesis (Option D) are invasive procedures used for definitive diagnosis or treatment (intrauterine transfusion) but are not used for routine surveillance. Thus, MCA-PSV is the modern mainstay for safe fetal monitoring
questions.learning: The monitoring of fetal anemia, particularly in cases of Rh isoimmunization, is primarily done using Middle Cerebral Artery Peak Systolic Velocity (MCA-PSV) Doppler ultrasound.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient is having the following hand movements. In which of the following conditions would this be seen?
questions.explanation: The image depicts asterixis, commonly known as "flapping tremors". This is a negative myoclonus characterized by a loss of muscle tone when the patient extends their wrists and fingers. Asterixis is a hallmark sign of metabolic encephalopathy. It is most classically seen in Hypercarbia (excess CO2 in the blood, often from COPD or respiratory failure) and Hepatic Encephalopathy (liver failure). It can also occur in uremia (renal failure). Thyrotoxicosis (Option A) causes a fine, fast tremor, not a slow flap. Hemiballismus (Option C) involves violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of the limbs. Hypoxia (Option D) causes confusion and cyanosis but is not the primary cause of flapping tremors. Recognizing asterixis at the bedside is a vital clinical clue for identifying systemic metabolic derangement. Treatment focuses on the underlying cause, such as non-invasive ventilation for hypercarbia or lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy
questions.learning: The image depicts asterixis, commonly known as "flapping tremors". This is a negative myoclonus characterized by a loss of muscle tone when the patient extends their wrists and fingers.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 16-year-old patient presents with diarrhoea and pellagra-like photosensitive skin eruptions for the last 5 years. Her vital examinations are normal. Urine analysis reveals an increase in the amino acid levels but normal levels of 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid (5-HIAA). What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hartnup disease

The above clinical history of a 16-year-old child presenting with diarrhoea and pellagra-like photosensitive skin eruptions with urine analysis showing an increase in the amino acid levels and normal 5-HIAA levels is suggestive of Hartnup disease.

Amino acids are reabsorbed in the kidneys in the proximal convoluted tubule. Aminoaciduria points towards a pathology.

Hartnup disease (pellagra-like dermatosis) is an autosomal recessive condition caused by a single defect in the renal and intestinal transport of neutral amino acids (eg, Tryptophan). Decreased intestinal absorption of tryptophan in conjunction with its increased renal loss leads to its reduced bioavailability. This hampers niacin synthesis, and Hartnup disorder can thus present with manifestations of niacin deficiency (pellagra) like diarrhoea, dermatitis, and dementia.

Clinical features:

* Most of the children are asymptomatic

* Symptomatic patients show cutaneous photosensitivity

* The skin becomes rough and red after moderate exposure to the sun, and with greater exposure, a pellagra-like rash may develop. The rash may be pruritic, and chronic eczema may also appear.

* Some patients may also have intermittent ataxia, manifested as an unsteady, wide-based gait, which usually lasts for a few days and recovers spontaneously.

The diagnosis of Hartnup disorder is established by typical clinical history and the presence of neutral amino acids in the urine.

The Obermeyer test will be positive for Hartnup disorder. The Obermeyer test detects the urinary excretion of indole compounds. Indole derivates such as indican are found in large amounts in patients due to bacterial breakdown of unabsorbed tryptophan in the intestines.

Urinary excretion of other amino acids remains normal, which differentiates it from causes of generalized aminoaciduria like Fanconi syndrome.

Treatment:

* Niacin or niacinamide supplements

* Nicotinamide for attacks

Other options:

Option A: In Carcinoid syndrome, there is an excess synthesis of serotonin. This consumes available tryptophan and leads to a deficiency of niacin and eventually pellagra-like symptoms. In carcinoid syndrome, excess serotonin is converted to 5-HIAA which is excreted in urine. This patient has normal levels of 5-HIAA.

Option B:  Nutritional pellagra can appear in patients with excessive maize-based diets. Maize has niacin in its unusable form. Additionally, they will not excrete amino acids in urine.

Option C: Fructosuria will present with fructose in urine instead of amino acids.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient with a reduced food intake over the past few months now presents with hypoglycemia. What is the most likely cause of hypoglycemia in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Impaired gluconeogenesis

The given clinical scenario of a chronic alcoholic presenting with hypoglycemia is suggestive of alcohol (ethanol) intoxication that inhibits the process of gluconeogenesis.

Alcohol is metabolized in the liver via the enzymes alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase. These reactions convert ethanol to acetaldehyde and then to acetate, using NAD⁺ as a cofactor and producing NADH. The excess NADH shifts the balance of metabolic processes, diverting key substrates (like pyruvate and oxaloacetate) away from gluconeogenesis, thus impairing the liver's ability to produce glucose.

The patient had decreased food intake over the past few months, leading to reduced dietary glucose consumption and increased reliance on the liver for blood glucose maintenance through gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. However, since alcohol inhibits these processes, it would further worsen hypoglycemia.

Other options:

Option A: Decreased glycogenolysis reduces the breakdown of glycogen into glucose, leading to impaired blood sugar regulation and potential hypoglycemia. This can result from enzyme deficiencies, liver dysfunction, or hormonal imbalances affecting glycogen metabolism.

Option C: Increased glycolysis accelerates the breakdown of glucose into pyruvate, leading to higher energy production in the form of ATP. This process can be upregulated in conditions like hypoxia, cancer, or insulin stimulation.

Option D: The HMP shunt is an alternative pathway to glycolysis and is used to produce ribose-5-phosphate and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH). It doesn't cause hypoglycemia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with shoulder pain following a hyperextension injury during exercise. On examination, there is evidence of avulsion of the long head of the triceps. What is the site of avulsion of triceps?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Infraglenoid tubercle

The long head of triceps brachii originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, crossing the shoulder joint.

A hyperextension injury can avulse this tendon at its origin.

The shaft of humerus gives origin to the lateral and medial heads, supraglenoid tubercle is for the long head of biceps, and deltoid tuberosity is for deltoid insertion.
questions.learning: Infraglenoid tubercle — The long head of triceps brachii originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, crossing the shoulder joint. A hyperextension injury can avulse this tendon at its origin.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old morbidly obese male patient presented with complaints of severe abdominal pain and urinary disturbances. His urine microscopy shows the following type of crystals and an ultrasound of the kidney revealed a renal stone of size 2.5 cm. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL)

Urine microscopy shows hexagonal crystals, typical of cystine stones that are radio-opaque (due to high sulfur content). The treatment of choice for renal calculi of size 2.5 cm is percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL).

Indications of PCNL:

* Staghorn calculi

* Stones >2 cm in size

* Stone composition - struvite, calcium oxalate monohydrate and cystine stones

* Multiple stones

* Obese patients in whom ESWL is contraindicated

* Stones not responding for ESWL

Endoscopic instruments are passed into the kidney using a percutaneous technique and stones are removed.

Complications of percutaneous nephrolithotomy include:

* Haemorrhage from the punctured renal parenchyma

* Perforation of the collecting system with extravasation of saline irrigant

* Perforation of the colon or pleural cavity during placement of the percutaneous track

Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy:

ESWL is a non-invasive method that generates shockwaves outside the body, which are focused on the stones. It is the commonest method of treating urinary tract stones nowadays. Stones up to approximately 2 cm in size are suitable for this form of treatment.Cystine stones are very hard stones as a result of disulphide bonds and do not fragment with ESWL. Other stones that are difficult to disintegrate by ESWL include cystine, brushite, and calcium oxalate monohydrate stones.

ESWL is only 45-60% effective in the treatment of large stones. It causes frequent complications including pain, hydronephrosis, fever, and occasional urosepsis, due to difficulties in the passage of stone particles, especially in cases of insufficient disintegration.

Complications: Infection, haematuria, parenchymal haemorrhage, and perirenal hematoma.

Contraindications: Obese patients, pregnant patients, and patients taking oral anticoagulants.

Stone fragments collecting in the distal ureter following ESWL are called steinstrasse  (a german word, which means 'street of stones'). The most common site of the column of stone fragments obstruction is the distal ureter, followed by the proximal ureter and mid ureter. The postoperative image is attached below.

Ureteroscopic removal: Ureteric calculi are directly visualized through semi-rigid ureteroscopes. Stones are then fragmented and extracted using a dormia basket.

These are generally preferred for stones <6mm and specifically those present in the distal ureter. The most significant complications relate to injury to the ureteric mucosa or wall and include ureteric perforation and extravasation, avulsion of the ureter and ureteric stricture.

Open surgery: A longstanding obstructing calculus can result in chronic inflammatory change in the kidney. Open surgeries are generally indicated for xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP). Generally, in such cases, a subcapsular nephrectomy is performed.

In extremely rare cases where both PCNL and ESWL are contraindicated open/laparoscopic surgery is used.
questions.learning: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) Urine microscopy shows hexagonal crystals, typical of cystine stones that are radio-opaque (due to high sulfur content).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 2-month-old girl child was brought to the hospital by her parents with the following presentation. What is the appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immediate surgery

For the 2-month-old girl presenting with leukocoria in the left eye, likely indicative of a congenital infantile cataract, immediate surgery is the most appropriate management.

Congenital infantile cataract refers to lens opacities present at birth, which can obstruct vision and potentially affect the child’s overall development. If left untreated, congenital cataracts, especially unilateral cataracts, can lead to amblyopia, a condition where one eye fails to develop normal vision due to insufficient visual input. Immediate surgical intervention is crucial not only to remove the cataract and restore visual clarity but also to minimize the risk of amblyopia, ensuring the best possible outcomes for the child's visual and developmental health. Prompt diagnosis and treatment can significantly enhance the chances of preserving and improving the child’s vision.

Leukocoria, or the white pupillary reflex or cat's eye reflex, is a critical sign that often indicates serious underlying eye disorders requiring prompt evaluation and management. Common causes of leukocoria include:

• Retinoblastoma
• Congenital cataract
• Coloboma of the choroid
• Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous
• Toxocara infestation
• Coat's exudative retinopathy.

Note: Retinoblastoma, a malignant tumour of the retina, often affects children under 6 years of age and can present with symptoms such as leukocoria, strabismus (crossed eyes), or vision problems. Treatment options vary widely depending on factors like the tumour's size, location, and whether it is unilateral or bilateral.
questions.learning: Immediate surgery For the 2-month-old girl presenting with leukocoria in the left eye, likely indicative of a congenital infantile cataract, immediate surgery is the most appropriate management.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the test depicted in the image below that is conducted on the victim's clothing to detect blood stains.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Teichmann test

The test shown in the image below is the Teichmann test, which is used to detect blood stains. It shows brownish-black rhombic crystals of haemin or haematin chloride.

Teichmann test (Haemin Crystal Test):

* This test is used to detect suspected bloodstains.

* A small piece of suspected material is placed on a glass slide. Then, 2-3 drops of glacial acetic acid and a small crystal of sodium chloride are added to the glass slide and covered with a coverslip. The slide is then heated.

* If bloodstain is present, faint yellowish-red to brownish-black rhombic crystals of haemin or haematin chloride appear.

* When hydrogen peroxide is added, the haematin crystals give bubbles of gas.

Other options:

Option A: Barberio test: It is used to detect seminal fluid. When a saturated aqueous or alcoholic solution of picric acid is added to the spermatic fluid, yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals of spermine picrate are produced.

Option B: Florence test: This test is used to detect semen. The suspected seminal stain is extracted with 10% hydrochloric acid, and a drop of it is placed over a slide. A coverslip is placed over it, and a drop of Florence solution (potassium iodide, iodine, and water) is made to run under the coverslip. If semen is present, dark brown rhombic or needle-shaped crystals of choline iodide appear immediately.

Option C: Takayama test (Haemochromogen crystal test): This test is used to detect suspected bloodstains. A small piece of suspected material is added to a glass slide. Then, 2-3 drops of Takayama reagent are added and covered with a coverslip. If it is a bloodstain, pink feathery crystals of haemochromogen or reduced alkaline haematin appear in a few minutes.

Pearl PF0395: Tests to detect seminal and blood stains

Tests for seminal stains

* Barberio's test

* Florence test

* Acid phosphatase test

* Creatine phosphokinase test

* Immunological test to detect Prostate Specific Antigen

Tests for blood stains

* Benzidine test

* Phenophthalein (Kastle Meyer) test

* Takayama hemochromogen crystal test

* Teichmann’s hemin crystal test

* Spectroscopic test
questions.learning: Teichmann test — The test shown in the image below is the Teichmann test, which is used to detect blood stains. It shows brownish-black rhombic crystals of haemin or haematin chloride.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman presents with palpitations, heat intolerance, unintentional weight loss, and anxiety over the past two months. Exam reveals warm, moist skin, fine resting tremor, brisk reflexes, lid retraction, and mild proptosis. Her heart rate is 118/min and irregularly irregular, and an ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. Echocardiography shows preserved ejection fraction with increased cardiac output. Her physician explains the arrhythmia and hemodynamic profile to a medical student, who proposes several possible mechanisms. Which of the following statements correctly describes the cardiovascular pathophysiology in this patient's condition?
options: The tachyarrhythmia is best explained by decreased density and sensitivity of myocardial β-adrenergic receptors, which paradoxically lowers the threshold for ectopic atrial activity

Increased sarcolemmal Ca²⁺-ATPase activity together with decreased phospholamban expression enhances sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium cycling, contributing to the increased chronotropy and contractility seen in this condition
Her elevated cardiac output is primarily due to increased systemic vascular resistance, which increases afterload and secondarily raises heart rate via baroreceptor-mediated reflex tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation is a rare and incidental finding in this condition, occurring no more frequently than in the general population, and should prompt a search for an alternative cardiac etiology
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased sarcolemmal Ca²⁺-ATPase activity together with decreased phospholamban expression enhances sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium cycling, contributing to the increased chronotropy and contractility seen in this condition

• This patient's presentation, including the ophthalmopathy with periorbital edema, exophthalmos, and lid retraction, is characteristic of Graves disease-associated hyperthyroidism.
• Thyroid hormone (T3) directly alters cardiac gene expression:

• ↑ SERCA2 (Sarcoplasmic Reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase) expression/activity
• ↓ Phospholamban (PLB) expression

• Normally, phospholamban inhibits SERCA2. Therefore:

• ↓ Phospholamban + ↑ SERCA2 → Faster reuptake of Ca²⁺ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum → Faster calcium cycling

• This results in:

• ✅ Increased contractility (positive inotropy)
• ✅ Faster relaxation (positive lusitropy)
• ✅ Increased heart rate (positive chronotropy)

• Additionally, thyroid hormone also:

• ↑ β₁-adrenergic receptor expression
• ↑ Sensitivity to catecholamines
• ↑ Cardiac output
• ↓ Systemic vascular resistance

• Hyperthyroidism is characteristically associated with tachycardia and increased cardiac output, not bradycardia, which is instead a feature of hypothyroidism.
• Atrial fibrillation is a recognized and clinically important arrhythmic complication of hyperthyroidism, related to the increased adrenergic sensitivity and metabolic demand on the heart.
questions.learning: Increased sarcolemmal Ca²⁺-ATPase activity together with decreased phospholamban expression enhances sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium cycling, contributing to the increased chronotropy and contractility seen in this condition • This patient's presentation,…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the primary mechanism of action of methotrexate?
options: Inhibits DNA synthesis by blocking thymidylate synthase
Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, leading to decreased DNA synthesis
Inhibits RNA synthesis by blocking RNA polymerase
Interferes with microtubule formation during cell division
questions.explanation: Methotrexate is an antimetabolite drug that functions as a folic acid analog. Its primary mechanism is the competitive inhibition of the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). DHFR is essential for converting inactive dihydrofolate into active tetrahydrofolate, which is a required cofactor for the synthesis of purines and thymidylate (needed for DNA). By depleting the cell's supply of active folate, methotrexate effectively halts DNA synthesis and cell division. Inhibition of thymidylate synthase (Option A) is the mechanism of 5-Fluorouracil. Blocking RNA polymerase (Option C) is how drugs like rifampicin work. Interference with microtubules (Option D) describes drugs like vincristine or taxanes. Methotrexate is widely used at high doses for chemotherapy and at lower doses for autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis. Its toxic side effects, such as bone marrow suppression, can be mitigated by "rescuing" normal cells with leucovorin (folinic acid), which bypasses the inhibited DHFR enzyme
questions.learning: Methotrexate is an antimetabolite drug that functions as a folic acid analog. Its primary mechanism is the competitive inhibition of the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with fatigue, anemia, and hepatomegaly, and hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrates the presence of HbS. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: The presence of Hemoglobin S (HbS) on electrophoresis confirms a diagnosis of Sickle Cell Anemia. Under low oxygen conditions, HbS polymerizes, causing red blood cells to sickle, leading to vaso-occlusion and chronic hemolysis. Hydroxyurea is the primary chronic therapy because it increases the production of fetal hemoglobin (HbF). Higher levels of HbF inhibit the polymerization of HbS, thereby reducing the frequency of painful crises and systemic complications. Blood transfusions (Option B) are reserved for acute severe anemia or emergencies rather than first-line long-term management. Iron supplementation (Option C) is contraindicated unless a concurrent iron deficiency is proven, as these patients are at risk for iron overload from hemolysis and transfusions. Vitamin B12 (Option D) treats macrocytic anemia and is not specific to sickle cell disease. Therefore, hydroxyurea remains the definitive treatment to modify the disease course
questions.learning: The presence of Hemoglobin S (HbS) on electrophoresis confirms a diagnosis of Sickle Cell Anemia. Under low oxygen conditions, HbS polymerizes, causing red blood cells to sickle, leading to vaso-occlusion and chronic hemolysis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is/are true about skeletal muscle?

1. Extracellular calcium is not important for contraction.
2. Calcium is mainly released from mitochondria.
3. Calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
4. Voltage-gated calcium channel on sarcolemma has no role in excitation-contraction coupling.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Only 3

The true statement about skeletal muscle is that the calcium is released from sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Excitation-contraction coupling refers to the process by which the membrane depolarization of the muscle fiber (excitation) leads to the contraction of the muscle.

For the maximum contraction of the skeletal muscle, the current has to penetrate deeply into the muscle fiber to the vicinity of the separate myofibrils. This penetration of current is achieved by transmission of action potentials along transverse tubules (T tubules). The T tubules penetrate through the muscle fiber, from one side of the fiber to the other.

Sarcoplasmic reticulum contains calcium ions in high concentration within its vesicular tubules. These ions are released from each vesicle when an action potential occurs in the adjacent T tubule. (Statement 3)

This action potential when it reaches the T tubule, it is sensed by the dihydropyridine receptors linked to calcium release channels. Actvation of this receptor leads to the opening of calcium release channels that releases the calcium ions into the sarcoplasm surrounding the myofibrils and causing contraction. (Statement 4)

In skeletal muscles, extracellular calcium supply partially contributes for the maintenance of skeletal muscle contraction.(Statement 1)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following organelles is absent in the area of the cardiac muscle marked:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lysosome

The area of the cardiac muscle marked is devoid of nuclei. Lysosomes are commonly observed in perinuclear areas. Other organelles are present in abundance throughout the cell.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 20-year-old male presenting with right flank pain, fever with chills, and pain on passive extension of the right hip, along with leukocytosis and characteristic findings on CT scan?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of fever, flank pain, and the classic "psoas sign" (pain on passive extension of the hip) is highly suggestive of a psoas abscess. The psoas muscle is located deep in the retroperitoneum, and its proximity to the hip joint causes inflammation there to manifest as pain when the muscle is stretched. While acute appendicitis (Option C), especially with a retrocecal appendix, can also cause a psoas sign, the primary location of the pain in the "flank" often shifts the differential toward an abscess or renal pathology. Pyelonephritis (Option A) causes flank pain and fever but typically does not produce a positive psoas sign. Torsion of an undescended testis (Option D) can cause lower abdominal or groin pain but would not typically involve the psoas sign and would show a missing testis in the scrotum. Therefore, the inflammatory symptoms localized to the psoas muscle confirm a psoas abscess diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of fever, flank pain, and the classic "psoas sign" (pain on passive extension of the hip) is highly suggestive of a psoas abscess.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the lesion in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Viral keratitis

The above image shows a dendritic ulcer caused by herpes simplex virus.

Herpes simplex causes epithelial keratitis and in severe forms, dendritic ulcers develop. Most of the patients present with redness, photophobia, watering, and blurred vision. On examination, visual acuity and corneal sensation are reduced. Follicular conjunctivitis and blepharitis may develop but are usually mild. Clinical reactivation occurs due to multiple stress factors and causes recurrent infections.

The fluorescein-stained image under slit-lamp examination shows dendritic ulcers, a pathognomic feature of epithelial keratitis. They are mostly treated with acyclovir 3% ointment or ganciclovir 0.15% gel.

* Punctate epithelial keratitis

* Dendritic ulcer

* Diffuse stromal necrotic keratitis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: 18-year-old female presented with high fever and pain in knee and ankle joints. On examination, the patient had a pan-systolic murmur at the apex. Rheumatoid factor is negative. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute Rheumatic Fever

Acute rheumatic fever presents with migratory polyarthritis of large joints and carditis following streptococcal infection.

A pan-systolic murmur at the apex indicates mitral regurgitation due to rheumatic carditis.

Diagnosis of ARF is based on Modified Jones Criteria.

Major Criteria

| Major feature

| -------------

| Carditis

| Migratory polyarthritis

| Chorea

| Erythema marginatum

| Subcutaneous nodules

Minor Criteria

| Minor feature

| -------------

| Fever

| Arthralgia

| Elevated ESR / CRP

| Prolonged PR interval

Evidence of recent streptococcal infection is also required.

Rheumatoid factor is negative, supporting a non-RA etiology.

Septic arthritis is usually monoarticular, and ankylosing spondylitis involves axial joints.
questions.learning: Acute Rheumatic Fever Acute rheumatic fever presents with migratory polyarthritis of large joints and carditis following streptococcal infection. A pan-systolic murmur at the apex indicates mitral regurgitation due to rheumatic carditis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following complication is specific to Monochorionic twins?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Twin to twin transfusion syndrome

Twin to twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) is a specific complication seen in monochorionic twins. Selective fetal growth restriction, polyhydramnios and neural tube defects are seen as complications to several conditions and are not specific to monochorionic twins.

In monochorionic diamniotic gestation, twins are separated solely by two amniotic membranes, with no intervening chorion. Monochorionic monoamniotic gestation lacks a dividing membrane.

All monochorionic placentas likely have some anastomotic connections, unique to this type. Chronic feto-fetal transfusion may lead to the following clinical syndromes:

• Twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS)
• Twin anemia–polycythemia sequence (TAPS)
• Twin reversed-arterial-perfusion (TRAP) sequence

Twin to twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS):

TTTS is a fetal syndrome in monozygotic twinning with two amnionic sacs and a shared chorion, allowing for anatomical sharing of fetal circulations through anastomoses of placental arteries and veins. This leads to transfusion from donor twin to recipient twin, resulting in donor anemia and restricted growth, while the recipient may suffer polycythemia, circulatory overload, and hydrops.

Features:

Donor twin
Recipient twin

Oliguria
Polyuria

Anemia
Polycythemia

Oligohydramnios
Polyhydramnios

Activation of Renin-angiotensin system (RAAS)
Activation of Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)

Decreased renal blood flow
Increased renal blood flow

Non-visible bladder

Over distended bladder, circulatory overload, hyperviscosity syndrome, hyperbilirubinemia, hypertension

Renal failure

Congestive cardiac failure (CCF), Hydrops twin (late cases )

The Quintero staging is as follows:

• Stage I—Discordant amnionic fluid volumes+ urine visible in donor's bladder.
• Stage II—Stage I + no visible urine in donor's bladder.
• Stage III— Stage II + abnormal Doppler studies of the umbilical artery, ductus venosus, or umbilical vein.
• Stage IV— frank ascites or hydrops in either twin.
• Stage V—the demise of either fetus.

Treatment:

• Laser photoablation of the placental vascular anastomoses is the preferred treatment for severe TTTS - Quintero stages 2 to 4.
• Septostomy is seldom done.
• Amnioreduction is a treatment modality that involves needle drainage of excessive amniotic fluid.
• Selective feticide is done only if the growth disturbances develop before 20 weeks.
• Of all, selective fetoscopic laser photocoagulation (SFLP) by Solomon technique is the preferred treatment modality as it is associated with better survival rates and a reduced likelihood of recurrence.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a method of direct transmission of communicable diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Droplet nuclei

Airborne transmission by droplet nuclei is not a method of direct transmission of diseases.

It is a method of indirect transmission of diseases.

Droplet nuclei are tiny particles of size 1-5 microns range that may be formed by either due to evaporation of droplets coughed or sneezed into the air or are formed from aerosols.

These droplet nuclei remain airborne for long periods of time and can transmit diseases like tuberculosis, influenza, chickenpox, measles, Q fever and other respiratory infections.

Droplet transmission, vertical transmission, and contact with soil are methods of direct transmission of diseases.

Differences between droplet and droplet nuclei are summarised below:

DROPLET NUCLEI
DROPLET

Indirect transmission
Direct transmission

It is the residue from evaporated droplets
It is produced while coughing, sneezing, talking

<5microns in diameter
≥5 microns in diameter

No need for close contact for transmission
Requires closeness and direct contact for transmission

Diseases transmitted: chickenpox, measles etc.
Diseases transmitted: diphtheria, meningococcal meningitis etc.
questions.learning: Droplet nuclei Airborne transmission by droplet nuclei is not a method of direct transmission of diseases. It is a method of indirect transmission of diseases.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nerves is not involved in olfaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypoglossal nerve

The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor cranial nerve and is not involved in olfaction.

The other three cranial nerves—trigeminal, glossopharyngeal, and vagus nerves are mixed cranial nerves and contribute to olfaction.

Vagal nerve stimulation modifies the electrical activity of the olfactory bulb.
questions.learning: Hypoglossal nerve — The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor cranial nerve and is not involved in olfaction. The other three cranial nerves—trigeminal, glossopharyngeal, and vagus nerves are mixed cranial nerves and contribute to olfaction.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A young child presented with mild intermittent upper abdominal pain. X-ray is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Morgagni hernia

The clinical features and the chest X-ray showing an opacity in the right cardiophrenic angle are suggestive of Morgagni hernia.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia(CDH) of anteromedial location is the Morgagni hernia. Here the defect is anterior and retrosternal. It is rarer than bochdalek hernia and accounts for only 2-5% of CDH. About 90% of the cases occur on the right side.

It is less symptomatic than bochdalek hernia and the diagnosis is usually delayed until childhood. The patient presents with respiratory or upper GI symptoms. Respiratory symptoms like distress, tachypnea, and recurrent pulmonary infections are common in children. Other symptoms are abdominal pain, dyspnea, flatulence, and indigestion.

Radiographic findings:

• Radiolucent paracardiac shadow may be seen retrosternally on lateral chest x-ray if there is bowel herniation.
• Rounded opacity in the right cardiophrenic angle may be seen if there is herniation of omentum or solid organs.
• A CT scan may be used to confirm the diagnosis.

Surgical repair is indicated in all cases either by a thoracic or abdominal approach.

Other options:

Bochdalek hernia: It is more common than Morgagni hernia. Here the defect is posterolateral in location. Respiratory distress is experienced by most infants. In the pediatric age group, symptoms are predominantly respiratory due to pulmonary hypoplasia. In adults, it is usually asymptomatic and is incidentally found. About 85% of the cases are left-sided.

Gastric volvulus: This is an uncommon condition and presents with the characteristic Borchardt triad which includes:

• Sudden-onset severe upper abdominal pain
• Recurrent retching with the production of little vomitus
• Inability to pass a nasogastric (NG) tube

It can be organoaxial or mesentroaxial. Chest X-ray may show intrathoracic upside-down stomach and retrosternal or mediastinal air-fluid level.

Image showing intrathoracic gastric volvulus with mediastinal gastric bubble-

Eventration of the diaphragm: It refers to the abnormal contour of the dome of the diaphragm without any disruption to the diaphragmatic continuity. It usually involves a segment of the hemidiaphragm. It can cause respiratory distress in newborns and is usually asymptomatic in adults.

Radiographic findings: The affected portion of the hemidiaphragm is elevated and is seen as a smooth hump, while the normal contour is seen in the remaining part. 'Double diaphragmatic contour' may be seen in frontal view and is confirmed with a lateral X-ray.

Image showing eventration of the right dome of the diaphragm-
questions.learning: Morgagni hernia — The clinical features and the chest X-ray showing an opacity in the right cardiophrenic angle are suggestive of Morgagni hernia. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia(CDH) of anteromedial location is the Morgagni hernia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for pneumoperitoneal bradycardia following CO2 insufflation during laparoscopic surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Peritoneal stretching

Vagal stimulation due to peritoneal stretching is responsible for bradycardia following CO2 insufflation during laparoscopic surgery.

Carbon dioxide (CO2) and nitrous oxide (N2O) are used in pneumoperitoneum, a technique that enhances laparoscopic surgery by distending the abdominal cavity and splitting up its contents.

The physiologic effects of CO2 pneumoperitoneum can be divided into local and systemic effects:

Local Effects
Systemic effects

Peritoneal distention
Hypercarbia

Vagal reaction
Acidosis

Elevated diaphragm
Increased afterload

Altered venous return
Increased catecholamines

CO2 pneumoperitoneum is associated with the risk of pathophysiological cardiovascular changes such as severe bradycardia, arrhythmia, and cardiac arrest requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation. These changes are known to be associated with vagal-mediated cardiovascular reflexes triggered by rapid peritoneum distension due to insufflation.

This can be managed by desufflation of the abdomen, the use of vagolytic medications (such as atropine), and sufficient volume replacement.

Most people can tolerate the hemodynamic and metabolic effects of pneumoperitoneum for a brief duration, and most healthy people can tolerate them for a longer period of time. Long laparoscopic procedures can be challenging for patients whose cardiovascular systems are compromised.

In such cases, alternative gases like helium, neon and argon can be used. They do not cause any metabolic effects, but if they get direct access to the venous system, they can cause gas emboli because they are not as soluble in blood as CO2 and N2O.

Gas embolism is treated by positioning the patient in a left lateral decubitus position, head down, to trap the gas in the right ventricle's apex. The gas can then be aspirated out of the right ventricle using a rapidly placed central venous catheter.

Limiting intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) below 12-15 mmHg during insufflation is also effective in preventing pathophysiological changes of pneumoperitoneum.
questions.learning: Peritoneal stretching Vagal stimulation due to peritoneal stretching is responsible for bradycardia following CO2 insufflation during laparoscopic surgery.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The true statement among the following is _____
options: The dose of telmisartan should be reduced in renal failure but not in hepatic failure.
The dose of irbesartan should be reduced in case of mild-moderate hepatic failure and renal failure.
The dose of candesartan should be reduced in mild-moderate liver failure but not in renal failure.
Losartan acts as thromboxane A2 antagonist and inhibits platelet aggregation.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Losartan acts as thromboxane A2 antagonist and inhibits platelet aggregation.

The true statement is losartan acts as a thromboxane A2 antagonist and inhibits platelet aggregation.

Losartan is a competitive angiotensin receptor antagonist. It binds to the AT1 receptor with high affinity. It is also a competitive antagonist of the thromboxane A2 receptor and attenuates platelet aggregation.

Losartan is the angiotensin receptor blocker used in the treatment of hypertension. Hyperkalemia is an important side effect of ARBs. It appears to be a safe and efficacious agent to lower serum uric acid levels in patients with hyperuricemia.

Other options:

Option A: The clearance of telmisartan is mainly by biliary secretion. The clearance is affected by hepatic insufficiency. The dose of telmisartan should be reduced in hepatic failure but not in renal failure.

Option B: Irbesartan is metabolized to glucuronide conjugate, and is cleared mainly by biliary excretion. The plasma clearance is unaffected by either renal or mild-to-moderate hepatic insufficiency. Hence, the dose need not be reduced in either of the cases.

Option C: The plasma clearance of candesartan is by biliary excretion and renal elimination. The clearance is affected by renal insufficiency. Hence, the dose should be reduced in case of renal failure and not in mild-moderate liver failure.
questions.learning: Losartan acts as thromboxane A2 antagonist and inhibits platelet aggregation. The true statement is losartan acts as a thromboxane A2 antagonist and inhibits platelet aggregation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text:
Which of the following is required for the cannulation of a newborn?

1. 22G needle
2. 24G needle
3. 5-mL syringe
4. Adhesive tape
5. Normal saline
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2,3,4,5

For cannulation in newborns, we would require a 24G needle, 5 mL syringe, adhesive tape, and normal saline.

Also, for a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC), we use a 24G needle for >1 kg neonate, and for <1 kg neonate, we use a 28G needle. We need to avoid using 1 mL syringes for flushing as it may lead to catheter rupture; preferably, use 5 or 10 mL syringes. Flushing of the cannulation is done using 0.9% sodium chloride or so-called normal saline (NS).

Dressing change: We change PICC line dressing only when visibly soiled, damp, or loosened. For making it easier and sterile, two persons should perform a dressing change.
questions.learning: 2,3,4,5 For cannulation in newborns, we would require a 24G needle, 5 mL syringe, adhesive tape, and normal saline. Also, for a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC), we use a 24G needle for >1 kg neonate, and for <1 kg neonate, we use a 28G needle.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: If a wide range of values are present in a community, what is the best measure of central tendency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Median

The best measure of central tendency if there are a wide range of values is median.

If we take an example of a dataset of (1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 11, 41), we can see that 41 seems to be well away from the mean of 7.45 of the dataset.  If we eliminate this outlier, we can get a new dataset of (1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 11) with a median of 4.5 and a mean of 4.1. We see that the median only changed by 10% (went down to 4.5 from 5), while the mean decreased by 45%. Therefore, the median is less affected by outliers or extreme values.

The median is not sensitive to extreme values or outliers and thus it is the preferred measure of central tendency in a distribution with a wide range of values.

* The median is the central element in a distribution when all the elements are arranged in order.

* In a distribution that has an odd number of elements, the median is the middle value.

* In a distribution that has an even number of elements, the median is the average of the middle values, i.e., the arithmetic mean of the two middle values.

* The drawback of the median is that it doesn’t respond to the actual values of the elements but only to the number of values above or below it.

* The median is the same as the 50th centile.

* It is sometimes symbolized by Mdn.

* The median can be arrived at in ordinal, interval and ratio data scales.
questions.learning: Median — The best measure of central tendency if there are a wide range of values is median. If we take an example of a dataset of (1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 11, 41), we can see that 41 seems to be well away from the mean of 7.45 of the dataset.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 7-year-old child from a low socioeconomic background presents with cerebrospinal fluid findings of lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose (30 mg%), and markedly elevated protein levels (300 mg%). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings of high protein, low glucose, and a predominant lymphocytic pleocytosis are classically seen in Tubercular Meningitis (TBM). This CSF profile reflects the chronic inflammatory response caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the meninges. Differential diagnosis reasoning: 1. Viral meningitis usually shows normal or mildly reduced glucose levels with only a modest rise in protein. 2. Acute bacterial meningitis characteristically presents with neutrophilic predominance and markedly reduced glucose levels. 3. Partially treated bacterial meningitis may show lymphocytic predominance, but the subacute to chronic course over two months strongly supports TBM rather than bacterial infection. Additionally, the patient’s low socioeconomic background increases the epidemiological likelihood of tuberculosis, especially in endemic regions
questions.learning: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings of high protein, low glucose, and a predominant lymphocytic pleocytosis are classically seen in Tubercular Meningitis (TBM).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which among the following serves as cofactor for Glycogen phosphorylase:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pyridoxal Phosphate

• Pyridoxal phosphate is a cofactor of glycogen phosphorylase, where the phosphate group is catalytically important.
• PLP also acts as the coenzyme for many enzymes involved in amino acid metabolism, especially transamination and decarboxylation.
• Glycogen phosphorylase is a debranching enzyme which cleaves alpha-1,4 bonds of the glycogen chain to produce glucose-1-phosphate in glycogenolysis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
All of the following cause a right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, except ___.

HbF- Fetal hemoglobin

2,3 BPG- 2,3 Bisphosphoglyceric acid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased HbF

Increased HbF (fetal hemoglobin) causes a left shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.

Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve:

This is a plot of the partial pressure of O2 and the percentage saturation of Hb with O2. It is normally sigmoid in shape. If the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is shifted to the right, it means that the affinity of Hb for O2 has become less, which favors O2 delivery. This means a higher P50, which implies that a higher PO2 is required to maintain 50% saturation (R - Right shift Releases oxygen). If the curve is shifted to the left, it means that affinity has increased for O2 ( which favors O2 binding ) i.e. lower P50 value ( L-Left shift Leashes oxygen ).

Causes of the right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve:

• Hypoxia and Hypercarbia - metabolically active tissues utilize O2 and tissues produce CO2
• ↓ pH - Secondary to increased CO2 production
• ↑ in temperature
• ↑ in 2,3-DPG - increased anaerobic glycolysis
• Growth hormone, thyroid hormone, androgen - by increasing 2,3 DPG
• Sickle cell anemia - reduced affinity for O2
• Exercise

Causes of the left shift of oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve:

• ↑ pH (alkalosis)
• ↓ PCO2
• ↓ 2,3-DPG
• ↓ Temperature
• HbF
• Carboxyhemoglobin

Bohr's effect- The decrease in the O2 affinity of hemoglobin when the pH of the blood falls
questions.learning: Increased HbF Increased HbF (fetal hemoglobin) causes a left shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve: This is a plot of the partial pressure of O2 and the percentage saturation of Hb with O2.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A tympanometry graph is displayed below. The arrow points to a sharp peak at pressure = 0 daPa. What type of tympanogram does the arrow represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type As

The given tympanograph is a type As tympanogram.

Tympanometry: It is used in evaluating the status of the middle ear and the functioning of the eustachian tube. Results of tympanometry are plotted in the form of a tympanogram with:

* Compliance on the Y axis (ease of mobility of TM)

* Middle ear pressure on the X axis (regulated by eustachian tube)

Principle: When a sound wave strikes the tympanic membrane, some of the sound energy is absorbed while the rest is reflected. A stiffer tympanic membrane would reflect more sound energy than a compliant one.

Tympanometry has also been used to evaluate the function of the eustachian tube in cases of intact or perforated tympanic membranes. A pressure of -200 or +200 mm H₂O is created in the middle ear, and the person is asked to swallow 5 times in 20 seconds. The ability to equilibrate the pressure indicates normal tubal function. It is also used in evaluating the patency of the grommet inserted in the tympanic membrane for treating serous otitis media.

By charting the compliance of the tympano-ossicular system against various pressure changes, different types of graphs called tympanograms are obtained. They are as follows:

Pearl PF1978: Pure tone audiometry (PTA)

A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its frequency can be increased or decreased by 5Hz.

The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram.

Normal thresholds:

* For AC: 15 dB

* For BC: 25 dB

Symbols used in pure tone audiometry:

Disease
Findings in PTA audiogram

Conductive hearing loss
AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present

Sensorineural hearing loss
Both AC and BC are abnormal and no air-Bone gap

Mixed hearing loss
Both AC and BC abnormal and air-bone gap present

Presbycusis, ototoxicity, noise-induced hearing loss (higher frequencies affected first)
Downsloping or descending audiogram

Early stages of Meniere's disease (lower frequencies affected first)
Upsloping or ascending audiogram

Congenital hearing loss and cochlear otosclerosis (mid-frequency hearing loss)
U-shaped or trough-shaped or cookie bite shaped audiogram

Early cases of noise-induced hearing loss

Acoustic dip - characteristic dip in both AC and BC at 4000 Hz

Otosclerosis
Carhart's notch- dip at 2000 Hz in BC curve

Pearl PF1696: Types of curves in tympanogram
questions.learning: Type As — The given tympanograph is a type As tympanogram. Tympanometry: It is used in evaluating the status of the middle ear and the functioning of the eustachian tube.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with gastrointestinal problems including abdominal pain and distension, bloody and mucus-filled diarrhea, and tenesmus, with rectal prolapse. A stool examination reveals the presence of typical barrel-shaped eggs. What is the possible causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trichuris trichiura

The given clinical picture and the barrel-shaped eggs are suggestive of infection with Trichuris trichiura (whipworm).

The characteristic features of whipworm eggs are:

• Eggs are barrel-shaped in the middle with a projecting mucus plug at each pole containing an unsegmented ovum. The plugs are colorless.
• They float in the saturated salt solution.
• It has a triple shell, the outermost layer of which is stained brown.

The below image shows the egg of Trichuris trichiura.

In moderate infections of 20 adult worms or less, the worms are confined to the caecum and ascending colon. The symptoms include epigastric and lower abdominal pain, diarrhea (rarely bloody), vomiting, flatulence and distention, weight loss, and increased blood and iron loss.

In heavy infections of 200 adults worms or more (trichuris dysentery syndrome), the worms are in the distal colon and rectum. The symptoms include bloody diarrhea with profuse mucus, abdominal pain, tenesmus, weight loss leading to cachexia, severe anemia, and rectal prolapse. On examination, clubbing may be present. Blood investigations may show moderate eosinophilia.

Chronic infection leads to growth retardation and nutritional deficiencies. Around 0.005 ml of blood is lost per day per worm. In heavy infections, as much as 4 to 5 ml can be lost per day per worm.

Treatment is mebendazole or albendazole.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is a primary lymphoid organ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thymus

Thymus and bone marrow are the primary lymphoid organs (also known as central lymphoid organs). It is the place where immature lymphocytes develop, differentiate, proliferate, and mature into immune competent cells.

A secondary lymphoid organ (also known as a peripheral lymphoid organ) is where the antigen is localized so that it can be effectively exposed to mature lymphocytes. These include the spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, appendix, and Peyer’s patches.

Both B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes are produced in the bone marrow. B lymphocytes also mature in bone marrow, while T lymphocytes mature in Thymus.

Given below is the histopathological image of the thymus.

The thymus is a lymphoid tissue that is arranged in the form of lobules. The lobules are separated from each other by connective tissue.

Each lobule is made up of an outer darker staining cortex and an inner pale-staining medulla. The medulla contains pink rounded masses called Hassell's corpuscles.
questions.learning: Thymus Thymus and bone marrow are the primary lymphoid organs (also known as central lymphoid organs). It is the place where immature lymphocytes develop, differentiate, proliferate, and mature into immune competent cells.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following does not form a boundary of the 'Triangle of Doom'? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inguinal ligament

The "Triangle of Doom" is an important anatomical danger zone encountered during laparoscopic hernia repair. This triangle contains critical structures, including the external iliac vessels that must be avoided during mesh fixation and dissection. This triangle is bounded by the vas deferens medially, the gonadal vessels laterally, and the peritoneal reflection forming the base. The inguinal ligament is not a boundary of this triangle in the laparoscopic perspective.
