questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which protein, having structural homology with plasminogen, is responsible for myocardial infarction and stroke?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. LP(a)

LP(a) or Lipoprotein(a) consists of one mole of LDL attached to one mole of apo(a). The apo(a) component shows structural homologies to plasminogen, which is clinically significant. This similarity to plasminogen, a key protein in the fibrinolytic system, allows LP(a) to inhibit fibrinolysis (the normal breakdown of blood clots). Consequently, LP(a) promotes both atherosclerosis and thrombosis, significantly increasing the risk of premature coronary heart disease, myocardial infarction, and stroke.
questions.learning: LP(a) LP(a) or Lipoprotein(a) consists of one mole of LDL attached to one mole of apo(a). The apo(a) component shows structural homologies to plasminogen, which is clinically significant.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the ideal number of antenatal visits?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 12-14

The ideal number of antenatal visits is 12-14.

The antenatal visits should ideally be: monthly once up to 28 weeks, once in two weeks between 28-36 weeks, and once weekly visits from 36 weeks onwards.

This translates to a total of 12-15 visits.

The WHO increased the minimum number of antenatal visits from 4 to 8 visits to reduce perinatal mortality.

In the Indian scenario, the earlier minimum of 4 visits were implemented as follows:

• 1st visit: within 12 weeks (preferably as soon as pregnancy is suspected)
• 2nd visit: between 14-26 weeks
• 3rd visit: between 28-34 weeks
• 4th visit: between 36 weeks and term

A booked case is one that has at least 3 antenatal visits with two visits in the third trimester.
questions.learning: 12-14 The ideal number of antenatal visits is 12-14. The antenatal visits should ideally be: monthly once up to 28 weeks, once in two weeks between 28-36 weeks, and once weekly visits from 36 weeks onwards.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old known case of Parkinson's disease presents with severe oropharyngeal dysphagia and recurrent episodes of aspiration pneumonitis. CXR reveals bilateral bronchiectasis. What is the most appropriate long-term management plan for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PEG tube

This patient has:

• Parkinson's disease → impaired swallowing
• Oropharyngeal dysphagia → aspiration risk
• Recurrent aspiration pneumonitis
• Result: Bronchiectasis

The root cause is aspiration, not just secretion retention.

Severe oropharyngeal dysphagia in Parkinson’s disease causes recurrent aspiration, leading to aspiration pneumonitis and secondary bronchiectasis.

The most effective long-term strategy is prevention of further aspiration, achieved by PEG tube feeding.

| Benefit | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Prevents aspiration | Bypasses oropharynx

| Ensures nutrition | Long-term feeding

| Reduces lung injury | Stops recurrent pneumonitis

Airway clearance methods or antibiotics do not address the primary problem of unsafe swallowing.

| Approach | Example | Role

| -------- | ------- | ----

| Cause control |  PEG in aspiration | MOST IMPORTANT

| Airway clearance | Physiotherapy | Supportive

| Mucolytics | NAC | Symptomatic

| Antibiotics | Macrolides | Exacerbations
questions.learning: PEG tube — This patient has: • Parkinson's disease → impaired swallowing • Oropharyngeal dysphagia → aspiration risk • Recurrent aspiration pneumonitis • Result: Bronchiectasis The root cause is aspiration, not just secretion retention.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What were the target goals for Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) and Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) to be achieved by 2023?
questions.explanation: India’s National Health Policy (NHP) 2017, aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), set specific targets to be achieved by 2023: Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR): < 70 per 100,000 live births Infant Mortality Rate (IMR): ≈ 28–30 per 1,000 live births Thus, the combined target is correctly represented as 70/30. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Option B (30/70): Reverses the indicators (MMR and IMR). 2. Option C (100/30): Reflects older benchmarks; many states had already reduced MMR below 100 before 2023. 3. Option D (30/100): Inconsistent with national priorities and epidemiological realities. Achieving the 70/30 target depends on improving institutional deliveries, quality antenatal and postnatal care, strengthening Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs), and effective implementation of programs like Janani Suraksha Yojana. These targets are key indicators of progress in maternal and child health

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient who is a known case of atherosclerosis underwent a circumflex artery bypass. The stent is now placed successfully. He is already taking lisinopril, verapamil, metoprolol. Which drug should be added?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. P2Y12 receptor blocker

P2Y12 receptor blocker should be added to prevent stent thrombosis.

Clopidogrel, a P2Y12 receptor blocker, along with aspirin is called dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT).

DAPT should be continued for at least 1 year following stent placement to prevent stent thrombosis. After the recommended duration of treatment with dual antiplatelet therapy, aspirin should be continued indefinitely.
questions.learning: P2Y12 receptor blocker P2Y12 receptor blocker should be added to prevent stent thrombosis. Clopidogrel, a P2Y12 receptor blocker, along with aspirin is called dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing dacryocystitis is being evaluated for surgical management. Which of the following procedures is most appropriate for her condition?
questions.explanation: Dacryocystitis is an infection of the lacrimal sac, usually due to nasolacrimal duct obstruction. For long-standing (chronic) dacryocystitis in an adult, dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the standard and most suitable surgical treatment. DCR creates a new permanent pathway between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity, bypassing the obstructed duct and restoring tear drainage. Dacryocystectomy (DCT) (Option B) involves the complete removal of the lacrimal sac; it is reserved for elderly patients, cases of malignancy, or where DCR is contraindicated, as it leaves the patient with permanent tearing (epiphora). Conjunctiva-cysto rhinostomy (Option C) is a more complex bypass used when the canaliculi are blocked. Balloon catheter dilation (Option D) is occasionally used for partial obstructions but is not the definitive treatment for chronic dacryocystitis. Therefore, DCR is the gold standard procedure for restoring function and preventing recurrent infection
questions.learning: Dacryocystitis is an infection of the lacrimal sac, usually due to nasolacrimal duct obstruction. For long-standing (chronic) dacryocystitis in an adult, dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the standard and most suitable surgical treatment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient involved in a road traffic accident with profuse bleeding and hypotension, which cannula gauge is most appropriate for rapid administration of large volumes of intravenous fluids?
questions.explanation: In trauma management (ATLS protocols), the goal for patients in hypovolemic shock is rapid volume resuscitation using wide-bore intravenous cannulae. According to Poiseuille's law, the flow rate is inversely proportional to the length and directly proportional to the fourth power of the radius. A 14 G (Gauge) cannula (Option A), which is typically orange-coded, is the widest standard bore used in emergency settings, allowing for the fastest possible infusion of fluids and blood products. A 16 G (Option C, grey) is also used for trauma but provides less flow than a 14 G. An 18 G (Option D, green) is standard for surgical patients but is insufficient for "large volume" rapid replacement in acute shock. 13 G (Option B) is not a standard medical cannula size. Clinicians should insert two 14 G cannulae in the antecubital veins for any patient presenting with trauma-induced hypotension. Therefore, 14 G is the appropriate choice for massive resuscitation

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In which color-coded disposal bag should cytotoxic drugs be discarded?
questions.explanation: According to the latest Biomedical Waste Management guidelines, cytotoxic drugs and contaminated items (such as vials, ampoules, and expired medicines) must be disposed of in a yellow bag or container. These items are specifically labeled as "cytotoxic" and are destined for high-temperature incineration at a common waste treatment facility. Red bags (Option B) are used for recyclable contaminated waste like plastics. Blue bags or cardboard boxes (Option C) are used for broken glassware and metallic implants. Black bags (Option D) were historically used for general municipal waste but are no longer the standard for biomedical segregation in many protocols. Cytotoxic drugs are highly hazardous and require specialized destruction to prevent environmental contamination and health risks to waste handlers. Therefore, the yellow bag is the designated disposal route for chemotherapy-related medications in an oncology unit
questions.learning: According to the latest Biomedical Waste Management guidelines, cytotoxic drugs and contaminated items (such as vials, ampoules, and expired medicines) must be disposed of in a yellow bag or container.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In ectopic pregnancy, where is the most frequent site of implantation?
questions.explanation: Ectopic pregnancy most commonly occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube, which is labeled as A in the image. The ampulla is the widest and longest part of the tube and is the usual site of fertilization. Because fertilization occurs here, any delay in the movement of the fertilized ovum toward the uterus can lead to implantation at this site. Approximately 70% of ectopic pregnancies occur in the ampullary region. Its relatively thin wall and rich blood supply make it prone to distension and rupture if implantation occurs. Why Other Options Are Wrong (B) Ovary: Ovarian pregnancy is rare (C) Cervix: Very rare site of ectopic implantation (D) Uterus: This is the normal site for implantation, not ectopic
questions.learning: Ectopic pregnancy most commonly occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube, which is labeled as A in the image. The ampulla is the widest and longest part of the tube and is the usual site of fertilization.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding thalidomide is false?
options: It is used in type 2 lepra reaction (ENL)
It is used in relapsing multiple myeloma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It acts as an antimetabolite

THALIDOMIDE-

Once infamous for birth defects, now reborn as a powerful immunomodulator and anti-cancer agent.

Multi-dimensional drug:

1. Immunomodulation

• ↓ TNF-α
• Alters cytokine balance

2. Anti-angiogenic

• ↓ VEGF → ↓ blood vessel formation

3. Anti-neoplastic

• Inhibits tumor growth (esp. multiple myeloma)

Thalidomide is an immunomodulatory and anti-angiogenic drug, not an antimetabolite. It is a potent teratogen causing limb defects and is strictly contraindicated in pregnancy. It is used in type 2 lepra reaction (ENL) and in relapsed multiple myeloma. Hence calling it an antimetabolite is incorrect.

| Feature | Details

| ------- | -------

| Class | Immunomodulator

| Mechanism | ↓ TNF-α, ↓ VEGF

| Uses | ENL, Multiple myeloma

| Major risk | Severe teratogenicity

| Other AE | Neuropathy, sedation

| Drug | Class | Mechanism

| ---- | ----- | ---------

| Thalidomide | Immunomodulator | TNF-α ↓, VEGF ↓

| Methotrexate | Antimetabolite | DHFR inhibition

| 5-FU | Antimetabolite | Thymidylate synthase inhibition

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented with pain and swelling of his left arm after a fall from height. An upper arm X-ray was done. Which nerve is most likely to be injured in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radial nerve

In the above clinical scenario, the history and radiograph suggest a closed fracture of the shaft of the humerus. The radial nerve is commonly damaged in this condition. This is because the radial nerve follows a superficial path around the humerus and can be stretched or compressed when there is significant trauma to the upper arm.

It manifests with wrist drop (inability to dorsiflex the wrist) and finger drop (inability to dorsiflex the digits). Numbness occurs on the dorsoradial aspect of the hand and the dorsal aspect of the radial 3 1/2 digits.

Management of humerus shaft fractures:

* Conservative management using a hanging cast or U-slab for 2-3 weeks followed by functional bracing

* Surgical fixation by compression plating, interlocking intramedullary nail, semi-flexible pins, or an external fixator is indicated in:

* Open fractures

* Pathological fractures

* Unstable humeral and forearm fractures (floating elbow)

* Radial nerve palsy

The below X-ray shows shaft of humerus fracture.

Other options:

* The axillary nerve is most commonly injured in shoulder dislocations or fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus.

* The ulnar nerve is more commonly injured in conditions like elbow dislocations, fractures of the medial epicondyle of the humerus, or entrapment at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome).

* The median nerve is more frequently associated with injuries in the forearm or wrist, such as carpal tunnel syndrome, or with certain systemic conditions like pronator teres syndrome.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Name the test depicted in the image provided.
questions.explanation: The image displays the results of the Teichmann test (also known as the Hemin Crystal Test), a confirmatory test for the presence of blood. The test is performed by heating a blood stain with glacial acetic acid and a halide (salt); a positive result is the formation of characteristic dark brown, rhombic, needle-like crystals of hemin chloride. The Barberio test (Option A) is used to identify semen (spermine). The Florence test (Option B) is also for semen (choline). The Takayama test (Option C) is another confirmatory test for blood that forms pink, feathery hemochromogen crystals, which look distinct from the brown needles shown. Because the image specifically captures the dark, rhomboid hemin crystals, it definitively identifies the Teichmann test. This forensic tool is used to prove that a suspected stain is indeed biological blood

questions.text: A 60-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy presents with complaints of palpitations. His ECG reveals a narrow complex tachycardia, and he is hemodynamically stable. The physician initiates amiodarone therapy for rhythm control. Amiodarone exerts its primary antiarrhythmic effect by acting on which phase of the cardiac action potential?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phase 3 – Repolarization

| Class | Target | Example

| ----- | ------ | -------

| Class I | Na⁺ channels | Lidocaine

| Class II | β-blockers | Propranolol

| Class III | K⁺ channels | Amiodarone

| Class IV | Ca²⁺ channels | Verapamil

Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic that primarily blocks potassium channels.

This action prolongs phase 3 repolarization, increasing action potential duration and refractory period.

Blocking potassium channels results in:

• Increased refractory period
• Reduced re-entry circuits
• Stabilization of cardiac rhythm

This makes amiodarone effective for:

• Atrial fibrillation
• Ventricular tachycardia
• Ventricular fibrillation

The effect helps terminate and prevent re-entry tachyarrhythmias.

Sodium (phase 0), calcium (phase 2), and phase 4 effects are secondary, not primary.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presented with serial blood pressure recordings of above 140/90 mmHg. Which one of the following signs is not a clue for an underlying cause of hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitiligo

Vitiligo is not a typical clinical clue for secondary hypertension.

• A. Radio-femoral delay — Clue for secondary hypertension

• Suggests coarctation of the aorta, a secondary cause of hypertension.
• Femoral pulses are delayed and weaker compared with radial pulses.

• B. Enlarged kidneys — Clue

• May suggest polycystic kidney disease, an important renal cause of secondary hypertension.

• C. Bull neck and buffalo hump — Clue

• Characteristic of Cushing syndrome, which can cause secondary hypertension through excess cortisol.

• D. Vitiligo — Not a typical clue

• Vitiligo is associated with autoimmune disorders but is not a characteristic clinical clue to a specific secondary cause of hypertension.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following murmur increases on standing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HOCM

The murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HOCM) increases with standing, as there is a reduction in preload. In conditions of reduced preload, there is lesser end diastolic volume in the left ventricle, leading to a narrower outflow tract, and a louder murmur is heard.

The murmur heard in HOCM is a mid-systolic murmur, which is loudest along the left sternal border. It increases in conditions of decreased preload and afterload (standing, valsalva, vagal maneuvers) or conditions of increased contractility (inotropic stimulation) and decreases when preload and afterload are increased (squatting, vasopressors).

Most murmurs decrease in intensity with reduced preload and afterload except HOCM and mitral valve prolapse (MVP).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which among the following radioactive isotopes is not employed in brachytherapy?
questions.explanation: Brachytherapy is a form of radiation therapy where a radioactive source is placed directly inside or next to the tumor. Common isotopes used for this purpose include Iridium-192 (Option D), which is frequently used for high-dose-rate brachytherapy, and Iodine-125 (Option A) or Palladium-103, which are used as permanent "seeds" for prostate cancer. Cobalt-60 (Option C) was historically used in both external beam therapy and brachytherapy applications. Iodine-131 (Option B), however, is NOT typically used for brachytherapy. Instead, it is used for "systemic" radionuclide therapy, specifically for the treatment of hyperthyroidism and differentiated thyroid cancer, where it is ingested or injected and concentrates naturally in thyroid tissue. Brachytherapy relies on sealed sources to deliver localized radiation, whereas I-131 is an unsealed liquid source used for systemic metabolic uptake. Thus, Iodine-131 is the correct "not employed" choice among the options provided

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a history of infertility is on treatment with HMG. She presented with the following finding in the USG. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

The given clinical scenario and the USG findings are suggestive of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is characterized by multiple ovarian follicular cysts accompanied by increased capillary permeability. It most often is a complication of ovulation induction therapy for infertility, although it may rarely develop in an otherwise normal pregnancy. It has also been reported with a partial molar pregnancy. Its etiopathogenesis is thought to involve the stimulation of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) expression in granulosa-lutein cells by hCG.

Human menopausal gonadotropin (HMG) is a medication that is composed of FSH and LH. It is used to stimulate the release of ova in women who do not ovulate spontaneously. It can lead to ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a middle-aged man who presents to the psychiatry OPD with a 7-month history of auditory hallucinations, believing that aliens are commanding him to harm his family?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with core psychotic symptoms: auditory hallucinations ("hearing voices from aliens") and command-type instructions with potential delusional content. According to ICD-10 and DSM-5 criteria, a diagnosis of Schizophrenia (Option C) requires the presence of these symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized speech) for a significant duration, typically at least one to six months. This patient’s symptoms have persisted for seven months, fulfilling the chronic duration criteria. Mania (Option A) is characterized by elevated mood, racing thoughts, and decreased need for sleep, which are not described here. Delusional disorder (Option B) involves non-bizarre delusions without prominent hallucinations like hearing alien voices. Brief psychotic disorder (Option D) is limited to symptoms lasting less than one month. Given the specific nature of the bizarre hallucinations and the seven-month duration, Schizophrenia is the most accurate psychiatric diagnosis. Management involves antipsychotic medication and psychosocial support
questions.learning: The patient is presenting with core psychotic symptoms: auditory hallucinations ("hearing voices from aliens") and command-type instructions with potential delusional content.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following best describes memantine’s mechanism of action in the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NMDA receptor antagonist

Memantine improves symptoms in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s disease by acting as a non-competitive NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor antagonist. It reduces excessive glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity, which contributes to neuronal injury and cognitive decline, while preserving normal synaptic transmission.

Why not the other options?

• A. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition: Mechanism of donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, which increase acetylcholine levels in the brain and are primarily used for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer’s disease.
• C. Blockade of A-beta amyloid: Mechanism of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies such as lecanemab and donanemab, which target amyloid plaques.
• D. Dopamine D₂ receptor antagonism: Mechanism of antipsychotic drugs (e.g., haloperidol, risperidone); not used to treat the cognitive symptoms of Alzheimer’s disease.
questions.learning: NMDA receptor antagonist Memantine improves symptoms in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s disease by acting as a non-competitive NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor antagonist.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Revised A primipara is being evaluated for hearing impairment which had worsened during her pregnancy. Rinne’s test is negative in both ears and Weber’s test is lateralized to the right side. On otoscopy, tympanic membranes appear normal. Audiometry shows a dip in BC at 2000 Hz. What is the treatment of choice for the above condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stapedotomy

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of otosclerosis and the treatment of choice for otosclerosis is stapedotomy.

Stapedotomy is the excision of the superstructure of stapes and drilling a hole in the footplate & placing a piston in the hole. This is the treatment of choice.

Other options:

Stapedectomy is the excision of the entire stapes (superstructure + footplate) and placing a piston in its place. It is outdated.

Sodium fluoride (NaF) is used in an active case of otosclerosis to hasten maturation.

Note:

* Both stapedectomy and stapedotomy have been described for the treatment of otosclerosis. Even in the stapedectomy procedure, stapedotomy (drilling) has been practiced. Hence stapedotomy is preferred over stapedectomy and is considered the treatment of choice.

* In the above case since Rinne’s test is negative on both ears, it indicates bilateral conductive deafness. Weber’s test will lateralize to the ear with greater conductive loss.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
A 4-week-old infant presented to the ER with projectile vomiting. USG abdomen findings of the infant are given below. Probable diagnosis is ______________

USG-Ultrasonography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

The probable diagnosis is Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric stenosis since the cervix sign and nipple sign are signs of Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric stenosis on USG.

• Double-layered hypertrophic mucosa protrudes into the stomach, creating the so-called Nipple sign.
• The sonographic appearance of the hypertrophied pylorus resembles that of the uterine cervix and is sometimes referred to as the cervix sign.

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis most presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. It is common between 2 and 8 weeks of age. Hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. Male infants are at a higher risk.

Clinically, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. When the infant is given a test feed, visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right across the abdomen.

Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality- hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-).

Ultrasound examination is the investigation of choice for this condition. The diagnostic criteria for pyloric stenosis are a muscle thickness of ≥4 mm and a pyloric length of ≥16 mm. The cervix sign and nipple sign are signs seen on USG.

As for the management, the child should be rehydrated and the metabolic abnormality has to be corrected before proceeding to surgery. The Ramstedt pyloromyotomy remains the standard surgical procedure for its treatment.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with bleeding. Evaluation reveals a 3 cm fibroid in the uterine wall and an endometrial thickness of 8 mm. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrial biopsy

Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) is considered endometrial carcinoma until proven otherwise. The first-line investigation is transvaginal ultrasonography (TVS) to measure endometrial thickness (ET).

In women with PMB:

• ET ≤4 mm → Very low risk of endometrial carcinoma; biopsy is usually not required unless bleeding persists.
• ET >4 mm → Endometrial biopsy is mandatory to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma, regardless of the presence of other uterine pathologies such as fibroids.

In this patient, although a 3 cm intramural fibroid is present, it does not explain the increased endometrial thickness (8 mm). Therefore, the priority is to obtain an endometrial tissue diagnosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. CECT: Has no role in the initial evaluation of PMB; used only if malignancy is diagnosed and extrauterine disease is suspected.
• C. Pap smear: Screens for cervical neoplasia, not endometrial pathology.
• D. MRI: Used for local staging of confirmed endometrial carcinoma, not for establishing the diagnosis.
questions.learning: Endometrial biopsy Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) is considered endometrial carcinoma until proven otherwise. The first-line investigation is transvaginal ultrasonography (TVS) to measure endometrial thickness (ET).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman with chronic pancreatitis undergoes a Puestow procedure. What is the preferred route for providing postoperative nutritional support in this patient?
questions.explanation: After a Puestow procedure (longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy) in chronic pancreatitis, the preferred postoperative nutritional support is TPN. This is because the primary goal is to provide adequate nutrition while ensuring complete pancreatic rest. Any enteral feeding (oral, gastric, or jejunal) can stimulate pancreatic exocrine secretion through hormonal and neural mechanisms, potentially stressing the anastomosis and worsening inflammation. TPN bypasses the gastrointestinal tract entirely, thereby minimizing pancreatic stimulation, reducing pain, and allowing optimal healing in the early postoperative period. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Oral feeding: Not advised early postoperatively, as it directly stimulates pancreatic secretion and may aggravate symptoms or disrupt healing. (C) Feeding gastrostomy: Feeding into the stomach triggers hormonal responses (like gastrin and CCK release), leading to pancreatic stimulation, which is undesirable. (D) Feeding jejunostomy: Although it reduces stimulation compared to gastric feeding, it still causes some pancreatic secretion. Hence, it is not preferred immediately after surgery when complete pancreatic rest is required
questions.learning: After a Puestow procedure (longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy) in chronic pancreatitis, the preferred postoperative nutritional support is TPN. This is because the primary goal is to provide adequate nutrition while ensuring complete pancreatic rest.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about triage, according to the internationally accepted four-color-coded system?
options: Yellow - Significant injuries, hemodynamically stable patients, required monitoring
Green - Patients in life threatening conditions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Yellow - Significant injuries, hemodynamically stable patients, required monitoring

The yellow color tag is given for the patients who have significant injuries but are hemodynamically stable, and need monitoring. They are the medium priority patients.

Triage is used to classify the priority of treatment.

It is carried out at the site of the disaster to determine the priority for immediate medical attention, transportation, and admission to the hospital.

The internationally accepted four-color coded system is commonly used. It includes:

Color code
Type of patients
Examples

Red (High priority) (option A).

Need for immediate resuscitation or surgery in the next 6 hours or transfer.

May survive if timely medical intervention can be given

• Tension pneumothorax
• Airway obstruction
• Hemothorax
• Cardiac tamponade
• Acute circulatory arrest
• Major intra-abdominal bleed etc.

Yellow (Medium priority)(option C).

Possible resuscitation or surgery in the next 24 hours.

Likely to survive if prompt treatment is given.

• Compound fractures
• Degloving injuries
• Pelvic fracture
• Spinal injuries
• Moderate head injury

Green (Low priority)(option D).

Ambulatory patients or minor illnesses.

Likely to survive if treatment is slightly delayed.

• Simple fractures
• Minor lacerations etc.

Black (Least priority)(option B).

• Severe brain injury
• Major damage / disruption to chest wall and abdominal structures
questions.learning: Yellow - Significant injuries, hemodynamically stable patients, required monitoring The yellow color tag is given for the patients who have significant injuries but are hemodynamically stable, and need monitoring.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Foreign body entry into the laryngeal inlet is prevented by the cough reflex. This reflex is sluggish in alcohol ingestion and some other conditions. Which nerve is likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Internal laryngeal nerve

The internal laryngeal nerve is the nerve implicated in the inhibition of the cough reflex in an alcoholic. Alcohol can cause chemical irritation of the nerve and it is also a potent inhibitor of the central nervous system.

The cough reflex is a protective mechanism of the larynx to expel irritants and keep the airway clear. Chemical or mechanical irritation of the respiratory mucosa stimulates the afferent internal laryngeal nerve, which is the branch of the superior laryngeal nerve of the vagus nerve.

Internal laryngeal nerve supplies the mucosa of the larynx above the level of the vocal cords (supraglottis). Hence, any injury to the internal laryngeal nerve results in aspiration and depressed cough reflex with no change in voice.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option D) gives sensory supply to the mucosa of the larynx at the level of vocal cords (glottis) and below the level of vocal cords (subglottis) and also motor supply to all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid.

Unilateral injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) may cause minimal or no change in voice, but it does not lead to aspiration or airway obstruction.

Bilateral injury to RLN can result in dyspnea and stridor due to the median or paramedian position of the vocal cords, which narrows and obstructs the airway. However, the voice remains unaffected.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (Option B) provides sensory supply to the oropharynx, posterior third of the tongue, and middle ear cavity. Damage to the glossopharyngeal nerve leads to the absence of the gag reflex.

The external laryngeal nerve (Option C) innervates the cricothyroid muscle, which is responsible for adjusting the pitch of sound during speech. Paralysis of the external laryngeal nerve results in the inability to increase the pitch of sound.
questions.learning: Internal laryngeal nerve — The internal laryngeal nerve is the nerve implicated in the inhibition of the cough reflex in an alcoholic. Alcohol can cause chemical irritation of the nerve and it is also a potent inhibitor of the central nervous system.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the underlying factor responsible for the occurrence of LH surge?
questions.explanation: The LH (Luteinizing Hormone) surge is the critical event that triggers ovulation. It is caused by a unique "positive feedback" mechanism. During the late follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, the dominant follicle produces increasingly high levels of estradiol. When estradiol levels remain above a certain threshold (typically pg/mL) for approximately 48 hours, the normal negative feedback on the pituitary switches to positive feedback. This triggers a massive, rapid release of LH from the anterior pituitary gland. FSH (Option A) also rises slightly during this time, but it is not the primary driver of the surge. Progesterone (Option C) levels are low during the follicular phase and only rise after ovulation occurs. LH (Option D) is the result of the surge, not its underlying cause. Therefore, the peak in estradiol is the definitive physiological trigger for the LH surge
questions.learning: The LH (Luteinizing Hormone) surge is the critical event that triggers ovulation. It is caused by a unique "positive feedback" mechanism.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common type of renal stones are:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calcium oxalate

The most common type of renal stone is calcium oxalate stone.

Note:

Uric acid stones are more common than calcium oxalate stones in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.

Calcium carbonate stone is the most common type of stone formed in chronic pancreatitis.

* Cystine stones: Hexagonal

* Uric acid stones: Varying shapes (rhomboids or parallelograms)

* Calcium oxalate

* Monohydrate: Dumbbell shaped

* Struvite stones: Rectangular or coffin lid

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 21-year-old girl who presented with multiple beefy-red painless ulcers over the vulval region is diagnosed with granuloma inguinale. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Klebsiella granulomatis

The causative organism of granuloma inguinale is Klebsiella granulomatis, a gram-negative bacillus.

Granuloma inguinale begins as a painless nodule that later ulcerates to form multiple beefy red painless ulcers. These ulcers tend to coalesce. There will be minimal adenopathy and progressive destruction of the vulva.

Microscopic examination of smears from the lesion/biopsy specimens reveals pathognomonic intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies and clusters of bacteria with a bipolar (safety-pin) appearance.

The microscopic image below shows the pathognomonic intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies. It also shows clusters of gram-negative bacteria with a bipolar/safety-pin appearance.

Management:

* Tetracycline 500 mg every 6 h for 2–3 weeks

* Gentamycin 1 mg/kg IM 8 h for 2 weeks

Other options:

Option A - Chlamydia trachomatis causes Lymphogranuloma Venereum.

Option C - Haemophilus ducreyi causes Chancroid.

Option D - Herpes simplex virus causes genital herpes.
questions.learning: Klebsiella granulomatis — The causative organism of granuloma inguinale is Klebsiella granulomatis, a gram-negative bacillus. Granuloma inguinale begins as a painless nodule that later ulcerates to form multiple beefy red painless ulcers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the embryological basis of the developmental defect shown in the image below?
options: Failure in closure of anterior neuropore of neural tube
Failure in closure of posterior neuropore of neural tube
Failure in closure of complete neural tube
Failure in closure of caudal neuropore of neural tube
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Failure in closure of anterior neuropore of neural tube

The image shows anencephaly.

Failure of the anterior end (cranial end) of the neural tube to close is known as exencephaly. As a result of this, the skull vault does not form. This leaves the malformed brain exposed. The exposed brain tissue degenerates, leaving a mass of necrotic tissue. This defect with the absence of a major portion of the brain, skull, and scalp is known as anencephaly. The brain stem remains intact.

In some cases, the closure defect of the neural tube extends caudally, and the spinal cord is affected. This condition is known as craniorachischisis, where there is anencephaly plus a large defect involving the spine.

Neurulation refers to the formation of the neural tube from the neural plate. The neural tube gives rise to the central nervous system.

Steps of neurulation

* The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken and form the neural plate.

* The neural plate lengthens and the lateral edges elevate to form the neural folds, and the mid-region gets depressed to form the neural groove.

* The neural folds approach each and fuse in the midline in a craniocaudal direction to form a tube-like structure called the neural tube.

* The anterior opening of the neural tube (cranial neuropore) closes by day 25 and the posterior opening (caudal neuropore) closes by day 28.

* The neural tube becomes the central nervous system.
questions.learning: Failure in closure of anterior neuropore of neural tube The image shows anencephaly. Failure of the anterior end (cranial end) of the neural tube to close is known as exencephaly.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with recurrent episodes of headache, palpitations, and profuse sweating, along with transient spikes in blood pressure. Investigations show elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrine levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A pheochromocytoma is a rare, catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla chromaffin cells. It classically presents with the triad of "paroxysmal" symptoms: pounding headache, palpitations (tachycardia), and profuse diaphoresis (sweating). These "spells" are caused by the episodic release of epinephrine and norepinephrine. Between episodes, the blood pressure may be normal, but transient, severe elevations during spells are characteristic. The definitive diagnostic test is the measurement of catecholamine metabolites—metanephrines and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)—in the blood or a 24-hour urine sample, which would be significantly elevated. Addison's disease (Option A) is adrenal insufficiency, which causes hypotension and hyperpigmentation. Renal artery stenosis (Option B) cause persistent, secondary hypertension but not episodic sweat/palpitation spells. Hyperthyroidism (Option D) can cause palpitations and sweating, but the symptoms are usually continuous, and metanephrines would be normal. Therefore, the combination of paroxysmal "5 Ps" (Pressure, Pain, Palpitations, Perspiration, Pallor) and elevated urinary metanephrines is diagnostic of pheochromocytoma
questions.learning: A pheochromocytoma is a rare, catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla chromaffin cells. It classically presents with the triad of "paroxysmal" symptoms: pounding headache, palpitations (tachycardia), and profuse diaphoresis (sweating).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the primary identification determined by a CBNAAT/ Gene-Xpert?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MTB + Rifampicin resistance

The Cartridge Based-Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (CBNAAT) is primarily done to check for Tuberculosis to detect DNA and rifampicin resistance.

CBNAAT (Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test) is a rapid molecular test that detects the DNA of TB bacteria in HIV-positive individuals. It uses sputum or any other biological specimen (except blood and blood-contaminated specimens). It can give a result in less than 2 hours. It can also detect the genetic mutations in the rpoB gene associated with resistance to the drug rifampicin.
questions.learning: MTB + Rifampicin resistance — The Cartridge Based-Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (CBNAAT) is primarily done to check for Tuberculosis to detect DNA and rifampicin resistance.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The cell shown below has it's origin from what type of cell?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. B cells

The image shows a Reed Sternberg cell and it is seen classically in Hodgkin's Lymphoma which is of B cell origin.

In classical Hodgkin's lymphoma , activation of the transcription factor NF-κB occurs. NF-κB may be activated by Epstein–Barr Virus (EBV) infection. EBV+ tumor cells express latent membrane protein-1 (LMP-1), a protein encoded by the EBV genome that transmits signals that upregulate NF-κB. Activation of NF-κB may occur in EBV tumors as a result of the acquired loss-of-function mutations in TNF alpha-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3). Activation of NF-κB by EBV or other mechanisms rescues “crippled” germinal center B cells that cannot express Igs from apoptosis, eventually leading to the formation of Reed–Sternberg cells.

Reed Sternberg cell: It is a giant cell. It has a classic owl-eyed appearance due to the presence of a symmetric or mirror image bilobed nucleus with prominent nucleoli surrounded by a clear space.

Reed Sternberg cells are not diagnostic for any condition since they are seen in many conditions such as:

* Hodgkin’s lymphoma

* Non Hodgkin’s lymphoma (commonly in immunoblastic type)

* Infectious mononucleosis

* Sarcomas
questions.learning: B cells — The image shows a Reed Sternberg cell and it is seen classically in Hodgkin's Lymphoma which is of B cell origin. In classical Hodgkin's lymphoma , activation of the transcription factor NF-κB occurs.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old female came to the clinic with headache and visual field loss. A pituitary adenoma was found compressing the optic chiasma. What visual field defect will be seen in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bitemporal hemianopia

The pituitary tumour compressing the optic chiasma results in bitemporal hemianopia.

Pituitary macroadenoma can compress the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopia, which leads to the loss of vision in the temporal halves of the visual fields in both eyes. This occurs when damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects the crossing fibres from the nasal retina of each eye while the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas remain intact. As a result, individuals retain central vision but lose peripheral vision on the sides.

The most common cause of bitemporal hemianopia is a pituitary adenoma. Other common causes include:

* suprasellar aneurysms

* chronic arachnoiditis

* suprasellar tumours like craniopharyngioma and suprasellar meningioma

Other options:

Option B: Loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes (e.g., right half of both eyes causes right homonymous hemianopia), but here it's the temporal fields of both eyes.

Option C: Homonymous anopia, sometimes used loosely, but strictly means loss of the same entire visual field ('an-' = absence) in both eyes.

Option D: Inferior quadrantanopia is seen in the lesion of parietal lobe optic radiation → “pie on the floor” defect.

Pearl PF2187: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which protein is present in the HPV vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. L1

The HPV vaccines use virus-like particles (VLPs) that consist of the HPV L1 major capsid protein. The L1 protein self-assembles into VLPs when expressed in eukaryotic cells.

These VLPs contain the same epitopes as the HPV virion. But they do not contain genetic material and cannot transmit infection. The immunogenicity of the HPV vaccines relies on the development of conformational neutralizing antibodies to epitopes displayed on viral capsids.

The nonavalent HPV vaccine works against strains 6,11,16,18,31,33,45,52 and 58. It is usually commercialized in the name of Gardasil 9.

Recent update: Gardasil 9 has received expanded indication which now includes the prevention of oropharyngeal and other head and neck cancers caused by HPV types 16,18,31,33,45,52,58.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents for an antenatal check-up and is currently on lithium for her bipolar disorder. This drug must be stopped, due to the risk of development of which of the following conditions in the fetus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ebstein anomaly

Lithium should be stopped as it can cause an Ebstein anomaly in the newborn.

Ebstein anomaly is characterized by the downward displacement of the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which results in a thin-walled, low-pressure, “atrialized” segment of the right ventricle due to the anomalous attachment of the tricuspid leaflets.

Lithium can also cause macrocephaly as a teratogenic effect.

Lithium use in early pregnancy causes Ebstein anomaly in the fetus. Fetal lithium exposure is associated with neonatal goiter, CNS depression, hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome), and cardiac murmur.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is brought to the OPD by his wife complaining about difficulty in expressing emotions and not taking part in daily activities. On examination, resting tremors and rigidity are noted. Given the possible diagnosis, which part of the brain is affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Basal ganglia

Based on the clinical findings given above the most likely diagnosis is Parkinson's disease and it is due to degeneration of the substantia nigra in the basal ganglia.

Parkinson’s disease, also known as paralysis agitans, results from widespread degeneration of the portion of the substantia nigra that sends dopamine-secreting nerve fibers to the caudate nucleus and putamen.

It is characterized by rigidity, resting tremors, akinesia, bradykinesia, postural instability, dysphagia, speech disorders, gait disturbances, and fatigue. Other non-motor features include anosmia, sensory disturbances, mood disorders (e.g., depression), sleep disturbances, autonomic disturbances, and cognitive impairment/dementia.

Other options:

Option B: Lesions of the hippocampus mainly affect learning, memory, emotional behavior, regulation of hypothalamic functions, and spatial navigation.

Option C: Features of cerebellar lesions are ataxia, intention tremors, nystagmus, speech defect (slurring speech), hypotonia or atonia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia (failure to perform rapid alternating movements), decomposition of movement (lack of smooth flow of movement), rebound phenomenon

Option D: Premotor cortex is concerned with setting posture at the start of a planned movement and with getting the individual prepared to move. It is most involved in the control of proximal limb muscles needed to orient the body for movement.
questions.learning: Basal ganglia — Based on the clinical findings given above the most likely diagnosis is Parkinson's disease and it is due to degeneration of the substantia nigra in the basal ganglia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the probable cause for hypotension, flushing, and nausea in a patient using anti- amoebic drugs?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of hypotension, flushing, nausea, and headache in a patient taking anti-amoebic drugs (specifically nitroimidazoles like Metronidazole or Tinidazole) are characteristic of a disulfiram-like reaction. This occurs when these medications inhibit the enzyme acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, leading to a toxic accumulation of acetaldehyde if the patient consumes alcohol. Delirium tremens (Option A) and alcohol withdrawal (Option B) occur after the cessation of alcohol in a chronic drinker and involve autonomic hyperactivity, seizures, and confusion. Hallucinosis (Option D) refers to perceptions in the absence of external stimuli, which is not the primary feature here. To prevent this highly distressing reaction, patients must be strictly counseled to avoid all forms of alcohol during treatment and for at least 48-72 hours after the final dose. This clinical interaction is a high-yield pharmacology topic due to its common occurrence and significant impact on patient safety
questions.learning: The symptoms of hypotension, flushing, nausea, and headache in a patient taking anti-amoebic drugs (specifically nitroimidazoles like Metronidazole or Tinidazole) are characteristic of a disulfiram-like reaction.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: While discharging a patient who underwent a vesicovaginal fistula repair, which of the following would you recommend?
options: Sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoid pregnancy for a year
Sexual abstinence for 3 weeks and avoid pregnancy for 6 months
Sexual abstinence for 6 weeks and avoid pregnancy for a year
Sexual abstinence for 6 months and avoid pregnancy for 6 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoid pregnancy for a year

While discharging a patient who underwent vesicovaginal fistula repair, sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoiding pregnancy for a year would be recommended.

Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) is a type of urinary fistula which commonly arises due to obstetric trauma. Small fistulas due to difficult childbirth can heal spontaneously. Most established fistulas need to be repaired vaginally usually after 3 months to allow the inflammation to subside. Post-operatively, continuous bladder drainage for 14 days along with antibiotics is recommended. Vaginal or speculum examination and intercourse are not advised for 3 months. Avoiding pregnancy for a year is also recommended. A cesarean section is usually done for future pregnancies.

Presenting features of VVF include constant dribbling of urine/ true incontinence. Excoriation of the vagina, vulva, and thighs can occur due to constant contact with urine. Few patients might develop bladder stones. Vaginal urine collection can be seen on retraction of the posterior vaginal wall with a speculum. A bimanual examination can be used to assess the fixity and scarring of the surrounding tissues. A cystourethroscopy can be used for localization and assessing bladder mucosa viability.
questions.learning: Sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoid pregnancy for a year While discharging a patient who underwent vesicovaginal fistula repair, sexual abstinence for 3 months and avoiding pregnancy for a year would be recommended.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the ICDS program in India, what is the calorie and protein supplementation provided to a child aged 6-72 months?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 500 kcal, 12-15 grams

Under the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme, children aged 6–72 months receive supplementary nutrition providing 500 kcal and 12–15 g of protein per day for approximately 300 days per year to bridge the gap between dietary intake and nutritional requirements, thereby preventing protein-energy malnutrition.

Why not the other options?

• A. 200 kcal, 6–8 g: Inadequate for the ICDS recommendation for children aged 6–72 months.
• B. 300 kcal, 8–10 g: Lower than the recommended supplementary nutrition under ICDS.
• D. 600 kcal, 18–20 g: Exceeds the routine supplementation provided to normal children under ICDS.

The supplementation values for each group under ICDS Program:

| Beneficiary | Calories | Protein

| ----------- | -------- | -------

| Child 6–72 months (normal) | 500 kcal | 12–15 grams

| Malnourished children | 800 kcal | 20–25 grams

| Pregnant and lactating mother | 600 kcal | 18–20 grams

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with irregular menstrual periods, acne, and excessive hair growth. Laboratory tests reveal elevated serum insulin and testosterone levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of irregular periods (ovulatory dysfunction), acne, and excessive hair growth (hirsutism), combined with laboratory findings of elevated testosterone and insulin, is pathognomonic for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is a complex endocrine disorder characterized by hyperandrogenism and insulin resistance. Endometriosis (Option B) typically presents with severe pelvic pain and infertility but not hyperandrogenic features. While certain virilizing ovarian tumors (Option C) can cause high testosterone, they usually present with rapid onset of symptoms rather than a chronic history. Hypothyroidism (Option D) can cause menstrual irregularities but is not associated with hirsutism or acne. Management of PCOS involves lifestyle modifications to address insulin resistance, along with hormonal contraceptives or anti-androgens to manage the skin and cycle issues. It is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility in reproductive-age women
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of irregular periods (ovulatory dysfunction), acne, and excessive hair growth (hirsutism), combined with laboratory findings of elevated testosterone and insulin, is pathognomonic for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify this sign in pregnancy.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hegar's sign

The image dipicts Hegar's sign.

Hegar's sign: the examiner performs a bimanual examination. Two fingers of one hand are placed in the anterior fornix of the vagina and the fingers of the other hand are placed, over the abdomen and behind the uterus. The abdominal fingers and the vaginal fingers appear to oppose each other below the body of the uterus. This can be elicited between 6-10 weeks.

This sign is based on the fact that the lower part of the body of the uterus is empty and extremely soft, and the upper part is enlarged by the growing fetus.

Other options :

Option A- Palmer's sign is regular rhythmic uterine contraction during the bimanual examination, which is seen as early as 4-8 weeks.

Option C- Osiander's sign is increased pulsation felt through lateral fornix by 8 weeks.

Option D- Goodell's sign is softening of the cervix by the 6th week.

Pearl PF1633: Clinical Signs in Obstetrics

*

Chadwick’s Sign: Bluish hue to the vestibule and anterior vaginal wall. Seen in the first trimester of pregnancy. The cause is increased blood flow to the pelvic organs. Also known as Jacquemier’s Sign. /

*

Cullen Sign: Bluish discoloration of the skin around the umbilicus. Occurs due to intraperitoneal hemorrhage. Seen in ruptured ectopic pregnancy

*

Goodell Sign: Marked softening of the cervix in contrast to a non-pregnant state. Also due to increased blood flow

* Hegar Sign: An indication of Pregnancy. The softening of the lower parts of the uterus enables the approximation of vaginal and abdominal fingers on bimanual pelvic examination.

*

Kustner’s Sign: Sign of placental separation. On pushing the uterus upwards does not move the cord with it due to the separation.

*

Ladin’s Sign: Softening in the midline of the uterus anteriorly at the junction of the uterus and cervix. It occurs at about 6 weeks gestation

* Osiander’s Sign: Pulsations in the lateral fornix due to the increased vascularity.

* Palmer’s Sign: Regular rhythmic contractions of uterus felt as early as 6-8 weeks. It is a sign of pregnancy

*

Piskacek’s Sign: Asymmetric growth occurs to the uterus in the initial stages of pregnancy due to the lateral implantation of the blastocyst. The area of implantation feels soft compared to the other parts.

*

Schroeder’s Sign: A sign of placental separation. Uterus rises up when the separated placenta is passed downwards

*

Stallworthy’s Sign: Slowing of fetal heart rate on pressing the head down into the pelvis and prompt recovery on the release of pressure is termed Stallworthy’s sign. This sign is suggestive of posterior placenta praevia.

*

Turtle Sign: This is when the fetal head suddenly retracts back against the mother's perineum after it has emerged from the vagina. This retraction of the fetal head is caused by the baby's anterior shoulder being caught on the back of the maternal pubic bone, preventing delivery of the remainder of the baby.

*

Von Braun-Fernwald's Sign: Irregular softening and enlargement of the uterine fundus during early pregnancy. It occurs at 5-8 weeks gestation.
questions.learning: Hegar's sign — The image dipicts Hegar's sign. Hegar's sign: the examiner performs a bimanual examination.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of these steps is followed first for the management of shoulder dystocia after McRoberts maneuver?
options: Flex the legs over the abdomen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Apply gentle supra pubic pressure

Applying a gentle suprapubic pressure is the first step in the management of shoulder dystocia after the McRoberts maneuver.

Shoulder dystocia drill to better organize emergency management:

* Call for help. Initially, a gentle attempt at traction is made. Drain the bladder if it is distended.

* Episiotomy

* McRoberts maneuver: involves flexing the legs on the abdomen with concurrent suprapubic pressure. This causes straightening of the sacrum relative to the lumbar vertebrae, rotation of the symphysis pubis toward the maternal head, and a decrease in the angle of pelvic inclination. This tends to free the impacted anterior shoulder. It is shown in the image below.

These maneuvers will resolve most cases of shoulder dystocia. If not -

* Delivery of the posterior arm is attempted.

* Woods screw maneuver is applied.

* Rubin maneuver is attempted.

Other techniques generally should be reserved for cases in which all other maneuvers have failed. These include intentional fracture of the anterior clavicle and the Zavanelli maneuver.
questions.learning: Apply gentle supra pubic pressure Applying a gentle suprapubic pressure is the first step in the management of shoulder dystocia after the McRoberts maneuver.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During a medical ethics discussion, students learn about the unethical practice in which doctors and radiologists exchange payments for patient referrals for CT scans. What is this practice called?
questions.explanation: In medical ethics and forensics, the practice of a doctor receiving a kickback or "fee-splitting" payment from a consultant or facility for a patient referral is termed Dichotomy (Option A). This is considered a highly unethical practice as it compromises the physician's objectivity and may lead to unnecessary testing for financial gain. Medical maloccurrence (Option B) refers to an unexpected, adverse clinical outcome that occurs despite proper care. Criminal negligence (Option C) involves a gross disregard for human life or safety during medical treatment. Commission (Option D) is a general financial term but "Dichotomy" is the specific ethical term used in medical jurisprudence to describe this illegal splitting of fees. This practice is prohibited under the Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette and Ethics) Regulations. Therefore, dichotomy is the definitive term for this referral-based kickback scheme
questions.learning: In medical ethics and forensics, the practice of a doctor receiving a kickback or "fee-splitting" payment from a consultant or facility for a patient referral is termed Dichotomy (Option A).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient who presented with a scrotal swelling underwent an orchidectomy. The image below shows the histopathology findings. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Seminoma

Based on the gross and microscopic appearance of the specimen, the diagnosis is seminoma.

The gross specimen shows a well-circumscribed, pale, gray-white, fleshy, homogenous mass, with a lobulated cut surface, usually devoid of hemorrhage or necrosis. Histopathology shows uniform tumor cells with abundant clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and large central nuclei. There is a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate. Classically, they have a fried egg appearance.

Other options:

Option B: Yolk-sac tumor has a yellowish-white, mucinous appearance. Histologically, they are typically composed of a lace-like (reticular) network of medium-sized cuboidal, flattened, or spindled cells, which generally show less cytologic atypia than embryonal carcinoma. In approximately 50% of tumors, structures resembling endodermal sinuses (Schiller-Duval bodies) may be seen; these consist of a mesodermal core with a central capillary and a visceral and parietal layer of cells resembling primitive glomeruli.

Option C: Embryonal cell carcinoma appears variegated with foci of hemorrhage or necrosis.  Histologically, the cells grow in alveolar or tubular patterns, sometimes with papillary folds. More undifferentiated lesions may display sheets of cells with cleft-like spaces. The neoplastic cells have an epithelial appearance, are large and anaplastic, and have hyperchromatic nuclei with prominent nucleoli. The cell borders are usually indistinct, and there is considerable variation in cell and nuclear size and shape (pleomorphism). Mitotic figures and tumor giant cells are frequently seen.

Option D: Teratomas also have a variegated appearance but have cysts reflecting the multiplicity of tissue types. Histologically, collections of differentiated cells or organoid structures originating in all 3 germ layers can be seen. Elements may be mature (resembling various adult tissues) or immature (sharing histologic features with fetal or embryonic tissue).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following clinical features: 1. Hypomimia 2. Dysphonia 3. Festination gait 4. Cogwheel rigidity Which of the features given above are generally present in Parkinsonism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Parkinsonism is a hypokinetic movement disorder resulting from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia. It is clinically characterized by bradykinesia, along with resting tremor, rigidity, and postural instability, and is associated with several characteristic motor features.

• Cardinal features: Bradykinesia (mandatory), resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, and postural instability.
• Hypomimia (masked facies): Reduced facial expression due to facial bradykinesia.
• Hypophonia/Dysphonia: Soft, monotonous speech.
• Festination gait: Short, rapid, shuffling steps with difficulty stopping.
• Other features:

• Micrographia
• Stooped posture
• Reduced arm swing
• Freezing of gait
• Decreased blinking
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 and 4 Parkinsonism is a hypokinetic movement disorder resulting from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following primitive reflexes do not disappear?
questions.explanation: Primitive reflexes are automatic movements present at birth that are eventually integrated into voluntary actions as the nervous system matures. Most, such as the Rooting reflex (Option A), Moro reflex (Option C), and Palmar grasp (Option D), disappear (integrate) within the first 6 months of life. However, the Parachute reflex is a protective reflex that appears around 6–9 months and does not disappear; it persists throughout life. It is elicited by suddenly tilting the infant forward; the child reflexively extends their arms to "break the fall." The persistence of primitive reflexes beyond their expected age or the absence of the parachute reflex can indicate central nervous system dysfunction or developmental delays. The parachute reflex is an essential marker of neurological maturity, ensuring the individual can protect their head and body during a fall. Clinicians assess these reflexes to determine the functional integrity of the infant's sensory and motor pathways
questions.learning: Primitive reflexes are automatic movements present at birth that are eventually integrated into voluntary actions as the nervous system matures. Most, such as the Rooting reflex (Option A), Moro reflex (Option C), and Palmar grasp (Option D), disappear…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are true?

1. Due to increasing mammography, there occurs over-diagnosis of breast carcinoma
2. Colon cancer screening is done by digital rectal examination
3. Oral cancer screening is done by visual inspection
4. Cervix cancer screening is done by a pap smear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3, 4

Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true.

Screening with noninvasive tests for common cancers aims to achieve early diagnosis, enable less invasive surgical treatments with reduced complications, and potentially improve surgical cure and overall survival rates.

Statement 1: Mammography as a routine screening tool has been found to lower breast cancer mortality at an acceptable cost. In the United Kingdom, an expert panel reported a 20% reduction in breast cancer mortality due to screening, despite the occurrence of overdiagnosis. The panel recommended continuing breast screening due to its significant benefits.

Statement 3: Visual inspection of the oral cavity is widely used for screening oral cancer. The target population includes individuals aged 30 and above who use tobacco and/or alcohol. Visual inspection is advantageous due to its feasibility, safety, acceptability, accuracy in detecting precancerous and cancerous lesions, and cost-effectiveness in reducing oral cancer mortality.

Statement 4: Pap smear is a screening test for cervical cancer. Cervical cancer screening should start at age 21. Women aged 21-29 should have Pap smear every 3 years, while women aged 30-65 should have both HPV and Pap co-test every 5 years.

Other statements:

Statement 2: American Cancer Society guidelines recommend colon cancer screening for average-risk individuals starting at age 50. Screening options include:

• Yearly fecal occult blood testing (FOBT) / fecal immunohistochemical testing (FIT)
• Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years,
• FOBT/FIT and flexible sigmoidoscopy in combination every 5 years, or
• Colonoscopy every 10 years.
questions.learning: 1, 3, 4 Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true. Screening with noninvasive tests for common cancers aims to achieve early diagnosis, enable less invasive surgical treatments with reduced complications, and potentially improve surgical cure and overall survival rates.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with muffled heart sounds, hypotension, and elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP). Which specific feature of the JVP waveform is most likely to be observed in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of muffled heart sounds, hypotension, and elevated JVP is known as Beck’s triad, which is diagnostic for cardiac tamponade. In tamponade, the heart is compressed by high-pressure pericardial fluid, which severely restricts ventricular filling. On the JVP waveform, the y-descent represents the rapid emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle during early diastole. Because the high intrapericardial pressure prevents rapid filling, the y-descent is characteristically blunted or absent. The x-descent (Option A) is typically preserved or even accentuated in tamponade. Enlarged C waves (Option C) and absent A waves (Option D) are not characteristic of tamponade; absent A waves are seen in atrial fibrillation. Recognizing these specific waveform nuances is essential for differentiating tamponade from other causes of high JVP like constrictive pericarditis, where a sharp, steep y-descent (Friedreich's sign) is seen. Immediate management of tamponade requires emergency pericardiocentesis to relieve the life-threatening cardiac compression

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: You have been called to declare the brain death of a 12-year-old child in the ICU. Which of the following is not seen in brain death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decorticate and decerebrate posturing

Decerebrate or decorticate posturing is not seen in brain death as they are motor responses to noxious stimuli that originate from the midbrain and cortex.

Brain death, also known as death by neurologic criteria refers to the irreversible and total cessation of all functions of the entire brain, including the brainstem.

The three components for diagnosing brain death are a demonstration of coexisting irreversible coma with a known cause, absence of brain stem reflexes, and apnea. Coma requires the patient to be unresponsive, even to noxious stimuli. The diagnosis of brain death can still be made despite positive spinal reflexes. (option B)

Brainstem reflexes (pupillary responses, oculocephalic reflex, oculovestibular responses, corneal reflex, jaw reflex, facial grimacing, pharyngeal gag reflex, coughing) are absent. Apnea is the absence of respiratory drive at PaCO2 of ≥60mmHg and > 20mmHg above baseline, which is consistent with brain death.

The following manifestations are occasionally seen and should not be misinterpreted as evidence of brainstem function:

• Normal systolic blood pressure - SBP >100 mmHg (option A)
• Movements originating from the spinal cord or peripheral nerve may occur
• Sweating, flushing, tachycardia (option C)
• Deep tendon reflexes; superficial abdominal reflexes; triple flexion response
• Babinski reflex
• Spontaneous movements of limbs other than pathologic flexion or extension response
• Respiratory-like movements (shoulder elevation and adduction, back-arching, intercostal expansion without significant tidal volumes)
questions.learning: Decorticate and decerebrate posturing Decerebrate or decorticate posturing is not seen in brain death as they are motor responses to noxious stimuli that originate from the midbrain and cortex.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: When radiotherapy is administered in combination with chemotherapy for bladder cancer, which drug usually requires a dose reduction because of an increased risk of toxicity?
questions.explanation: In the concurrent chemoradiotherapy (trimodality therapy) used for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, Cisplatin is the primary radiosensitizing agent of choice. When used in combination with radiation, cisplatin carries a significantly increased risk of synergistic toxicity, most notably nephrotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy. To minimize these risks, the dosage must be carefully adjusted, often being delivered in lower, frequent weekly doses rather than high-dose pulses used in standard systemic therapy. Gemcitabine (Option B) is also used but is a more potent radiosensitizer with a higher risk of local bowel and bladder inflammation (toxicity). Paclitaxel (Option C) and Ifosfamide (Option D) are typically reserved for salvage therapy or metastatic disease rather than primary concurrent radiosensitization protocols. Therefore, because of its gold-standard status and dose-limiting renal and neurological side effects during radiation, Cisplatin is the medication most critical for dosage adjustment
questions.learning: In the concurrent chemoradiotherapy (trimodality therapy) used for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, Cisplatin is the primary radiosensitizing agent of choice.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The given set of instruments are used in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Airway management

The image shows a tray in an airway cart with the instruments necessary for airway management.

An airway cart may include:

• Laryngoscope blades of various sizes, including a rigid fibreoptic.
• Tracheal tubes of various sizes, and tracheal tube guides such as semirigid stylets, ventilating tube changer, light wands, and forceps that are required to manipulate the distal portion of the tracheal tube.
• Masks of various sizes.
• Laryngeal mask airways of various sizes.
• Flexible fiberoptic intubation equipment.
• Retrograde intubation equipment.
• At least one device to perform emergency noninvasive airway ventilation such as esophageal tracheal tube, a hollow jet ventilation stylet.
• Equipment required for emergency invasive airway access.
• An exhaled CO2 detector.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old girl was brought by her mother with complaints of enlarged clitoris. Karyotype revealed 46XX. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 21 hydroxylase deficiency

The given clinical scenario of a girl (46XX) with an enlarged clitoris is highly suggestive of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia/adrenogenital syndrome is a family of autosomal-recessive disorders caused by the deficiency of enzymes involved in the synthesis of steroid hormones in the adrenal cortex. The majority of cases of CAH are caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency. This deficiency leads to a lack of synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone, resulting in the salt-wasting form of the disease, which is the most severe form.

Severe 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents with symptoms including weight loss, dehydration, weakness, hypotension, and electrolyte imbalances. Accumulated steroid precursors like 17-hydroxyprogesterone, are shunted into the pathway of androgen synthesis leading to elevated levels of androstenedione and testosterone. This can result in abnormal genital development in affected female fetuses during early gestation.

Females may have masculinized external genitalia. This can include enlargement of the clitoris, partial or complete labial fusion, and a shared opening of the vagina and urethra (urogenital sinus).

Untreated individuals develop signs of androgen excess after birth.  These signs include accelerated skeletal maturation, premature epiphyseal closure leading to stunted adult stature, excessive muscular development, the appearance of pubic and axillary hair, acne, and deepening of the voice. In males, enlargement of the penis, scrotum, and prostate. In females, the clitoris may become further enlarged.

Diagnosis of confirmed by elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels. Glucocorticoid replacement with hydrocortisone is done. In a salt-wasting crisis, fludrocortisone supplementation is given. Vaginoplasty and clitoral recession are done for females with ambiguous genitalia.
questions.learning: 21 hydroxylase deficiency The given clinical scenario of a girl (46XX) with an enlarged clitoris is highly suggestive of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Gamma radiation is used for sterilization of ____?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Syringes, needles and catheters

Gamma radiation is used for the sterilization of articles such as syringes, needles, catheters, and gloves.

Gamma particles show maximum penetration and since there is no increase in temperature during the process it is called as cold sterilisation.

* When a nucleus disintegrates, it will emit radiation either as photons (X or gamma rays) or as high velocity particles.

* Gamma rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation (EMR) similar to X-rays, however, distinguished from the latter by the fact that they are emitted from an excited nucleus.
