questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presented with easy fatigability, irritability and inability to concentrate. Labs revealed the following findings a and b (light and oil immersion respectively) on the bone marrow aspiration. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficient in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glucocerebrosidase

The given clinical scenario of a child with easy fatiguability, irritability, and inability to concentrate with the images showing a crumpled tissue paper appearance(Gaucher's cell) is suggestive of Gaucher's disease. The deficient enzyme is glucocerebrosidase (also known as beta-glucosidase). I

Gaucher's disease is an inborn error of metabolism caused due to a deficiency of beta glucocerebrosidase. It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and the mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive. There is an accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, and other tissues.

There are three clinical subtypes - type I (chronic non-neuronopathic), type II (acute neuronopathic), and type III (intermediate). Clinical features include anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological features depending on the subtype.

Gaucher's cells - These are formed as a result of the accumulation of massive amounts of glucocerebrosides within the phagocytes. The cells have a fibrillary cytoplasm and give a crumpled tissue paper appearance.

Option A: Deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A is seen in Tay-Sachs disease. The deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A and B causes Sandhoff's disease. Clinical features are seizures, macrocephaly, and hyperacusis.

Option C: Deficiency of sphingomyelinase leads to Niemann-Pick disease. It is characterized by the presence of foam cells in the bone marrow. There may be pulmonary infiltrates leading to lung failure.

Option D: Deficiency of N-acetylglucosaminidase leads to Sanfillipo's disease. It is a type of mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS - III). There is an accumulation of heparan sulfate leading to severe cognitive degeneration.
questions.learning: Glucocerebrosidase — The given clinical scenario of a child with easy fatiguability, irritability, and inability to concentrate with the images showing a crumpled tissue paper appearance(Gaucher's cell) is suggestive of Gaucher's disease.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A radiopaque density may be noticed in poisoning by which of the following agents?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chloral hydrate

Certain drugs and toxins are radiopaque and can be visualized on a plain abdominal X-ray after ingestion. Chloral hydrate is one of these radiopaque substances and may appear as a radiopaque density in the gastrointestinal tract following overdose or poisoning.

Why not the other options?

• A. Phenazopyridine: Not reliably radiopaque.
• B. Ethylene glycol: A colorless liquid; not radiopaque on X-ray.
• C. Chloroquine: Not consistently radiopaque and cannot be relied upon for radiographic detection.
questions.learning: Chloral hydrate Certain drugs and toxins are radiopaque and can be visualized on a plain abdominal X-ray after ingestion. Chloral hydrate is one of these radiopaque substances and may appear as a radiopaque density in the gastrointestinal tract following…

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What type of fracture is caused by a hammer?
questions.explanation: A hammer is a heavy, blunt object with a relatively small impact surface. When it strikes the skull with significant force, it typically causes a depressed fracture. In this type of injury, bone fragments are pushed inward toward the brain, often creating an indentation that may even mirror the shape of the hammer's head. Regarding other options, a linear or fissured fracture (Option A) is caused by impact against broad surfaces, like a fall onto a flat floor, and shows cracks without bone displacement. A hinge fracture (Option (C) is a transverse fracture at the skull base often seen in side impacts or motorcyclist accidents. A ring fracture (Option D) circles the foramen magnum and is usually caused by vertical force transmitted through the spine, such as falling from a height and landing on the feet. Therefore, the focused, high-energy impact of a hammer uniquely leads to a localized depression of the skull vault
questions.learning: A hammer is a heavy, blunt object with a relatively small impact surface. When it strikes the skull with significant force, it typically causes a depressed fracture.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: Histopathological examination of myocardium from a patient with myocardial infarction shows predominant neutrophilic infiltration along with loss of nuclei. What is the most likely time elapsed since the infarction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1–3 days

Following myocardial infarction (MI), histopathological changes occur in a predictable chronological sequence. Predominant neutrophilic infiltration with coagulative necrosis (loss of nuclei and striations) is characteristic of the 1–3 day period after infarction.

Why is B correct?

• 1–3 days: Extensive coagulative necrosis with loss of nuclei, eosinophilic myocytes, and dense neutrophilic infiltration.

Why not the other options?

• A. 0–4 hours: Minimal or no light microscopic changes; early wavy fibers may be seen.
• C. 7–10 days: Macrophages have replaced neutrophils, with well-developed granulation tissue.
• D. 2 months: Dense collagenous scar with little or no inflammatory infiltrate.

| Time after MI | Histological Finding

| ------------- | --------------------

| 0–4 hours | No significant LM changes; early wavy fibers

| 4–24 hours | Early coagulative necrosis, edema, beginning neutrophils

| 1–3 days | Extensive coagulative necrosis + dense neutrophilic infiltration

| 3–7 days | Macrophages predominate; maximal tissue breakdown

| 7–10 days | Granulation tissue with angiogenesis and fibroblasts

| Weeks to months | Progressive collagen deposition → fibrous scar
questions.learning: 1–3 days Following myocardial infarction (MI), histopathological changes occur in a predictable chronological sequence. Predominant neutrophilic infiltration with coagulative necrosis (loss of nuclei and striations) is characteristic of the 1–3 day period…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 53-year-old woman underwent hip replacement surgery. A week after the surgery, the patient developed swelling of the legs associated with pain on palpation. Her heart rate is 70 beats per min. There is no history of hemoptysis or significant weight loss. There is no previous history of pulmonary embolism. What is the risk of developing pulmonary embolism in the patient based on Well's score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High

The risk of developing pulmonary embolism in this patient is high (Option B) according to the three-tiered Well’s clinical risk assessment score.

Calculation of Well's score:

• Clinical signs of DVT = 3;  - swelling of legs, pain on palpation (Moses sign)
• No alternative diagnosis = 3
• Heart rate is <100 BPM = 0; - 70 BPM
• Surgery in previous 4 weeks = 1.5; - hip replacement surgery 1 week ago
• No previous pulmonary embolism = 0
• No Hemoptysis = 0
• No malignancy = 0; - no significant weight loss

Total score = 7.5

Risk stratification:

• High risk =  > 6.0
• Moderate risk =  2.0 to 6.0
• Low risk = <2.0 (in patients with low risk, to further confirm the risk - pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria (PERC) may be referred)

Note: There is no other alternative diagnosis which is more likely in this condition, where there is a clear clinical presentation of a deep vein thrombosis, with the associated risk factors of a recent surgery and immobilization. Hence, 3 points can be added to the score.
questions.learning: High — The risk of developing pulmonary embolism in this patient is high (Option B) according to the three-tiered Well’s clinical risk assessment score.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 4-year-old-boy was brought to emergency department with complaints of acute radiating pain in right iliac region and during surgery the following structure was found. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meckel’s Diverticulum

The clinical history and the image are both suggestive of Meckel's Diverticulum.

Meckel’s diverticulum is a true diverticulum, which extends from the antimesenteric side of the small bowel. The diverticula which contain all the layers of the intestine are called true diverticula. It is caused by a failure of normal regression of the vitelline duct that develops during weeks 5-7 of gestation.

The rule of 2's (Mnemonic for Meckel’s diverticulum) :

* 2 types of heterotopic mucosa (gastric & pancreatic)(Option d).

* 2% incidence

* located within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve

* approximately 2 inches in length

* Usually symptomatic by 2 years of age

The most common presentation is painless, massive, lower GI bleed in children younger than 5 years. Meckel's diverticulum can be the lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception.

A bleeding Meckel's diverticulum may be confirmed by a 99 mTc-pertechnetate isotope scan to detect ectopic gastric mucosa.

Surgical treatment is the definitive therapy for Meckel’s diverticulum. A simple V-shaped diverticulectomy with transverse closure of the ileum is the ideal surgical approach.

The following diagram shows the various anomalies that arise as a result of the failure of normal regression of vitellointestinal duct:

Other Options:

Option A: The most common tumor of the appendix is the well-differentiated neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumor. This neoplasm, which is almost always benign, most frequently forms a solid bulbous swelling at the distal tip of the appendix.

Option B: Adenocarinoma of  the appendix is very rare, accounting for 0.5% of all gastrointestinal cancers. They are detected in 0.08 to 0.1% of appendectomy specimens. Mucinous is a subtype of the adenocarinoma of  the appendix.

Option D: In bowel loop obstruction, the obstructed bowel loops are centrally located and lie transversely. In cases of jejunal obstruction, valvulae conniventes, which are mucosal folds that span the entire diameter of the bowel, create a ladder effect. Additionally, a distended cecum may exhibit a gas shadow in the right iliac fossa.
questions.learning: Meckel’s Diverticulum — The clinical history and the image are both suggestive of Meckel's Diverticulum. Meckel’s diverticulum is a true diverticulum, which extends from the antimesenteric side of the small bowel.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-year-old child presents with bedwetting. The parents report a single episode of falling from the bed, but there is no other significant medical history. Examination shows no evidence of urinary tract infection or neurological abnormality. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: In an 8-year-old with primary nocturnal enuresis and no medical or neurological symptoms, the established first-line management is behavioral modification. This includes strategies like limiting fluid intake in the evening, scheduled voiding before bed, and positive reinforcement reward systems. Enuresis alarms can also be utilized if these simple measures are insufficient. Anticholinergic drugs (Option B) and oxybutynin (Option C) are indicated for urge incontinence rather than simple nocturnal enuresis. Desmopressin therapy (Option D) is a second-line pharmacological option reserved for cases where behavioral measures fail or when rapid, short-term control is needed for specific events like camps. Thus, starting with non-pharmacological behavioral changes is the mandated clinical standard
questions.learning: In an 8-year-old with primary nocturnal enuresis and no medical or neurological symptoms, the established first-line management is behavioral modification.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old presents with absent menses. Examination shows widely spaced nipples, webbed neck, and Tanner grade 1 breast development. USG shows streak ovaries. Investigation shows raised FSH, raised LH, and reduced estradiol. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Turner syndrome

The patient’s clinical features are strongly suggestive of Turner syndrome.

Turner's syndrome is the most common sex chromosome abnormality in females. The classical karyotype is 45, XO. It is characterized by hypogonadism in phenotypic females.

The clinical features of Turner’s syndrome include short stature, short webbed neck, shield chest with widely spaced nipples, primary amenorrhea, congenital heart defects, and renal anomalies. Two X chromosomes are required for the development of ovaries. The loss of one X chromosome results in streak ovaries with inadequate estrogen production. The loss of negative feedback from reduced estrogen raises the FSH and LH levels causing hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

Other options:

Option B: Kallmnann syndrome presents with delayed puberty due to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from deficiency of GnRH. It is associated with olfactory dysfunction and anosmia.

Option C: Androgen insensitivity syndrome occurs due to a defect in the androgen receptor in a genotypic male (XY). These individuals are phenotypic females with no male or female internal genitalia. They have normal female external genitalia with an absent or shallow vagina, well-developed breasts, and scanty body hair (axillary and pubic) and are present with primary amenorrhea.

Option D: Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome, commonly referred to as Mullerian agenesis, has primary amenorrhea due to failure of development of the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina. They have normally functioning gonads and external genitalia.
questions.learning: Turner syndrome — The patient’s clinical features are strongly suggestive of Turner syndrome. Turner's syndrome is the most common sex chromosome abnormality in females.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A boy presents with multiple bullous lesions on the trunk and periostitis evident on X-rays. What is the next appropriate investigation to perform?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a neonate or young child with multiple bullous lesions (syphilitic pemphigus) and radiological evidence of periostitis (bone inflammation) is highly diagnostic of Congenital Syphilis . The most appropriate next step in the diagnostic workup is to perform a VDRL test on both the mother and the child (Option A). This non-treponemal screening test is used to detect antibodies against Treponema pallidum. PCR for TB (Option B) and HBsAg (Option C) or general ELISA (Option D) are unrelated to this specific orthopedic-cutaneous presentation. Congenital syphilis is also associated with findings like snuffles, Hutchinson's teeth, and saber shins later in life. Therefore, because the combination of bullae and periostitis is pathognomonic for fetal-maternal transmission of spirochetes, VDRL is the definitive next investigation. Prompt diagnosis is essential for initiating penicillin therapy to prevent further systemic damage and long-term sequelae
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a neonate or young child with multiple bullous lesions (syphilitic pemphigus) and radiological evidence of periostitis (bone inflammation) is highly diagnostic of Congenital Syphilis .

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a history of a previous cesarean section is currently in labor. She presents with mild contractions (3 in 10 minutes), intact membranes, and no signs of fetal distress. Partograph finding is given below. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Perform artificial rupture of membrane (ARM) and monitor
Wait and watch for labour to progress
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Perform artificial rupture of membrane (ARM) and monitor

In the clinical scenario of a woman in labor with mild contractions (3/10), no fetal distress, intact membranes, and the partograph showing rate of cervical dilatation of 0.5 cm/hour with the tracing crossing the alert line, the next best step is to augment labor with artificial rupture of membranes (ARM), followed by monitoring, as the membranes are still intact.

It is evident from the partograph that in 4 hours, the cervical dilatation has only gone from 4cm to 6 cm at a rate of 0.5 cm/hour, which is slower than the expected rate of dilatation (1cm/hour), indicating a protracted active phase. Since the membranes are intact and there is no fetal distress, artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) can be done to accelerate labour.

Artificial rupture of membranes is one of the surgical methods of induction of labor. It is done by pricking the membranes with an amnihook (Kocher’s forceps). Labor is induced by prostaglandins released by the separation of the membranes. There is also stretching of the cervix.

Other options:

Option A: If ARM fails to initiate labor within 4 hours, it should be supplemented by oxytocin.

Option C: Since the partograph tracing has crossed the alert line, expectant management is no longer appropriate, and intervention is necessary.

Option D: If the tracing crosses the action line, a repeat cesarean section is necessary.

Pearl PF2194: Partograph

Partograph types:

WHO Modified Partograph (2000)

* No latent phase

* Vaginal examination: This should be done no less than every 4 hours to assess cervical dilatation, descent of the fetal head, and moulding of skull bones. More frequent examination is only undertaken if indicated.

* Charting starts at 4 cm of cervical dilation.

* Colour of liquor mentioned as C-clear, B-blood stained, M-meconium stained.

* Moulding mentioned:

* bones are separated and sutures can be easily felt - (0)

* bones touching (1+)

* bones overlapping but can be reduced(2+)

* bones severely overlapping and irreducible ( 3+).

* Alert line reflects the average rate of cervical dilation of the slowest quintile of term primigravidas, if dilation slows or ceases, the partograph plot will cross the alert line.

* Alert line: at 4 cm dilation and expected dilation of 1 cm/hour.

* Action line is 2–4 hours after the alert line, which prompts interventions to accelerate labor or perform cesarean delivery.

* Higher rates of perinatal mortality are associated with delays of 4 hours or more after the alert line.

* Contractions measured for a span of 10 min (duration noted) and measured every 30 min (1 square = half hour).

* Pulse: record every 30 minutes and mark with a dot (•).

* Blood pressure: record every 4 hours and mark with arrows, unless the patient has a hypertensive disorder or pre-eclampsia, in which case record every 30 minutes.

* Temperature: record every 4 hours.

WHO Composite Partograph: It is same as modified except for it has latent phase and charting done at 3 cm.

WHO Simplified Partograph: WHO further modified the partograph for use by skilled attendants in health centers. This simplified partograph is colour coded.

* The area to the left of the alert line in the cervicograph is coloured green, representing normal progress.

* The area to the right of the action line is coloured red, indicating dangerously slow progress in labour.

* The area in between the alert and action line is coloured amber, indicating the need for greater vigilance.
questions.learning: Perform artificial rupture of membrane (ARM) and monitor In the clinical scenario of a woman in labor with mild contractions (3/10), no fetal distress, intact membranes, and the partograph showing rate of cervical dilatation of 0.5 cm/hour with the tracing…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A woman at 37 weeks of gestation comes to the OPD for an antenatal checkup. She is on warfarin for prosthetic valves. What would be the management of this patient?

LMWH- Low molecular weight heparin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Change to LMWH

The next appropriate step in the management of a pregnant woman with a prosthetic valve on warfarin therapy at 37 weeks of gestation is to stop warfarin and start low molecular weight heparin (LMWH).

Warfarin is safe and effective in preventing thromboembolism in the mother during the 2nd trimester. However, it is teratogenic and can lead to miscarriage, stillbirths, fetal anticoagulation, and fetal embryopathy if used in the 1st trimester.

Heparin is safe for the fetus as it does not cross the placenta but is less effective than warfarin in preventing thromboembolism.

Period of gestation
Anticoagulant

Till 12 completed weeks

LMWH or UFH

13 to 36 weeks
Warfarin

36 weeks till just before delivery
LMWH or UFH

6 hours after vaginal delivery and 24 hours after cesarean section
Warfarin, LMWH or UFH

LMWH- Low molecular weight heparin, UFH- Unfractionated heparin

For patients taking LMWH, factor Xa levels should be monitored weekly.

Heparin should be discontinued just before (at least 6 hours before) delivery. If delivery occurs before discontinuation and there is extensive bleeding, then iv protamine sulfate can be given. Warfarin or heparin anticoagulation can be restarted after 6 hours of vaginal delivery, usually without any problem.

Warfarin, LMWH, and UFH do not accumulate in breast milk and do not have an anticoagulant effect in the newborn. They are compatible with breastfeeding.
questions.learning: Change to LMWH — The next appropriate step in the management of a pregnant woman with a prosthetic valve on warfarin therapy at 37 weeks of gestation is to stop warfarin and start low molecular weight heparin (LMWH).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The commonest surgical approach to a retrosternal goiter is via:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neck

The commonest surgical approach to a retrosternal goiter is via the neck and the most common type of goitre approached is the secondary retrosternal goiter.

A goiter is considered to be retrosternal if at least 50% of the thyroid tissue is located intrathoracically. They can be primary or secondary.

Primary retrosternal goiter
Secondary retrosternal goiter

Occurrence
1%
Majority of retrosternal goiters

Origin

Arise from ectopic thyroid tissue in the chest

No connection with the thyroid tissue in the neck

Arise from the downward extension of cervical thyroid tissue along the fascial planes of the neck

Blood supply
Intrathoracic blood vessels
Superior and inferior thyroid arteries

Retrosternal goiter presents with dyspnoea, stridor, and dilated neck veins. Pemberton’s sign (venous congestion of the neck on the raising of hands above the head) is seen.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the neck is performed to assess the location of the thyroid. The definitive treatment is surgical excision of the ectopic thyroid.

Other options:

Option B & C: Median sternotomy (via chest) is indicated in:

• Primary mediastinal goiter
• Malignant retrosternal goiter
• Very large retrosternal goiter
• Recurrence in the mediastinum
questions.learning: Neck — The commonest surgical approach to a retrosternal goiter is via the neck and the most common type of goitre approached is the secondary retrosternal goiter.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young man is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. His left leg is shortened, internally rotated, and adducted, with absent femoral artery pulsation. A plain radiograph is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these findings?
options: Fracture neck of femur with injury to femoral vessels
Anterior dislocation of hip with femoral artery injury
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of a shortened, internally rotated, and adducted limb following high-energy trauma is pathognomonic for a Posterior Dislocation of the Hip (Option D) . This position is the classic "orthopedic posture" for this injury. The provided radiograph confirms the diagnosis, showing the femoral head out of its socket, typically appearing smaller and more superior than the contralateral side. In an anterior dislocation (Option C), the leg would instead be externally rotated and abducted. Fractures of the femur (Options A and B) typically result in an externally rotated limb. While vascular injury can occur, the characteristic "adducted and internally rotated" deformity is the definitive hallmark of a posterior dislocation. This is a medical emergency requiring urgent reduction to prevent avascular necrosis of the femoral head and sciatic nerve injury. Therefore, Option D is the accurate clinical and radiological diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical triad of a shortened, internally rotated, and adducted limb following high-energy trauma is pathognomonic for a Posterior Dislocation of the Hip (Option D) .

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is true about BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry)?
options: It can be used for screening of hearing loss.
It can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss.

BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) or ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response) is an objective test that records electrical activity occurring in the auditory pathway and can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss.

* The recording is made from brain stem potentials

* Click stimulus is used

* Responses are not frequency specific

* Can be performed in awake and restless patients

* Responses begin after 1 -10 milliseconds after stimuli

* Suitable for even younger children

Uses:

* To objectively find hearing threshold- wave-V appears 10dB above the hearing level obtained through PTA

* Best audiometric test for:

* Confirming hearing loss in infants

* Diagnosing acoustic neuroma

*

* Differentiating cochlear and retro-cochlear hearing loss

* Diagnosing non-organic hearing loss.

Auditory brainstem response:

* Used to elicit brainstem responses to auditory stimulation by clicks or tone bursts.

* Non-invasive technique to find the integrity of central auditory pathways through the eighth nerve, pons and midbrain.

TYPE
SITE OF ORIGIN

Wave I
Distal part of CN VIII

Wave II
Proximal part of CN VIII near the brainstem.

Wave III
Cochlear nucleus

Wave IV
Superior olivary complex

Wave V
Lateral lemniscus

Wave VI and VII
Inferior colliculus

Pearl PF1553: BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) or ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response)

It is an objective test that records electrical activity occurring in the auditory pathway.

Normally, 7 waves are produced in the first 10ms.

* Wave I – distal part of the cochlear nerve

* Wave II –proximal part of the cochlear nerve

* Wave III – cochlear nucleus

* Wave IV – superior olivary complex

* Wave V – lateral lemniscus

* Wave VI – inferior colliculus

* Wave VII - medial geniculate body

Findings:

* Conductive or cochlear pathology- delayed wave-I but inter-peak latency of I-V is normal

* Retrocochlear pathology- wave-I present, rest of the waves absent

* Acoustic neuroma or vestibular schwannoma- increased inter-peak latency of wave I-V and increased inter-aural latency of wave V > 0.2ms.

Uses:

* To objectively find hearing threshold- wave-V appears 10dB above the hearing level obtained through PTA

* Best audiometric test for:

* Confirming hearing loss in infants

* Diagnosing acoustic neuroma

*

* Differentiating cochlear and retro-cochlear hearing loss

* Diagnosing non-organic hearing loss.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A medical student presented with complaints of repeated episodes lasting approximately 30 minutes, characterized by breathlessness, palpitations, sweating, hyperventilation, and a fear of an impending heart attack. The patient has experienced these episodes 5-6 times per month over the last 6 months, and investigations did not reveal any obvious abnormalities. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Panic Disorder

Panic attacks typically include palpitations, sweating, tremors, dyspnea, chest pain, dizziness, paresthesias, and fear of dying or losing control, usually peaking within minutes and resolving within about 20–30 minutes.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD): Characterized by persistent, excessive worry for ≥6 months, not sudden episodic attacks.
• Depression: Core features include low mood, anhedonia, sleep/appetite changes, not acute panic episodes.
• Social Phobia (Social Anxiety Disorder): Anxiety occurs specifically in social or performance situations, not spontaneous attacks.
questions.learning: Panic Disorder Panic attacks typically include palpitations, sweating, tremors, dyspnea, chest pain, dizziness, paresthesias, and fear of dying or losing control, usually peaking within minutes and resolving within about 20–30 minutes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with a known history of breast cancer has previously received Cobalt-60 radiotherapy. She now presents with respiratory distress, and chest imaging reveals haziness in the left lung. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of Cobalt-60 radiotherapy for breast cancer, combined with subsequent respiratory distress and localized lung haziness, points to radiation pneumonitis. This condition typically occurs 4–12 weeks post-radiotherapy as an inflammatory response to lung tissue damage. Recurrence of breast cancer (Option B) usually presents as distinct lung nodules or pleural effusion rather than diffuse, localized haziness. Pulmonary embolism (Option C) causes sudden chest pain but typically leaves the lung fields clear on standard X-rays. Infective pneumonia (Option D) presents with a productive cough and fever, whereas radiation pneumonitis causes non-infective inflammation specifically within the irradiated field. CT imaging of radiation pneumonitis often shows hazy ground-glass opacities or consolidation. Treatment primarily involves corticosteroids like prednisone and supportive care
questions.learning: The patient’s history of Cobalt-60 radiotherapy for breast cancer, combined with subsequent respiratory distress and localized lung haziness, points to radiation pneumonitis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Fluid leaving the proximal convoluted tubule in the absence of antidiuretic hormone is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Isotonic

Fluid leaving the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) in the absence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is isotonic.

The PCT is the site of maximum water reabsorption under normal physiological conditions. It reabsorbs around 60% of the filtered NaCl and water and other nutrients such as glucose and amino acids. Isosmotic reabsorption occurs in the PCT, so the amount of solute and water reabsorbed are coupled and proportional to each other. Here, sodium is reabsorbed along with the water. The large amounts of sodium and water reabsorption are essential in maintaining the ECF volume.

In addition to the isosmotic reabsorption, the water reabsorption in the PCT also occurs through aquaporin-1 which are active water channels. Reabsorption of sodium and water in PCT is not affected by ADH levels. Thus even in the absence of ADH, fluid is isotonic in PCT.
questions.learning: Isotonic Fluid leaving the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) in the absence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is isotonic. The PCT is the site of maximum water reabsorption under normal physiological conditions.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient with a history of kidney stone removal two years ago presents with fever and flank pain. Imaging reveals findings suggestive of residual stones or a retained foreign body. What is the most appropriate management approach for this patient?
options: Perform a Laparotomy to remove the stones
Undertake Cystoscopic retrieval of the foreign body
Opt to leave the foreign body inside
Utilize Lithotripsy to remove recurrent stones
questions.explanation: In a patient with a history of urological surgery who presents with fever and flank pain (potential signs of infection or obstruction), imaging showing a "retained foreign body" often refers to a forgotten or migrated double-J stent. Stents left in place for too long become encrusted with minerals, mimicking new kidney stones. The most suitable management approach is the Cystoscopic retrieval of the foreign body. This minimally invasive procedure allows for the visualization and removal of the stent or foreign object via the urethra. Laparotomy (Option A) is excessively invasive for standard retrieval. Leaving the body inside (Option C) would lead to worsening infection (pyelonephritis), stone formation, and eventual renal failure. Lithotripsy (Option D) is used to break up large stones but would not be the primary choice for removing a mechanical foreign object like a stent. Clinicians must meticulously track all stents placed and ensure they are removed within the recommended timeframe (usually 6-12 weeks) to avoid these common urological complications
questions.learning: In a patient with a history of urological surgery who presents with fever and flank pain (potential signs of infection or obstruction), imaging showing a "retained foreign body" often refers to a forgotten or migrated double-J stent.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about pegylated-filgrastim?
options: Duration of action is shorter than normal filgrastim
Added advantage is that it can be taken orally
It should not be administered in sickle cell patients
It is not effective in the treatment of severe neutropenia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It should not be administered in sickle cell patients

Patients with sickle cell anemia should not receive pegylated filgrastim as it can trigger a sickle cell crisis.

Filgrastim is a recombinant human G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor). The pegylated forms of filgrastim, pegfilgrastim, and lipefilgrastim, are longer-acting forms. It is administered subcutaneously or by slow intravenous infusion only.

Indications of recombinant G-CSF:

• Severe neutropenia after autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
• Severe neutropenia after high dose cancer chemotherapy
• Severe congenital neutropenias
• Neutropenia of patients with AIDS receiving zidovudine
questions.learning: It should not be administered in sickle cell patients Patients with sickle cell anemia should not receive pegylated filgrastim as it can trigger a sickle cell crisis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following culture media is used in the identification of Salmonella?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wilson and Blair medium

Wilson and Blair bismuth sulphite medium is used for the identification of Salmonella. It is a type of selective and indicator media.

Salmonella typhi reduces sulphite to sulphide in the presence of glucose and produces jet black colonies with a metallic sheen due to the production of H2S on Wilson and Blair bismuth sulphite medium. It is an example of indicator media. It is also a selective media because inhibiting substances are added to inhibit the growth of unwanted bacteria.

On the Wilson-Blair medium, S. paratyphi A produces green colonies due to the absence of H2S production.

On Deoxycholate citrate media and XLD (xylose lysine deoxycholate), colonies show blackheads due to H2S production.

Other options:

Option 1) PLET medium is used to isolate B. anthracis. It is a selective medium consisting of polymyxin, lysozyme, ethylene diamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA), and thallous acetate added to heart infusion agar.

Option 2) BCYE medium (Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar) is used to culture Legionella.

Option 4) Stuart Transport Medium is recommended for the preservation and transportation of Neisseria species and other fastidious organisms from the clinic to the laboratory.

The image below shows black colonies of Salmonella.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man is found to have a rectal mass on digital rectal examination, despite having no history of altered bowel habits. If rectal carcinoma is suspected, what is the most appropriate next step in the evaluation or management of this patient?
questions.explanation: In a patient with a rectal mass detected on digital rectal examination, the next step is to confirm the diagnosis and evaluate the entire colon. A full colonoscopy allows direct visualization of the rectal lesion and enables biopsy for histopathological confirmation, which is essential before planning treatment. Importantly, colonoscopy also helps detect synchronous lesions elsewhere in the colon, which are present in a small but significant number of patients with colorectal cancer. Although rigid sigmoidoscopy can visualize and biopsy a rectal lesion, it is limited to the distal bowel and may miss proximal pathology. Therefore, it is not sufficient as a complete evaluation. A CT scan of the abdomen is used for staging after diagnosis, not for initial confirmation. A barium enema is largely outdated and has been replaced by endoscopic techniques. Thus, the most appropriate next step is full colonoscopy with biopsy, as it provides both diagnostic confirmation and complete colonic assessment

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A person has recently traveled from Nigeria to the United States. Which vaccination is mandatory for international travel from Nigeria to the USA?
questions.explanation: Nigeria is classified as a Yellow Fever endemic zone. Under the WHO's International Health Regulations, travelers moving from endemic areas to other countries, including the USA, are required to present a valid international certificate of vaccination for Yellow Fever to prevent the global spread of the virus. The Yellow Fever (17D) vaccine is a live-attenuated viral vaccine given as a single subcutaneous dose, which provides life-long immunity. The certificate is valid starting 10 days after vaccination. The JE vaccine (Option B) is recommended for travel to rural Asia-Pacific regions, not for Nigeria–USA travel. Measles (Option C) and Rabies (Option D) vaccines are part of general public health or high-risk group immunization but are not mandatory regulatory requirements for international transit on this specific route

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is associated with the clinical condition shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malignant melanoma

The given image showing a black, heterogeneous, hairy palpable lesion in a child is suggestive of congenital melanocytic nevus. Malignant melanoma is more commonly associated with a congenital melanocytic nevus.

Congenital melanocytic nevi (CMN) are benign, pigmented, melanocytic nevi present at birth. They are most commonly brown, black, purplish, or red, usually a palpable lesion with heterogeneous color and texture. CMN often have thick hair at birth, which grows at a significantly greater rate than the surrounding scalp hair.

Congenital melanocytic nevi can be classified based on size: small (<1.5 cm), medium (1.5-19.9 cm), and large or giant (>20 cm). Larger CMN have a higher risk of developing malignant melanoma. Management of CMN depends on the size and location of the lesion. Smaller nevi may be observed, while larger nevi or those at a higher risk for complications may require surgical excision, particularly if there is a concern for malignant transformation. Complications of CMN include neurological abnormalities (intraparenchymal melanosis is the commonest finding), malignant melanoma, and other tumors like rhabdomyosarcoma.

The lifetime risk of malignant transformation in large or giant CMN ranges from 5% to 10%. Regular follow-up and monitoring for changes in size, color, or texture are essential for early detection of potential complications.

Note: More than 50% of patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome have glaucoma as an ocular complication. The image given below shows port-wine staining in a child with Sturge-Weber syndrome.
questions.learning: Malignant melanoma — The given image showing a black, heterogeneous, hairy palpable lesion in a child is suggestive of congenital melanocytic nevus. Malignant melanoma is more commonly associated with a congenital melanocytic nevus.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of local anesthetics?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Block sodium channels

Local anesthetics primarily act by blocking the sodium channels bound to the membrane.

Sodium channels have one larger α subunit and one or two smaller β subunits. These voltage-gated sodium channels exist in 3 states :

* Resting (non conducting)

* Open (conducting) and

* Inactivated (non conducting)

The local anesthetics bind to the α subunit of sodium channels, thereby preventing their activation and inhibiting the influx of sodium.

Local anesthetics have a higher affinity for the sodium channels in open and inactivated state than in the resting state.

Local anesthetic inhibition is both voltage and frequency-dependent and is higher when nerve fibers are firing rapidly than with slow, infrequent depolarizations.

Note:

Local anesthetics may also bind and inhibit calcium, potassium, transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and many other channels and receptors. But blocking of sodium channels is the best answer, of all the given options.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following hepatitis viruses is most commonly transmitted via the fecal–oral route?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis A Virus (HAV) and Hepatitis E Virus (HEV) are the two primary hepatotropic viruses transmitted through the fecal-oral route, often via contaminated food or water. HAV is a non-enveloped RNA virus that causes acute, self-limiting hepatitis and does not lead to chronic infection. In contrast, Hepatitis B (Option B), Hepatitis C (Option C), and Hepatitis D (Option D) are primarily transmitted through parenteral routes, such as contaminated needles, blood transfusions, or sexual contact. Hepatitis B is a DNA virus that can cause both acute and chronic liver disease. Hepatitis C is an RNA virus notorious for its high rate of chronicity and association with cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Hepatitis D is a "satellite virus" that requires concurrent Hepatitis B infection to replicate. Understanding the transmission dynamics is critical for public health interventions; while HAV and HEV are managed through improved sanitation and vaccination, the management of HBV, HCV, and HDV focuses on blood safety and antiviral therapy
questions.learning: Hepatitis — A Virus (HAV) and Hepatitis E Virus (HEV) are the two primary hepatotropic viruses transmitted through the fecal-oral route, often via contaminated food or water.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida at 39 weeks of gestation presents with good uterine contractions, normal vital signs, and a fetal heart rate of 150 bpm. On examination, the cervix is 6 cm dilated (6 hours after labor onset), the fetal head is at +2 station, and the membranes are absent. What is the appropriate management in this case?
options: Rupture of membranes and confirm cord prolapse
questions.explanation: This primigravida at 39 weeks of gestation is in the active phase of labor, with the cervix dilated to 6 cm after 6 hours of regular, good uterine contractions. The fetal heart rate is normal (150 bpm), maternal vitals are stable, and the fetal head is at +2 station, indicating good descent. The membranes are already absent, ruling out the need for artificial rupture. In a primigravida, labor progression is typically slower than in multiparous women, and the current cervical dilatation and descent are within normal limits for active labor. Since there is no evidence of fetal distress, uterine inertia, or arrest of labor, the appropriate management is expectant management with close observation. Emergency cesarean section (Option A) is not indicated in the absence of maternal or fetal compromise. Oxytocin augmentation (Option C) is unnecessary because uterine contractions are already adequate. Rupture of membranes (Option D) is inappropriate, as the membranes are already ruptured. Therefore, continued observation with routine monitoring of maternal vitals and fetal heart rate is the correct management to allow for a safe vaginal delivery
questions.learning: This primigravida at 39 weeks of gestation is in the active phase of labor, with the cervix dilated to 6 cm after 6 hours of regular, good uterine contractions.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby assessed 5 minutes after birth is found to be pink, with blue extremities, and irregular respiration. Heart rate is 80 beats per minute. There is grimace and some flexion. What is the Apgar score for this baby?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 5

The Apgar score for this baby will be 5.

• Color; body pink, extremities blue: score-1
• Heart rate; 80 beats per minute: score 1
• Grimace: Score-1
• Some flexion: Score-1
• Irregular respiration: Score-1

The Apgar score is a systematic way of assessing the infant after birth at 1 and 5 minutes of life. It gives a maximum score of 10 which indicates the newborn is in the best possible condition. Scores between 0-3 require immediate resuscitation.

Changes in the Apgar scores denote the response of the infant to resuscitation. If the score at 5 minutes remains less than 7, the infant should be assessed again every 5 minutes for the next 20 minutes.

Causes for false positive Apgar score are:

• Prematurity
• Drugs like analgesics, narcotics, sedatives, magnesium sulfate
• Acute cerebral trauma
• Precipitous delivery
• Airway obstruction (choanal atresia)
• Congenital pneumonia or sepsis
• Hemorrhage- hypovolemia

False-negative Apgar score is seen in maternal acidosis and high fetal catecholamine levels.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 23-year-old man wants to become a fighter pilot in the Indian Air Force. He is made to undergo tests for positive-G in a flight simulator. Which of the following physiological effects is not seen in this individual during exposure to positive-G?
options: Increased hydrostatic pressure in lower limb veins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased cerebral arterial pressure

Exposure to positive G-forces (+Gz) (e.g., during rapid upward acceleration in fighter aircraft) causes blood to shift toward the lower parts of the body due to gravity.

Physiological effects:

• Pooling of blood in lower limbs → increased hydrostatic pressure in leg veins.
• Reduced venous return to the heart → decreased cardiac output.
• Reduced cerebral perfusion → visual disturbances (grey-out/blackout) and possible loss of consciousness.

Therefore, cerebral arterial pressure decreases, not increases.
questions.learning: Increased cerebral arterial pressure Exposure to positive G-forces (+Gz) (e.g., during rapid upward acceleration in fighter aircraft) causes blood to shift toward the lower parts of the body due to gravity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: OCPs are not protective for?
questions.explanation: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs) are not protective against breast cancer and may actually be associated with a slight increase in risk (approximately 25%), especially in long-term users who started at a young age. However, this risk generally disappears within ten years of stopping the medication. In contrast, OCPs provide significant, well-documented protection against other malignancies. They reduce the risk of endometrial cancer (Option C) by over 30% and ovarian cancer (Option D) by 30–50% by suppressing ovulation and endometrial proliferation. There is also evidence that OCP use is protective against colorectal cancer (Option B), reducing the risk by roughly 15–20%. Cervical cancer risk may also be increased by OCPs, but breast cancer is the most classic "non-protected" malignancy listed. Therefore, while OCPs have significant non-contraceptive benefits, breast health requires separate screening protocols
questions.learning: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs) are not protective against breast cancer and may actually be associated with a slight increase in risk (approximately 25%), especially in long-term users who started at a young age.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are correctly matched?

1. Pre-contemplation phase - A person is thinking about commencing morning walks due to their increased health benefits.

2. Contemplation phase - A smoker is considering giving up his habit of smoking.

3. Maintenance phase - A person who quit smoking one year back and has abstained from smoking ever since

4. Action -  A person who is overweight says he can't do anything as his entire family is overweight
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Statement 2,3

True statements are:

• Contemplation phase - A smoker is considering giving up his habit of smoking. (Recognizes his problem and thinks about to bring about a change)
• Maintenance phase - A person who quit smoking one year back and has abstained from smoking ever since. (He has sustained his abstinence from smoking)

Motivation enhancement therapy (MET) is a systematic intervention approach for bringing about change in the addictive behaviour seen in people with substance use disorders. It is based on the principle of motivational psychology and aims to enable the patient to deal with his addiction by producing internally motivated change.

Addictive behaviors do not change abruptly, and go through gradual stages. The stages of motivation enhancement therapy (MET) include:

Precontemplation - individuals in this stage are often unaware that their behaviour (eg. alcohol abuse) is problematic or is producing negative consequences.

Contemplation - individuals in this stage recognize their problems and begin to think about changing their behaviour. They weigh the pros and cons of change. They may still feel ambivalent about changing their behaviour.

Preparation or determination - individuals in this stage make decisions to change their habits and are ready to take action. They start to take small steps toward behaviour change.

Action - individuals in this stage change their behaviour and intend to keep moving forward with this change in behaviour

Maintenance - individuals in this stage sustain their change in behaviour for a while and intend to maintain this change going forward. People work to prevent relapse to earlier stages.

Other statements:

Statement 1: This statement is false as people in the pre-contemplation stage are unaware that their behaviour is problematic.

Statement 4: This statement is also false as people in the action stage make strides to change their behaviour.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Examine the radiograph of the foot and identify the bone marked by the arrow.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Navicular

The navicular is a boat-shaped tarsal bone located on the medial side of the foot, between the talus proximally and the three cuneiforms distally.

It is a key component of the medial longitudinal arch and is prone to stress fractures, especially in athletes.

Cuboid lies laterally, while cuneiforms are distal to the navicular and smaller in size.
questions.learning: Navicular — The navicular is a boat-shaped tarsal bone located on the medial side of the foot, between the talus proximally and the three cuneiforms distally.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Chvostek's sign is seen in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypocalcemia

The Chvostek's sign is seen in hypocalcemia.

Chvostek's sign is a clinical indicator of hypocalcemia, seen in conditions like hypoparathyroidism and vitamin D deficiency. It is elicited by gently tapping the facial nerve just anterior to the ear, which triggers involuntary twitching of the facial muscles, particularly around the mouth and eye.

While a positive Chvostek's sign suggests neuromuscular excitability due to low calcium levels, it is not always specific, as mild twitching can also occur in healthy individuals. This sign is often assessed alongside Trousseau's sign to confirm hypocalcemia. Trousseau’s sign indicates hypocalcemia and is demonstrated by inflating a blood pressure cuff above the systolic level for 180 seconds. This causes an involuntary carpal spasm, resulting in contraction of the hand and fingers. It signifies increased neuromuscular excitability due to low calcium levels.

Symptoms and signs of hypocalcemia include:

* laryngeal spasms

* mild digital circumoral numbness

* cardiac arrhythmias

* paresthesia

* Chvostek's sign and Trousseau's sign, as shown in the images below.
questions.learning: Hypocalcemia — The Chvostek's sign is seen in hypocalcemia. Chvostek's sign is a clinical indicator of hypocalcemia, seen in conditions like hypoparathyroidism and vitamin D deficiency.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 75-year-old female presented with urinary incontinence. She also has cognition decline and dementia. Which of the following drugs is useful for treating urinary incontinence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tolterodine

For managing urinary incontinence in a 75-year-old female with cognitive decline and dementia, tolterodine is useful.

Tolterodine is a muscarinic receptor antagonist specifically effective for treating urinary incontinence. It exhibits selectivity for the urinary bladder, which helps to minimize side effects compared to other antimuscarinic agents. This selectivity is beneficial for patients with cognitive decline or dementia, as it reduces the risk of adverse effects. Tolterodine is metabolized by CYP2D6, so its dosage may need adjustment based on individual CYP2D6 activity, making it a suitable option for managing urinary incontinence while minimizing potential side effects.

Other muscarinic antagonists for urinary incontinence include oxybutynin, trospium chloride, darifenacin, solifenacin, and fesoterodine. Oxybutynin, though effective, often causes antimuscarinic side effects such as xerostomia. Trospium chloride, being a quaternary amine, is better tolerated and excreted primarily via the kidneys, requiring dosage adjustments in renal impairment. Darifenacin and solifenacin have selectivity for M3 receptors, which helps balance efficacy and side effects, while fesoterodine, a prodrug, provides a stable pharmacokinetic profile due to its conversion to tolterodine’s active metabolite.

Other Options:

Option A: Tiotropium and Option C: Ipratropium are muscarinic antagonists used primarily for respiratory conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma, rather than urinary incontinence. Tiotropium is a long-acting agent with selectivity for M1 and M3 receptors, while Ipratropium is used more frequently for its short-acting effects.

Option D: Telenzepine, an analogue of Pirenzepine, displays higher potency and selectivity for M1 receptors compared to pirenzepine and is used in treating acid-peptic disease, not urinary incontinence.
questions.learning: Tolterodine For managing urinary incontinence in a 75-year-old female with cognitive decline and dementia, tolterodine is useful. Tolterodine is a muscarinic receptor antagonist specifically effective for treating urinary incontinence.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old asymptomatic woman undergoes routine ultrasonography, which reveals a 6 cm unilocular ovarian cyst. Her tumor markers and other serological investigations are within normal limits. What is the most appropriate approach to management?
options: Follow-up after 1-2 cycles of Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs)
questions.explanation: In a 35-year-old asymptomatic woman with a 6 cm unilocular ovarian cyst and normal tumor markers, the most appropriate management is watchful waiting with follow-up CA-125 monitoring. Since all tumor markers are normal and the cyst is unilocular with no suspicious features, immediate surgery is not warranted. Serial CA-125 monitoring along with repeat ultrasonography after 3 months is the recommended conservative approach to assess for resolution or change in characteristics. Why other options are wrong: (A) Laparotomy is incorrect because laparotomy is reserved for suspicious, complex, or malignant ovarian masses. An asymptomatic unilocular cyst with normal markers does not justify major surgery. (B) Follow-up with OCPs is incorrect because OCPs are useful for functional cysts which are typically smaller (<5 cm). A 6 cm cyst in a 35-year-old warrants monitoring with tumor markers rather than OCP suppression therapy alone. (C) Ovariotomy is incorrect because surgical removal of the ovary is not indicated as first-line management for a simple unilocular cyst with normal tumor markers in a premenopausal woman
questions.learning: In a 35-year-old asymptomatic woman with a 6 cm unilocular ovarian cyst and normal tumor markers, the most appropriate management is watchful waiting with follow-up CA-125 monitoring.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 70-year-old man with a BP of 170/100mmHg. What is the reason for the increased pulse pressure in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased arterial compliance

Pulse pressure increases with age due to decreased arterial wall compliance.

Diastolic blood pressure falls after 60 years of age due to increased arterial stiffness and decreased compliance, often associated with arteriosclerosis. As the left ventricle contracts against stiffer, less compliant arteries, systolic blood pressure also increases.

As a result of these two changes, pulse pressure increases (↑PP = ↑SBP - ↓DBP)

The factors that affect the pulse pressure:

• the stroke volume output of the heart
• the compliance or total distensibility of the arterial walls
• the character of ejection from the heart during systole (less important)

Pulse pressure = Stroke volume/ arterial compliance

Widened pulse pressure (> 40 mm Hg) occurs with several diseases such as:

• Aortic regurgitation
• Aortic sclerosis
• Severe iron deficiency anaemia
• Arteriosclerosis
• Hyperthyroidism

In the majority of these cases, systolic pressures increase while diastolic pressures remain near normal.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient develops a broad QRS complex tachycardia following a myocardial infarction. His blood pressure is 120/85 mm Hg, and the ECG findings are provided. What is the most appropriate management in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with a broad QRS complex (>120 ms), regular, monomorphic tachycardia following an MI, which is diagnostic of sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT). With a blood pressure of 120/85 mm Hg, the patient is hemodynamically stable. According to ACLS guidelines, the first-line pharmacological treatment for stable VT is IV amiodarone. Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic that suppresses ventricular ectopy and is safe in structural heart disease. Labetalol (Option B) is an antihypertensive and has no role in acute VT termination. Metoprolol (Option C), while used post-MI for prevention, is not the primary choice for terminating an active VT episode and carries a risk of hypotension. Nitroglycerin (Option D) is used for ischemic chest pain but does not treat the underlying arrhythmia. Therefore, IV amiodarone is the most appropriate intervention for this stable, post-MI tachycardia
questions.learning: The patient presents with a broad QRS complex (>120 ms), regular, monomorphic tachycardia following an MI, which is diagnostic of sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the National Health Mission (NHM), the RMNCH+A strategy has been formulated to provide quality health care to various vulnerable age groups. Which of the following is a component of the RMNCH+A strategy? 1. Adolescent health 2. Family planning 3. Geriatric health 4. Maternal health 5. Infant Health
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 4, 5

RMNCH+A stands for Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health, covering the life-cycle approach from adolescence through childhood, including family planning. The “+” represents linkages with other health services like family planning, nutrition, gender issues & universal immunization. The strategy was introduced to provide continuum of care from adolescence → pregnancy → childbirth → childhood.

Geriatric health is not part of RMNCH+A; hence the included components are adolescent health, family planning, maternal health, and infant/child health.

Major Programs Under RMNCH+A-
questions.learning: 1, 2, 4, 5 RMNCH+A stands for Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health, covering the life-cycle approach from adolescence through childhood, including family planning.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure done in the given image.
options: Bilateral Orchidectomy with bilateral inguinal node dissection
Total penectomy with inguinal node dissection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Total penectomy with inguinal node dissection

The given post-operative image suggests that this patient underwent Total penectomy with inguinal lymph node dissection.

Total penectomy is done in cases of penile carcinoma if the stump is < 2cm after resection of the tumour and partial penectomy is done if the stump is >2cm. Carcinoma of the penis is commonly a squamous cell carcinoma. It arises from the skin of the glans penis or the prepuce. The lesion can be flat or warty in appearance.

The first lymph node to be involved is the superficial inguinal lymph node and thus, superficial inguinal lymph node dissection or sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) helps evaluate the spread of penile cancer.

Tumours of low-grade and low-stage are managed by Mohs’ surgery. Tumors involving the glans penis require glansectomy, and in advanced cases require partial penectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Testis is visible in the given image, therefore it is unlikely to be a specimen of Bilateral Orchidectomy with bilateral inguinal node dissection.

Option B: Hernia repair would be done higher up at the inguinal region.

Option C: SLNB will be done through a smaller incision.
questions.learning: Total penectomy with inguinal node dissection — The given post-operative image suggests that this patient underwent Total penectomy with inguinal lymph node dissection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male patient presents with erectile dysfunction and bilateral leg pain that worsens with rest. The patient reports a history of smoking and high blood pressure. Physical examination reveals reduced sensation in both legs and weak pulses in the feet. Identify the location of the lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aortoiliac bifurcation

Erectile dysfunction + bilateral claudication + absent pulses → Leriche syndrome, caused by occlusion at the aortoiliac bifurcation. Peripheral distal artery disease does not explain impotence.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All are normal physiological changes in pregnancy except? (NEET PG 2019)
options: Mild ST changes in inferior leads
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pansystolic murmur

A pansystolic murmur is not a normal finding in pregnancy. It suggests pathological regurgitation — mitral, tricuspid, or a ventricular septal defect — and warrants full cardiac evaluation.

Why the other three are normal:

A. Left axis deviation — as the uterus enlarges, the diaphragm is pushed upward, mechanically displacing the heart to the left and superiorly. This produces an average \~15° left axis shift on ECG, which is entirely physiological.

B. Mild ST changes in inferior leads — the same diaphragmatic elevation alters the heart's positional relationship to the chest wall, producing mild non-specific ST and T-wave changes in the inferior leads. These are positional, not ischaemic.

C. Atrial and ventricular premature contractions — the hyperdynamic circulation, increased sympathetic tone, and expanded plasma volume of pregnancy make ectopic beats relatively common and generally benign in structurally normal hearts.

Normal cardiovascular findings in pregnancy — quick reference:

| System | Normal finding | Mechanism

| ------ | -------------- | ---------

| Murmurs | Ejection systolic (aortic/pulmonary areas) | Increased cardiac output → flow murmur

| Murmurs | Mammary soufflé (2nd–4th ICS, continuous) | Increased breast blood flow

| Murmurs | Venous hum | Increased venous return

| Heart sounds | Loud, widely split S1 | Increased flow + hyperdynamic state

| Heart sounds | Increased P2, split S2 | Increased pulmonary flow

| Apex beat | Shifted to 4th ICS, 2.5 cm lateral to MCL | Diaphragmatic elevation displacing heart

| ECG | \~15° left axis deviation | Diaphragm elevation

| ECG | Mild inferior ST/T changes | Positional cardiac shift

| ECG | Atrial/ventricular ectopics | Hyperdynamic circulation

| ECG | T-wave inversion, bi-atrial enlargement | Volume overload physiology

| Echo | Increased LV mass, increased LA end-diastolic dimension | Volume overload

| Echo | Trivial tricuspid regurgitation | Annular dilatation from volume load
questions.learning: Pansystolic murmur — A pansystolic murmur is not a normal finding in pregnancy. It suggests pathological regurgitation — mitral, tricuspid, or a ventricular septal defect — and warrants full cardiac evaluation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 33-year-old female patient comes with complaints of menorrhagia for the past 3 months. The duration and regularity of her menstrual cycles are normal. Non-hormonal management has been tried without success. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hormonal therapy

Hormonal therapy is the next best step in the given scenario of menorrhagia that is unresponsive to non-hormonal therapy.

Menorrhagia/heavy menstrual bleeding is defined as heavy but regular menstrual bleeding, >80mL of blood loss, or >8 days of bleeding per menstrual period. It can be acute (<6 months) or chronic (>6 months).

It is managed as follows:

• Medical - first line of treatment.

• NSAIDs
• Tranexamic acid
• OCPs/progestogens - if non-hormonal management fails
• Mirena IUCD
• GnRH agonists
• Blood transfusion, if required

• Surgical - if medical management fails, depending on the diagnosis:

• Endometrial ablation - hysteroscopic, TCRE, RITEA, microwave, NovaSure, etc (option B)
• Uterine artery embolization (option A)
• Uterine tamponade
• Hysterectomy - if all minimally invasive methods fail (option D)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
What is the repair mechanism associated with CRISPR-Cas9?

CRISPR- Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Non-homologous end joining

The repair mechanism associated with CRISPR-Cas9 is non-homologous end-joining.

Non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) is a mechanism by which a group of proteins mediates the recognition, processing, and direct ligation of the ends of two DNA fragments where a double-strand break in DNA has occurred. This is in contrast to homologous recombination (HR), another mechanism to repair a double-strand break, where DNA repair needs an undamaged homologous DNA template to replace an adjacent damaged one.

Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats-associated gene 9 or CRISPR-Cas9 is a DNA editing/gene regulatory system. It involves two essential components, Cas9, an endonuclease that causes a double-stranded DNA break, allowing modifications to the genomic DNA to be made; and a synthetic single guide RNA or sgRNA responsible for guiding Cas9 to its target.

Once the sgRNA has directed the Cas9 to the section of the genomic DNA to be edited, the 3’ end of the sgRNA comes to lie across a specific sequence of DNA adjacent to the editing side called the protospacer adjacent motif or PAM. The Cas9 now causes a double-stranded break in the DNA at the PAM site which is then repaired by a non-homologous end-joining.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A pregnant couple presented to the OPD with concerns about thalassemia in their baby due to a positive family history. Genetic studies revealed that both she and her husband are carriers. What is the probability that the child will have thalassemia major?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 25%

There is 25% probability that their child will have thalassemia major.

β-thalassemia occurs due to mutations causing an impaired synthesis of β-globin chains of hemoglobin (Hb), leading to anemia, hypoxia, and hemolysis. The mutations can be of two types:

* Absent β chain synthesis (β0)

* Reduced β chain synthesis (β+)

Being an autosomal recessive disease, disease occurs only when both alleles are defective. When only one is defective, they are called carriers or trait. Here as both the parents are carriers, their alleles will be β/β0 or β/β+ (1 β-thalassemia allele and 1 normal allele). As the clinical disease doesn't alter much based on it being β+ or β0, its safe to use use β+ to represent a thalassemia allele.

Thalassemia major means both alleles are mutated. And from the table, that can occur in one of the four ways possible. Hence the answer is 25%

Clinical syndromes of β-thalassemia depending on the genetic defect:

Major:

* Severe microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells, basophilic stippling, and fragmented red cells (typical Hb: 3 to 6 g/dL), requiring regular blood transfusions

* Crewcut appearance of facial bones and skull (due to cortical bone erosion by expanding marrow and new bone formation)

* Speen, liver, and lymph node enlargement (due to extramedullary hematopoiesis)

Minor:

* More common

* Usually asymptomatic

* Mild microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells and basophilic stippling (important to rule out iron deficiency anemia by serum iron studies)

* Mild erythroid hyperplasia in bone marrow

Other features:

A third clinical syndrome of moderate severity is called β-thalassemia intermedia. The genotype in this type includes milder variants of β+/β+ or β0/β+ and does not require regular transfusions.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A deceased male was posted for a post-mortem examination. His relatives reported that he had a tattoo over his skin, which was not found during the autopsy. Which of the following would you examine to determine the absence of his tattoo?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lymph nodes

The lymph nodes should be examined in this case.

Some amount of material or dye used for creating tattoo marks is transported through lymph to the regional lymph nodes.

A faded tattoo mark can be visualized by:

* Ultraviolet light

* Infrared photography

* Rubbing the part and examining it with a magnifying lens

In decomposed bodies, the tattoo marks can be visualized by removing the epidermis with a moist cloth. The lymph nodes near a tattoo mark also show a deposit of the pigment.

Hence in cases where a tattoo mark has disappeared naturally or has been removed, the lymph nodes must be examined before making any conclusions.
questions.learning: Lymph nodes — The lymph nodes should be examined in this case. Some amount of material or dye used for creating tattoo marks is transported through lymph to the regional lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not an advantage of USG over Mammography?
options: Can be used for screening mammographically undetectable clinically non palpable breast mass
Useful in young females with dense breast
Differentiates between solid and Cystic lesions in the Breast
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Can be used for screening mammographically undetectable clinically non palpable breast mass

USG cannot be used for screening mammographically undetectable clinically nonpalpable breast mass. Although ultrasound has its advantages in certain scenarios, mammography remains the primary screening tool for breast tumor detection.

Mammography is complementary to physical examination and can detect clinically non-palpable breast mass. The primary purpose of mammography is to detect small breast tumors. While mammography is typically the initial screening tool for breast cancer detection, there are specific scenarios where ultrasound may be preferred or used in conjunction with mammography. Advantages of USG over mammography include:

• USG is preferred in pregnant women, lactating women, and young women since breast tissue is dense (Option B) in these populations.
• USG can differentiate between solid and cystic lesions (Option C) of the breast and is able to detect abnormal axillary lymph nodes.
• Ultrasound can assist in guided breast biopsy (Option D) procedures.
questions.learning: Can be used for screening mammographically undetectable clinically non palpable breast mass USG cannot be used for screening mammographically undetectable clinically nonpalpable breast mass.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child is diagnosed with von Willebrand disease. To understand the disorder, it is important to know the function of von Willebrand factor (vWF). With which molecule does von Willebrand factor primarily combine?
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand factor (vWF) is a multi-functional glycoprotein essential for normal hemostasis. Its primary role in platelet adhesion is to act as a bridge between the subendothelial collagen of a damaged vessel wall and platelets. It achieves this by binding specifically to the Glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) receptor on the platelet membrane. This interaction allows platelets to adhere to the injury site even under conditions of high shear stress. Regarding the distractors, Platelet factor 3 (Option B) is a phospholipid surface that facilitates coagulation but does not bind vWF. ADP (Option C) is an agonist released by platelets to promote aggregation, not adhesion. Prothrombin (Option D) is a precursor to thrombin in the coagulation cascade and has no direct interaction with vWF. Thus, GpIb is the specific platelet receptor associated with vWF function
questions.learning: Von Willebrand factor (vWF) is a multi-functional glycoprotein essential for normal hemostasis. Its primary role in platelet adhesion is to act as a bridge between the subendothelial collagen of a damaged vessel wall and platelets.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman who recently received a kidney transplant 2 months ago develops a high fever and severe dyspnea with a dry hacking cough. Chest x-ray reveals bilateral interstitial infiltrates that are diffuse and urine examination shows 'owl-eye' appearance of cells. Which of the following agents is most likely responsible for her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cytomegalovirus

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is an important cause of morbidity and mortality after allogeneic transplant. Interstitial pneumonia (IP) is the most common manifestation of CMV, in transplant recipients.

The predominant pathogen to infect the renal transplant recipients in the period around 1 to 4 months following the transplantation is cytomegalovirus (CMV).The most common CMV presentation in kidney transplant patients is fever (most common), leukopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, myalgia, and arthralgia.

CMV infection in immunocompromised hosts:

The infection is contained by host immune response where virus remains latent in leukocytes. Then reactivates when host becomes immunocompromised, and may cause:

* Retinitis (especially in AIDS patients)

* Pneumonia (especially in transplant patients)

* Esophagitis

Diagnosis:

* Giant cells with “owl’s eye” intranuclear inclusionbodies found in tissues/urine

* Serology (negative monospot test as compared to EBV mononucleosis)

* Detection in buffy coat culture (CMV infects WBCs)

Other options:

* Option a: Adenovirus is associated with conjunctivitis and acute respiratory disease in military recruits, among other diseases.

* Option c: Although influenza can cause pneumonia, there is no mention of season, and CMV is still the most common cause in transplant patients.

* Option d: Respiratory syncytial virus is usually seen in children (especially premature infants).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which among the following is associated with Cryoglobulinemia?
questions.explanation: Cryoglobulinemia refers to the presence of abnormal proteins in the blood that thicken and clump together in cold temperatures. It is most strongly associated with chronic Hepatitis C infection, which accounts for approximately 80-90% of cases of mixed cryoglobulinemia. The virus triggers a chronic immune response leading to the production of monoclonal or polyclonal immunoglobulins that form immune complexes. These complexes can cause vasculitis, leading to symptoms such as purpura, arthralgia, and weakness (Meltzer's triad). While certain hematological malignancies like B-cell Leukemia (Option D) or lymphoma can cause Type I cryoglobulinemia, Hepatitis C is the classic and most frequent association in clinical exams. Ovarian cancer (Option B) and Diabetes (Option C) are not standard associations for this condition. Treatment primarily focuses on managing the underlying viral infection, often with direct-acting antivirals, to reduce the stimulus for cryoglobulin production
