questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with itchy, flat- topped, polygonal, violaceous papules on the inner wrists and flexor surfaces of the forearms. The lesions have a shiny surface and appear in a linear arrangement. There is no history of recent medication use. What is the appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of itchy, flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules on the flexor surfaces of the wrists is pathognomonic for Lichen Planus. These lesions often display a characteristic shiny surface known as Wickham striae and can demonstrate the Koebner phenomenon, where lesions appear in a linear pattern along sites of trauma. The first-line treatment for localized Lichen Planus is topical steroids, which work by reducing the T-cell mediated inflammatory response at the dermo-epidermal junction. Antibiotics (Option B), immunosuppressants (Option C), and anti-fungals (Option D) are not the primary treatments for this autoimmune condition. While systemic steroids or other immunosuppressants may be used for widespread or recalcitrant disease, topical therapy remains the standard of care for initial management. Clinicians should also screen these patients for Hepatitis C infection, which has a documented association with Lichen Planus
questions.learning: The clinical description of itchy, flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules on the flexor surfaces of the wrists is pathognomonic for Lichen Planus.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man with no prior medical history presents with abdominal pain at an airport. An X-ray reveals an abnormal internal finding, and he is found to be carrying laxatives and an enema device. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The scenario—a healthy young man at an airport with sudden abdominal pain and an X-ray showing multiple uniform internal foreign bodies—is the classic presentation of Body Packer Syndrome. Body packers ingest wrapped packets of illicit drugs (usually cocaine or heroin) for international transport. The laxatives and enema apparatus are carried to facilitate the expulsion of these packets once they reach their destination. Bezoar syndrome (Option A) involves an accumulation of indigestible material like hair or fiber over time. Pica (Option B) is the ingestion of non-food items like clay or ice. Fecaliths (Option D) are hardened stool causing constipation. In body packing, the primary danger is the rupture of a packet, leading to massive, life-threatening drug toxicity. Treatment involves watchful waiting if the patient is asymptomatic or emergency surgery if packet rupture or intestinal obstruction occurs. Given the "airport" context, Body Packer Syndrome is the definitive forensic and clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: The scenario—a healthy young man at an airport with sudden abdominal pain and an X-ray showing multiple uniform internal foreign bodies—is the classic presentation of Body Packer Syndrome.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient complaining of vertigo without hearing loss has consulted an ENT surgeon. The surgeon performs a diagnostic maneuver and cautiously performs a therapeutic maneuver. What is the diagnostic maneuver?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dix-Hallpike maneuver

The given clinical scenario of a patient with vertigo without hearing loss is suggestive of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). The diagnostic maneuver used in BPPV is the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, the gold standard for diagnosing BPPV. The therapeutic maneuver is Epley's maneuver.

BPPV is characterized by vertigo, recurrent brief (<1 minute) episodes triggered by specific head movements, and is not associated with hearing loss or other neurological symptoms.

It is thought to be caused by the dislodgement of crystals of calcium carbonate from the degenerating macula of the utricle. When this crystal settles on the cupula of the posterior canal, it causes displacement of the cupula and vertigo.

A patient presenting with vertigo should be evaluated for ruling out the central lesions (like a tumor in the fourth ventricle, cerebellum, temporal lobe, or multiple sclerosis) before confirming the diagnosis of BPPV. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver helps to differentiate a peripheral from a central lesion.

Dix-Hallpike maneuver: The maneuver starts with the patient in a sitting position. Their head is turned 45 degrees towards the ear to be tested. Then the examiner quickly brings the patient to a supine position with their head 30 degrees below the horizontal. The 45-degree head rotation is maintained during the procedure. Now the examiner observes the patient for nystagmus.

The features of nystagmus differentiate between BPPV and central lesions:

The therapeutic maneuver is the Epley maneuver which displaces the otolith out of the posterior canal. This ends the sensation of vertigo with positional changes relieving the symptoms.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with a phobic disorder. Which of the following defense mechanisms is likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Displacement

Displacement is the defense mechanism in phobias. It is the shifting of emotions about one object/individual onto another object/individual.

Pearl PF0613: Defense mechanisms that operate in various diseases

* OCD - reaction formation, undoing

* Phobia - displacement

* Neurosis - repression

* Grief - denial

* Borderline personality - Splitting

* Schizophrenia - projection

* Enuresis - Regression

Pearl PF0612: Defense mechanisms

Narcissistic-psychotic defenses

Denial: Used to avoid becoming aware of some painful aspects of reality.

• Eg: I know I do not have cancer.

Distortion: Grossly reshaping the experience of external reality to suit inner needs.

• Eg: I possess special powers and abilities and am superior to others.

Projection (psychotic): Attributing your own wishes, thoughts, or feelings onto someone else.

• Eg: I’m sure my wife is cheating on me.

Splitting: External objects are divided into all good or all bad.

• Eg: The morning staff is perfect, the evening staff is terrible.

Immature defenses

Acting out: Behavioral or emotional outburst.

• Eg: My 10-year-old started getting into trouble right after his mother and I got divorced.

Blocking: Temporary block in thinking.

• Eg: I have known him for years but can never seem to remember his name.

Hypochondriasis: A defense style in which people say that no one understands their pain.

• Eg: No one understands the depth of my pain.

Introjection: Features of the external world are taken and made part of the self.

• Eg: The resident physician dresses like the attending whom he admires.

Passive-aggressive behavior: Aggressive intent is cloaked by a passive method.

• Eg: Procrastinating at work for not getting the promotion.

Projection (non-psychotic): Unwanted feelings are displaced onto another person.

• Eg: A man who has been unfaithful to his wife but accuses his wife of cheating on him.

Regression: Return to an earlier stage of development, most immature.

• Eg: Ever since my divorce, my 5-year-old has begun to wet the bed.

Schizoid fantasy: Tendency to retreat into fantasy in order to resolve inner and outer conflicts.

• Eg: Adolescents day dreaming on pornographic materials.

Somatization: Psychic derivatives are converted into bodily symptoms.

• Eg: Just thinking of the exam I get butterflies in my stomach.

Neurotic defenses

Externalization: Perceiving one’s personality, impulses, moods and attitudes in the external world.

• Eg: An argumentative person perceives the doctor as argumentative whilst believing himself to be blameless.

Displacement: Shifting emotions about one object/ individual onto another object/ individual.

• Eg: Getting angry at your parents because you had a bad day at work.

Inhibition: conscious or unconscious constraint of a process or behavior.

• Eg: A desire to eat dessert versus the desire to lose weight.

Intellectualization: Excessive use of intellectual processes to avoid affective expression or experience.

• Eg: It is interesting to note the specific skin lesions which seem to arise as a consequence of my end-stage disease.

Isolation: Separation of an idea from the affect that accompanies it.

• Eg: As she arrived at the station to identify the body, she appeared to show no emotion.

Rationalization: Rational explanations are used to justify unacceptable attitudes, beliefs, or behaviors.

• Eg: I did not pass the test because it was harder this year than ever before.

Reaction formation: An unacceptable impulse is transformed into its opposite; results in the formation of character traits.

• Eg: Listen to him tell his family he was not afraid when I saw him crying.

Repression: An idea or feeling is withheld from consciousness; unconscious forgetting.

• Eg: I do not remember having had a dog.

Sexualization: Endowing an object or function with sexual significance.

Undoing: Acting out the reverse of unacceptable behavior; consists of an act.

• Eg: I need to wash my hands whenever I have these thoughts.

Retroflexion: Self-destruction due to rage.

• Eg: A person cutting his wrist because he is angry with himself.

Mature defenses

Altruism: Getting pleasure from giving to others what the individual would have liked to receive.

• Eg:  A former alcoholic funding a rehabilitation center.

Anticipation: Realistically planning or anticipating future inner discomfort.

• Eg: Moderate amount of anxiety before surgery.

Asceticism: Gratification derived from renunciation.

Humor: Permits the expression of feelings and thoughts without personal discomfort.

• Eg: Before execution, firing squad leader offers the man a cigarette. He replies "no thanks I'm trying to quit".

Sublimation: Impulse gratification has been achieved, but the aim or object has been changed from unacceptable to acceptable; allows instincts to be channeled. Most mature of the defenses.

• Eg: Jack the Ripper becomes a surgeon.

Suppression: Conscious forgetting. The only conscious defense mechanism.

• Eg: I would rather talk about my operation after the party is over.
questions.learning: Displacement Displacement is the defense mechanism in phobias. It is the shifting of emotions about one object/individual onto another object/individual.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Sodium benzoate is given for urea cycle defects for scavenging ammonia. Which amino acid donates amino group to the scavengers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycine

In urea cycle disorders, toxic ammonia accumulates because the body cannot efficiently convert ammonia to urea. Nitrogen scavenger drugs such as sodium benzoate are used to remove excess nitrogen through alternative metabolic pathways.

Mechanism of Sodium Benzoate:

• Sodium benzoate conjugates with glycine in the liver.
• This reaction forms hippuric acid (benzoylglycine).
• Hippuric acid is then excreted in urine, removing one nitrogen atom from the body.

| Drug | Amino acid used | Product excreted

| ---- | --------------- | ----------------

| Sodium benzoate | Glycine | Hippurate

| Sodium phenylacetate / phenylbutyrate | Glutamine | Phenylacetylglutamine

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Contraceptive failure is assessed using which of the following methods?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pearl index

Pearl index is the common method used to measure contraceptive failure rate.

It is defined as the number of failures per 100 woman-years of exposure (HWY). This rate is given by the formula:

Pearl index = Total accidental pregnancies x 1200/Total months of exposure

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the structure marked in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Buccopharyngeal Fascia

The structure marked in the given image is the buccopharyngeal fascia.

The structures forming the tonsillar bed from within outward are

* Pharyngobasilar Fascia (number 10- option A)

* Superior Constrictor

* Buccopharyngeal Fascia (number 11)

* Styloglossus

* Glossopharyngeal Nerve

* Facial Artery

In a retropharyngeal abscess, the pus collects between the buccopharyngeal fascia and the prevertebral fascia.

An acute retropharyngeal abscess commonly occurs in children below 3 years of age due to infections of adenoids or tonsils that cause suppuration in the retropharyngeal lymph nodes and lead to abscess formation. Since the retropharyngeal lymph nodes disappear after this age, an adult retropharyngeal abscess is uncommon and usually occurs secondary to trauma.

Other options:

Option B: Danger space in neck: The danger space or alar space is the space that is present between the alar fascia and the prevertebral fascia.

Option C:  Prevertebral fascia - It forms the floor of the posterior triangle and the axillary sheath. Inferiorly, it blends with the anterior longitudinal ligament.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-month-old male infant is found to have an empty scrotum on clinical examination. Ultrasonography reveals the right testis located in the right inguinal canal, while the left testis is positioned in the perineal region. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Right-side undescended testis and left-sided ectopic testis
Right side ectopic testis and left side undescended testis
questions.explanation: The terminology for abnormal testicular positions depends on whether the testis followed the normal path of descent. An "undescended testis" (cryptorchidism) is one that stopped somewhere along the normal anatomical path of descent (abdominal, inguinal, or high scrotal). Since the right testis is in the inguinal canal, it is an undescended testis. An "ectopic testis" is one that has strayed from the normal path of descent and is found in an abnormal location, such as the perineum, femoral canal, or superficial inguinal pouch. Since the left testis is in the perineum, it is classified as ectopic. Therefore, Option C is the correct diagnosis. Options A and B are incorrect because the locations of the two testes represent different pathological entities. Surgical management (orchidopexy) is usually recommended around 6–12 months of age to maximize fertility potential and reduce the risk of malignancy, though ectopic testes always require surgical repositioning as they will never descend spontaneously

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with symptoms of peripheral neuropathy and macrocytic anemia. She was given folate 5mg and the blood picture improved. However, the neurologic manifestations were aggravated. What is the most likely cause?
options: Treatment with folate unmasking pyridoxine deficiency
Deficiency of folate reductase in CNS
Folate therapy using the B12 stores
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Folate therapy using the B12 stores

The most likely cause is folate therapy which used up the B12 stores, aggravating the symptoms.

Administration of folic acid for patients with macrocytic anemia can partially reverse the hematologic abnormalities associated with vitamin B12 deficiency. However, the neurologic manifestations of vitamin B12 deficiency are not treated by folic acid.

Administration of folic acid to an individual with vitamin B12 deficiency can potentially mask untreated vitamin B12 deficiency or even worsen the neurologic complications. Hence, testing for and/or treatment of vitamin B12 deficiency is required in all patients being treated with folic acid.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man was admitted to the emergency ward with severe, sudden-onset chest pain radiating to the left arm and profuse sweating. ECG showed ST-segment elevation in precordial leads. The person succumbed after 3 hours. During the autopsy, his heart was taken out and immersed in a solution. The normal area of the heart turned brick red whereas the infarcted portion turned white. Which of the following can be the likely component of the solution?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride

Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride stain imparts a brick red color to the intact non-infarcted myocardium whereas the infarcted portion appears white.

* Myocardial infarcts less than 12 hours old are usually not apparent on gross examination. However, if the infarct preceded death by 2 to 3 hours, it is possible to highlight the area of necrosis by immersion of tissue slices in a solution of triphenyl tetrazolium chloride.

* This gross histochemical stain imparts a brick-red color to intact, noninfarcted myocardium where lactate dehydrogenase activity is preserved.

* Because dehydrogenases leak out through the damaged membranes of dead cells, an infarct appears as an unstained pale zone.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Consider the following statements about behavior change stages and choose the correct answer : • Statement 1: Contemplation – A person who smokes is thinking of quitting smoking. • Statement 2: Precontemplation – A person is considering starting morning walk considering its benefits to health. • Statement 3: Maintenance phase – A person quit smoking one year back and has not smoked since then. • Statement 4: Action phase – A person with obesity says he can't do anything as it runs in his family.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Statement 1 and 3 are correct

This question is based on the Transtheoretical Model (Stages of Behaviour Change).

Statement 1: Contemplation – A person who smokes is thinking of quitting smoking.

This is correct. In the contemplation stage, the person is aware of the problem and is considering change, usually within the next 6 months.

Statement 2: Precontemplation – A person is considering starting morning walk considering its benefits to health.

This is incorrect. In precontemplation, the person does not intend to change behaviour and may be unaware of the problem. Considering starting a morning walk indicates contemplation, not precontemplation.

Statement 3: Maintenance phase – A person quit smoking one year back and has not smoked since then.

This is correct. The maintenance stage involves sustaining behaviour change for more than 6 months and preventing relapse.

Statement 4: Action phase – A person with obesity says he can't do anything as it runs in his family.

This is incorrect. This reflects precontemplation (no intention to change), not the action phase, where the person is actively modifying behaviour.

Therefore, the correct option is A. Statement 1 and 3 are correct.
questions.learning: Statement 1 and 3 are correct — This question is based on the Transtheoretical Model (Stages of Behaviour Change). Statement 1: Contemplation – A person who smokes is thinking of quitting smoking.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presented to Ayushman Arogya Mandir with blood pressure measurements of 148/93 and 153/99 on two separate occasions. What is the next step in management?
options: Admit the patient and give IV antihypertensives
Start the patient on Amlodipine 5mg per day and follow up after 1 month
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start the patient on Amlodipine 5mg per day and follow up after 1 month

Blood pressure readings ≥140/90 mmHg on two separate occasions confirm hypertension.

As per NPCDCS / Ayushman Arogya Mandir guidelines, uncomplicated Stage 1–2 hypertension is managed at the primary level by initiating first-line antihypertensive therapy (e.g., Amlodipine 5 mg daily) with follow-up after 1 month for titration and monitoring.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What hormone levels are typical during days 21–25 of a 28-day cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Estrogen ↑, Progesterone ↑ ; FSH ↓, LH ↓

Days 21–25 correspond to the mid-luteal phase, when the corpus luteum is fully functional. Progesterone peaks, and estrogen remains moderately elevated. High steroid levels exert negative feedback on the pituitary, suppressing FSH and LH, matching option A.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following zymogens requires gamma-glutamyl carboxylase?
options: Factors II, VII, IX, and X
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Factors II, VII, IX, and X

Clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X are zymogens of serine proteases that contain glutamic acid residues. These residues undergo vitamin-K-dependent carboxylation via gamma-glutamyl carboxylase to form gamma-carboxyglutamic acid residues. These residues chelate calcium ions, allowing the binding of clotting factors to the platelet surface.

Zymogens are the proprotein form of enzymes (proenzymes) that require proteolytic activation to carry out their function.

The reduced form of vitamin K acts as a cofactor in the post-synthetic modification of these zymogens and their activation. This reduced form of vitamin K is recycled back from its oxidized form by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase, which is inhibited by warfarin.

The absence of vitamin K or the presence of warfarin inhibits carboxylation of the glutamate residues, leading to the release of abnormal precursors of clotting factors in the blood.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A professional singer presents with difficulty in raising the pitch of her voice. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ELN

Inability to raise the pitch of voice indicates dysfunction of the cricothyroid muscle, which is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve (ELN).

·    Cricothyroid muscle:

o    Tenses and elongates vocal cords → produces high-pitched sounds

·  External laryngeal nerve (branch of superior laryngeal nerve):

o    Supplies cricothyroid muscle

·   Injury leads to:

o    Monotonous voice

o    Inability to sing high notes (important in professional voice users)

Why not other options:

·         Internal laryngeal nerve (ILN): Sensory above vocal cords, no role in pitch

·         Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN): Supplies all other intrinsic muscles → causes hoarseness, not specifically loss of high pitch

questions.text: Which visual field defect is shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Enlarged blind spots

Enlarged blind spot-on visual field testing indicates pathology involving the optic nerve head or peripapillary retina.

• Enlargement of the normal physiological blind spot
• Seen temporal to fixation in visual field charts
• Often bilateral if due to raised intracranial pressure

Common causes:

• Papilledema (most important cause)
• Optic disc edema
• Optic neuritis (early)
• Peripapillary lesions

Why not others:

• Altitudinal defect: Seen in ischemic optic neuropathy
• Arcuate scotoma: Seen in glaucoma (follows nerve fiber layer)
• Nasal step (Roenne’s): Early glaucomatous defect

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old man can only hear when words are shouted. What is the degree of his hearing impairment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Severe hearing loss > 70%

In the given clinical scenario, the patient can only hear when words are shouted, which is a severe hearing loss. The degree of his hearing impairment will be Severe hearing loss > 70%.

Our normal conversational speech is only up to 60 dB. If we have to shout, it means the patient is having a hearing loss greater than 60 dB.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of colchicine in the acute treatment of gout?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inhibition of chemotaxis

Colchicine relieves an acute gout attack by inhibiting microtubule polymerization through binding to tubulin, thereby preventing neutrophil chemotaxis, adhesion, phagocytosis, and degranulation. This suppresses the inflammatory response to monosodium urate crystals without affecting serum uric acid levels.

Why not the other options?

• A. Inhibition of xanthine oxidase: Mechanism of allopurinol and febuxostat, which reduce uric acid production for long-term gout management.
• B. Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase (COX): Mechanism of NSAIDs (e.g., indomethacin, naproxen), which reduce prostaglandin-mediated inflammation.
• D. Blockade of IL-1 receptors: Mechanism of anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist), used in selected refractory cases of acute gout.
questions.learning: Inhibition of chemotaxis Colchicine relieves an acute gout attack by inhibiting microtubule polymerization through binding to tubulin, thereby preventing neutrophil chemotaxis, adhesion, phagocytosis, and degranulation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 24-month-old child weighing 11 kg was brought to the pediatric OPD. He had a respiratory rate of 38/min. On examination, chest indrawing was observed. What is the next step of management?
options: Urgent referral to the tertiary care centre immediately
Administer IV antibiotics and ask the patient to be brought after 24 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral amoxicillin for five days

From the given clinical picture, it appears that the child has pneumonia as diagnosed from the presence of chest indrawing. The next best step of management is to give oral amoxicillin for five days and send the child home.

This is based on the revised WHO classification and treatment of childhood pneumonia at health facilities. Pneumonia with general danger signs like inability to drink, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargic or unconscious, stridor in a calm child or severe malnutrition needs antibiotics with urgent referral to higher centre.

The following image distinguishes the previous and revised classification and treatment of the childhood pneumonia.
questions.learning: Oral amoxicillin for five days From the given clinical picture, it appears that the child has pneumonia as diagnosed from the presence of chest indrawing.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 13 year old male patient presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent episodes of epistaxis for past 6 months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

The most likely diagnosis is juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA), as there is unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is a highly vascular and locally aggressive tumor seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, associated with significant morbidity and occasional mortality.

Patients usually present with:

• Epistaxis (most common presentation): Profuse, recurrent, and spontaneous
• Mass: A mass may be present in either the postnasal space, resulting in progressive nasal obstruction, or nasopharynx, where it may obstruct both choanae. The mass is firm in consistency, but digital palpation of the same should not be done. If the mass obstructs the eustachian tube, conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion may be observed.
• Proptosis, swelling of the cheeks, broadening of nasal bridge, and involvement of 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 6th cranial nerves may occur

JNA can be diagnosed using CT, MRI, and carotid angiography.

Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus due to the presence of a mass in the pterygomaxillary space is a characteristic CT finding of JNA. This is known as the Holman-Miller sign or antral sign.

Recurrence has been reported up to 35%. Surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Recurrent angiofibroma is treated with revision surgery or radiotherapy when the tumor is inaccessible.
questions.learning: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma — The most likely diagnosis is juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA), as there is unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is a primary use of this imaging modality?
questions.explanation: The image depicts Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS), a high-resolution modality that combines endoscopy with ultrasonography to visualize the gastrointestinal wall layers. Its primary and most critical use is the clinical staging of esophageal cancer. It allows for the precise assessment of the depth of tumor invasion (T stage) and the identification of regional lymph node involvement (N stage). GERD (Option B) is typically evaluated using pH monitoring or manometry rather than EUS. Dysphagia (Option C) is initially investigated with a barium swallow or standard endoscopy; EUS is reserved for assessing specific submucosal lesions identified thereafter. Cardiac and aortic pathologies (Option D) are better assessed using Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE). EUS provides unique detail for staging malignancies and guiding fine-needle aspiration of adjacent structures, making it indispensable for oncology
questions.learning: The image depicts Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS), a high-resolution modality that combines endoscopy with ultrasonography to visualize the gastrointestinal wall layers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A pregnant woman was prescribed indomethacin. Which of the following effects does the drug have on the fetus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Premature closure of ductus arteriosus

Indomethacin can cause premature closure of ductus arteriosus if given to a pregnant woman.

Indomethacin is approved for the closure of persistent ductus arteriosus in premature infants. It is given intravenously. One of its limiting factors is the development of renal toxicity in neonates.

Indomethacin is a nonselective COX inhibitor. It has anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic properties. It can be used in the management of conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, gouty arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, etc. But its use is limited due to the high rate of intolerance and availability of safer agents.

Adverse effects: Diarrhea with ulcerative bowel lesions, acute pancreatitis, and hepatitis are seen. Frontal headache is the most frequent CNS effect. Dizziness, light-headedness, vertigo, and mental confusion can occur. Neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and rarely aplastic anemia can also occur.

Note:

Prostaglandin analogs are indicated in the maintenance of patency of the ductus arteriosus.
questions.learning: Premature closure of ductus arteriosus Indomethacin can cause premature closure of ductus arteriosus if given to a pregnant woman. Indomethacin is approved for the closure of persistent ductus arteriosus in premature infants.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Interpret the audiogram displayed in the image below and identify the pattern.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conductive loss in both ears

Recognize conductive hearing loss on an audiogram by the presence of a significant air–bone gap, where bone conduction thresholds are normal or near normal while air conduction thresholds are elevated. In this audiogram, both ears show a clear air–bone gap with preserved bone conduction, indicating bilateral conductive hearing loss.

Why not the other options?

• A. Conductive loss in right ear: Incorrect; both right and left ears demonstrate an air–bone gap.
• C. Sensorineural loss in left ear: In sensorineural hearing loss, air and bone conduction are equally reduced with no air–bone gap.
• D. Sensorineural loss in right ear: Incorrect for the same reason; the audiogram shows preserved bone conduction with impaired air conduction, consistent with conductive rather than sensorineural loss.

| Audiogram Finding | Diagnosis

| ----------------- | ---------

| Air conduction ↓, Bone conduction normal (Air–bone gap >10 dB) | Conductive hearing loss

| Air conduction ↓ = Bone conduction ↓ (No air–bone gap) | Sensorineural hearing loss

| Air conduction ↓ + Bone conduction ↓ with air–bone gap | Mixed hearing loss

Remember:

• Conductive hearing loss → External or middle ear pathology (e.g., otitis media, otosclerosis, wax, tympanic membrane perforation).
• Sensorineural hearing loss → Inner ear or auditory nerve pathology (e.g., presbycusis, noise exposure, Meniere disease, acoustic neuroma).
questions.learning: Conductive loss in both ears Recognize conductive hearing loss on an audiogram by the presence of a significant air–bone gap, where bone conduction thresholds are normal or near normal while air conduction thresholds are elevated.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Fructose is absent in the seminal fluid, which of the following statements is true regarding this:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Both

Fructose is absent in seminal fluid in case of congenital absence of seminal vesicle and obstruction of the ejaculatory duct.

The ejaculatory duct is formed by the fusion of the ductus deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle. A major portion of the semen volume is contributed by the seminal vesicles. Seminal fluid is alkaline and protects sperm from acidity in prostatic secretions and in the vagina. Seminal fluid also provides fructose as an energy source for sperm. If seminal vesicle is absent or if there is an obstruction at the level of the ejaculatory duct then semen analysis will reveal low ejaculate volume, oligospermia or azoospermia, low pH, and absence of fructose.
questions.learning: Both Fructose is absent in seminal fluid in case of congenital absence of seminal vesicle and obstruction of the ejaculatory duct. The ejaculatory duct is formed by the fusion of the ductus deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which source and cell produce testosterone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cholesterol and Leydig cells

Testosterone production is mainly contributed by Leydig cells from cholesterol.

Testosterone is also synthesized from androstenedione secreted by the adrenal cortex. Luteinizing hormone(LH) helps in the secretion of testosterone by increased formation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) via the G-protein- coupled LH receptor and Gs. 99% of the testosterone in plasma is bound to protein, 65% is bound to gonadal steroid–binding globulin (GBG) or sex steroid–binding globulin, and 33% to albumin.

Actions of testosterone:

* Development of secondary sexual characters in males.

* Increases protein synthesis and decreases protein destruction.

* Maintain spermatogenesis along with FSH.

* Libido

In some target cells testosterone is primarily converted into dihydrotestosterone(DHT) by 5α reductase. DHT helps in the development of male external genitalia, enlargement of the prostate and penis at the time of puberty, facial hair and acne development, and the temporal recession of the hairline.
questions.learning: Cholesterol and Leydig cells Testosterone production is mainly contributed by Leydig cells from cholesterol. Testosterone is also synthesized from androstenedione secreted by the adrenal cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the thickened nerve marked in the arrow in the image shown below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Great auricular nerve

The thickened nerve marked with the arrow in the above image is the great auricular nerve and the thickened nerve visible below the great auricular nerve is the transverse cervical nerve.

Nerve thickening in this case is likely to be due to leprosy.

Great auricular nerve:

It is the largest ascending branch of cervical plexus and arises from the second and the third cervical spinal nerves.

It winds over the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and ascends upwards. On reaching the parotid gland it divides into the anterior and posterior branches:

• Anterior branch - supplies the facial skin over the parotid gland and joins the facial nerve in the gland.
• Posterior branch - supplies the skin over the mastoid process, posteroinferior part of the auricle, lobule, and concha.

Clinical considerations:

• Leprosy - Nerve thickening is present. The nerve is palpable over the upper part of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. (as seen in the above image)
• Frey's syndrome - An aberrant connection between the auriculotemporal nerve and great auricular nerve causes gustatory sweating.
questions.learning: Great auricular nerve — The thickened nerve marked with the arrow in the above image is the great auricular nerve and the thickened nerve visible below the great auricular nerve is the transverse cervical nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident with severe head trauma. His GCS is 5. On examination, there is a loss of sensation below the level of the neck and flaccid paralysis of all four limbs. Which of the following structures pass through the same cranial foramen as the structure involved in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spinal root of accessory nerve

The spinal root of the accessory nerve (CN XI) enters the skull through the foramen magnum, ascends briefly into the cranial cavity, and then exits the skull with the cranial root of CN XI through the jugular foramen. Structures passing through the foramen magnum:

• Medulla oblongata
• Spinal roots of the accessory nerve (CN XI)
• Vertebral arteries
• Anterior and posterior spinal arteries
• Meninges

Why others are incorrect:

A. Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) → passes through the hypoglossal canal.

B. Cranial root of accessory nerve → exits through the jugular foramen.

D. Middle meningeal artery → enters through the foramen spinosum.
questions.learning: Spinal root of accessory nerve — The spinal root of the accessory nerve (CN XI) enters the skull through the foramen magnum, ascends briefly into the cranial cavity, and then exits the skull with the cranial root of CN XI through the jugular foramen.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wrist and knee joint

Wrist and knee joint radiographs will be ordered to solve this discrepancy as lower end of radius and upper end of tibia fuse at 18-19 years. If these joints are fused, It is certain that the boy is more than 18 years and his claim is false.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: According to the neonatal resuscitation protocol, below what heart rate are chest compressions initiated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 60

According to the neonatal resuscitation protocol, chest compressions are started when heart rate is below 60/min

The response to neonatal resuscitation at various steps is assessed based on the heart rate.

* If the heart rate is less than 100/min, PPV is initially provided with bag and mask on room air, and SPO2 monitoring is done. Increasing concentration of oxygen is used to ensure adequate ventilation.

* If the heart rate is below 60, chest compressions are initiated over the lower third of the sternum at a rate of 90 compressions/min. The ratio of compressions to ventilation is 3: 1.

* If the heart rate still remains <60, despite effective compressions and ventilation, then IV epinephrine is given.

questions.text: Identify the foramen marked in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Foramen rotundum

The image shows the sphenoid bone. The foramen marked is the foramen rotundum. Maxillary branch of trigeminal nerve passes through it.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 34-year-old female presented to the psychiatric OPD with low mood, loss of energy, loss of interest in pleasurable activities, decreased sleep, and appetite for the past 2 months. What is the most appropriate treatment to be started?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fluoxetine

The clinical vignette point towards major depressive disorder. SSRIs like fluoxetine are the most appropriate treatment for major depressive disorder. SSRIs should be continued for 6-9 months after complete remission of symptoms in case of a single episode of depression.

The diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder are as follows:

A. Five or more of the following symptoms have been present during the same 2-week period. At least one of the symptoms is either depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure.

* Depressed mood most of the day

* Markedly diminished interest or pleasure in activities (anhedonia)

* Significant weight loss when not dieting or weight gain, decrease or increase in appetite

* Insomnia or hypersomnia

* Psychomotor agitation or retardation

* Fatigue or loss of energy

* Feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt

* Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness

* Recurrent thoughts of death, recurrent suicidal ideation

B. The symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

C. The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or to another medical condition.

D. The occurrence of the major depressive episode is not better explained by schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, schizophreniform disorder, delusional disorder, or other specified and unspecified schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders.

E. There has never been a manic episode or a hypomanic episode.

Treatment of depression according to NICE guidelines:

* In recent‐onset, mild depression, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is preferred and antidepressants are not recommended.

* Antidepressants (SSRIs) are recommended for the treatment of moderate to severe depression and for dysthymia along with CBT.

* For treatment‐resistant depression, recommended strategies include augmentation with lithium or an antipsychotic or the addition of a second antidepressant.

* The use of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is supported in severe and treatment-resistant depression.
questions.learning: Fluoxetine — The clinical vignette point towards major depressive disorder. SSRIs like fluoxetine are the most appropriate treatment for major depressive disorder.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A homeless man comes with diarrhea, dementia, and dermatitis. He consumes alcohol occasionally. He admits to having 'X' as his staple diet. Which of the following is X most likely to be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Maize

This patient with symptoms of dementia, diarrhea and dermatitis most likely has niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency. X  is likely to be maize in his diet.

Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, found mostly among people eating corn/maize-based diets, which is low in niacin and tryptophan. Excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin.

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds- nicotinic acid, and nicotinamide have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes NAD ( nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) and NADP (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck.

The 4Ds of pellagra:

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis
• Dementia, leading to
• Death

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone.

It is treated by oral supplementation of 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

Casal’s necklace finding in niacin deficiency
questions.learning: Maize — This patient with symptoms of dementia, diarrhea and dermatitis most likely has niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency. X is likely to be maize in his diet.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for the negative charge in fibrinopeptide A?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspartate and glutamate

Aspartate and glutamate are responsible for the negative charge in fibrinopeptide A and B of fibrinogen.

The negative charges contribute to the solubility of fibrinogen in plasma and importantly also serve to prevent aggregation by causing electrostatic repulsion between fibrinogen molecules.
questions.learning: Aspartate and glutamate Aspartate and glutamate are responsible for the negative charge in fibrinopeptide A and B of fibrinogen. The negative charges contribute to the solubility of fibrinogen in plasma and importantly also serve to prevent aggregation by…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young boy presents with joint swelling after a fall. Lab investigations show normal PT and raised aPTT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Joint swelling (hemarthrosis) following minor trauma is a classic indicator of a coagulation factor deficiency, most notably hemophilia. Laboratory findings of a normal PT combined with a prolonged aPTT confirm a defect in the intrinsic pathway. Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency) and Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency) both manifest with this specific pattern. Von Willebrand Disease (Option A) also shows a raised aPTT but is typically characterized by mucocutaneous bleeding (like epistaxis) rather than deep joint bleeds. Iron Deficiency Anemia (Option C) causes fatigue and pallor but has no effect on coagulation times. Platelet function disorders (Option D) lead to mucosal bleeding and petechiae, while both PT and aPTT usually remain within normal limits. Thus, the isolated aPTT elevation and hemarthrosis identify hemophilia
questions.learning: Joint swelling (hemarthrosis) following minor trauma is a classic indicator of a coagulation factor deficiency, most notably hemophilia. Laboratory findings of a normal PT combined with a prolonged aPTT confirm a defect in the intrinsic pathway.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which one of the following groups of drugs is ineffective against gram positive bacteria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Monobactams

Monobactams (e.g., Aztreonam) are β-lactam antibiotics with activity primarily against aerobic Gram-negative bacteria and have virtually no activity against Gram-positive organisms or anaerobes.

Spectrum of Activity of Monobactams

• Effective against:

• Gram-negative bacilli
• Pseudomonas infection
• Enterobacteriaceae

• Ineffective against:

• Gram-positive cocci
• Anaerobic bacteria

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect

• A. Glycopeptides (e.g., Vancomycin): Excellent activity against Gram-positive organisms, including MRSA.
• C. Fluoroquinolones: Later generations (e.g., levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) have significant Gram-positive coverage.
• D. First-generation cephalosporins: Strong activity against Gram-positive cocci such as streptococci and methicillin-sensitive staphylococci.
questions.learning: Monobactams Monobactams (e.g., Aztreonam) are β-lactam antibiotics with activity primarily against aerobic Gram-negative bacteria and have virtually no activity against Gram-positive organisms or anaerobes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient has a fever, cough, and cold. The chest x-ray is given below. What will be the examination finding in the infrascapular region?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dull note on percussion

The above X-ray and symptoms are suggestive of pleural effusion secondary to a lower respiratory tract infection. On examination, dullness to percussion will be observed.

Pleural effusion refers to the pathological accumulation of fluid in the pleural space due to

• excess fluid formation from the interstitial spaces of the lung, parietal pleura, or peritoneal cavity
• decreased fluid removal by the lymphatics

Pleural effusion may present with dyspnea, pleuritic pain, dry cough, and associated symptoms like fever, weight loss, edema, and ascites depending on the etiology. On examination, there may be tachypnea, dullness on percussion and decreased/absent breath sounds at the base(s).

The etiology of pleural effusion can be of two types:

• Exudative: disruption in pleural fluid formation and drainage because of local factors. Examples include malignancy, infections, and pulmonary embolism.
• Transudative: disruption in pleural fluid formation and drainage due to systemic factors. Examples include congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome.

Option A: Hyperresonance is a sign of pneumothorax or emphysema.

Option B: Crackles are heard in cases of pulmonary edema or pneumonia.

Option D: Stridor is due to a lesion in the upper airways, usually tracheal or laryngeal.
questions.learning: Dull note on percussion — The above X-ray and symptoms are suggestive of pleural effusion secondary to a lower respiratory tract infection. On examination, dullness to percussion will be observed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Dohlman's procedure is used for the treatment of which condition?
questions.explanation: Dohlman’s procedure is a specialized endoscopic surgical technique used to treat Zenker’s diverticulum (Option B), a pharyngeal pouch that occurs at Killian's dehiscence. The procedure involves using a double-lipped endoscope to visualize the common wall between the diverticulum and the esophagus. This wall, which contains the cricopharyngeus muscle, is then divided using electrocautery or a laser. This "stapling" or division converts the pouch and the esophagus into a single cavity, preventing food entrapment and relieving dysphagia. Meckel's diverticulum (Option A) is an intestinal anomaly requiring abdominal resection. Bochdalek hernia (Option C) is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia treated with abdominal or thoracic repair. Menetrier’s disease (Option D) is a rare hypertrophic gastropathy involving the stomach. Because Dohlman’s is an endoscopic approach to a pharyngeal pouch, Zenker’s diverticulum is the correct clinical association. It offers a shorter recovery time compared to open diverticulectomy
questions.learning: Dohlman’s procedure is a specialized endoscopic surgical technique used to treat Zenker’s diverticulum (Option B), a pharyngeal pouch that occurs at Killian's dehiscence.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a reaction, the substrate is available in a concentration that is 1000 times the Km value of the enzyme. After 9 minutes of reaction, 1% of substrate is converted to product (12 microgram/ml). If the concentration of the enzyme is changed to 1/3 and concentration of substrate is doubled, what is the time taken to convert the substrate into the same amount of product that i.e. 12 microgram/ml?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 27 minutes

The time taken for the formation of the same amount of product is 27 minutes.

In this reaction, the substrate concentration becomes 1000 times i.e much greater than the Km value. Thus, the rate of this reaction is equal to Vmax and is thus independent of the substrate concentration i.e. it follows zero-order kinetics. Thus, doubling the substrate concentration does not change the velocity of the reaction i.e. it remains as Vmax.

No matter the substrate concentration, the rate of the reaction is directly proportional to the concentration of the enzyme. In this situation the enzyme concentration becomes 1/3rd. Thus, the velocity of the reaction (Vmax) also becomes 1/3rd. This means that the time taken for the formation of the same amount of product will become tripled i.e 9 × 3 = 27 minutes.
questions.learning: 27 minutes The time taken for the formation of the same amount of product is 27 minutes. In this reaction, the substrate concentration becomes 1000 times i.e much greater than the Km value.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is the best sign to indicate adequate growth in an infant with a birth weight of 2.8 kg?
options: Increase in length of 25 centimeters in the first year
Weight gain of 300 grams per month till 1 year
Anterior fontanelle closure by 6 months of age
Weight under 75th percentile and height under 25th percentile
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase in length of 25 centimeters in the first year

The best sign to indicate adequate growth in an infant is an increase in length of 25 centimeters in the first year. The growth velocity is the rate of increase in height in one year and varies with age.

The average growth velocity is 25 cm/year in the first year (birth-12 months) and an infant will be 75 cm tall at 1 year. The height velocity is 10 cm/year from 12-24 months and at 2 years, the height is 90 cm. The height velocity is 8 cm/year from 24-36 months. At 4 years, the child is 100 cm tall. After this, the child gains about 6 cm every year until 12 years.

If growth velocity is lower than expected for age, the child is likely to be suffering from a pathological cause of short stature.

Other options:

Option B: During the first 3 months of age, the weight gain is about 20-40 grams per day. From 4 months of age till 1 year of age, the weight gain is about 400 grams per month. The weight of an infant doubles his birth weight at 5 months of age and triples at 1 year of age and quadruples at 2 years of age.

Option C: The anterior fontanelle closes by 18 months of age.

Option D: According to WHO growth charts, weight under the 75th percentile and height under the 25th percentile do not indicate adequate growth.
questions.learning: Increase in length of 25 centimeters in the first year The best sign to indicate adequate growth in an infant is an increase in length of 25 centimeters in the first year.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is non-pulsatile dosing of GnRH agonist not used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Male infertility

Pulsatile dose of GnRH agonist is used in the treatment of male infertility.

Pulsatile administration of GnRH agonists results in increased FSH and LH secretion and is used to treat male and female infertility.

Non-pulsatile or continuous dose of GnRH agonist results in suppression and decreased concentrations of gonadotropins LH and FSH. They are used in:

1. Endometriosis
2. Uterine fibroids
3. Central precocious puberty
4. Ca prostate
5. Ca ovary and breast
6. Controlled ovary stimulation
questions.learning: Male infertility Pulsatile dose of GnRH agonist is used in the treatment of male infertility. Pulsatile administration of GnRH agonists results in increased FSH and LH secretion and is used to treat male and female infertility.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A young child with absent thymus is brought to the OPD with features of hypoparathyroidism and tetany. Which of the following marked area in the picture is defective in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The image shows pharyngeal pouches and based on the clinical history, the patient most likely has DiGeorge syndrome(thymic and parathyroid defects). It may be caused by defective development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouch. In the given stem, it is clearly mentioned that the thymus is absent. Thus, the better of the two options is 3.

DiGeorge syndrome is a complex embryopathy that is caused by hemizygous interstitial deletion of chromosome 22, leading to multiple developmental defects, including conotruncal defects, hypoparathyroidism, and dysmorphic syndrome. Microdeletion at chromosome 22q11 can lead to variable presentations including

• Cleft palate
• Abnormal facies
• Thymic aplasia leading to T-cell deficiency
• Cardiac defects
• Hypocalcemia 2° to parathyroid aplasia. (Mnemonic: CATCH-22)

Velocardiofacial syndrome - palate, facial, and cardiac defects.

In the diagram, I-IV are the branchial arches, 1-4 are pharyngeal pouches (inside), and/or pharyngeal grooves (outside)

1. Tuberculum lateral
2. Tuberculum impar
3. Foramen cecum
4. Ductus thyroglossus
5. Sinus cervicalis

1. First pharyngeal pouch, middle ear cavity, and epithelial lining of the auditory tube.
2. Second pharyngeal pouch, palatine tonsils
3. Points towards third pharyngeal pouch which gives rise to inferior parathyroid gland and thymus.
4. Fourth pharyngeal pouch, Superior parathyroid gland, and ultimobranchial body.
questions.learning: 3 The image shows pharyngeal pouches and based on the clinical history, the patient most likely has DiGeorge syndrome(thymic and parathyroid defects).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient has profuse bleeding after the removal of an IV cannula. He underwent a small bowel resection and was given broad-spectrum antibiotics during his hospital stay. The deficiency of which of the following vitamins is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin K

The deficiency of vitamin K is responsible for this condition.

Vitamin K deficiency in adults may be seen in patients with chronic small-intestinal diseases like celiac disease, Crohn’s disease, obstructed biliary tracts, and after small-bowel resection. Additionally, broad-spectrum antibiotics can precipitate Vitamin K deficiency by reducing the number of gut bacteria, which synthesize menaquinones.

It is a fat-soluble vitamin that has two natural forms: Vitamin K1, also known as phylloquinone, from vegetable sources, and vitamin K2, or menaquinones, which are synthesized by bacterial flora and found in hepatic tissue.

Vitamin K is required for the posttranslational carboxylation of glutamic acid, which is necessary for calcium binding to γ-carboxylated proteins such as

* prothrombin (factor II)

* factors VII, IX, and X

* protein C, protein S

Patients with vitamin K deficiency usually present with a history of bleeding either at venipuncture sites or minor trauma.

It is diagnosed on the basis of an elevated prothrombin time or reduced clotting factors. It is treated with supplementation by oral or IV route.

Other options:

Option A: Riboflavin or Vitamin B2 deficiency manifests as angular stomatitis, magenta tongue, seborrhea, corneal vascularization. It is seen in alcoholism, and individuals with a poor diet and decreased intake of dairy products.

Option B: Vitamin E deficiency manifests as peripheral neuropathy, spinocerebellar ataxia, skeletal muscle atrophy, and retinopathy. Usually seen with fat malabsorption or genetic abnormalities of vitamin E metabolism.

Option C: Niacin deficiency manifests as pellagra, which includes symptoms of diarrhea, a pigmented rash over sun-exposed areas, bright red tongue, memory loss, and altered sensorium. Alcoholism, vitamin B6 deficiency, riboflavin, and tryptophan deficiencies predispose to this condition.
questions.learning: Vitamin K — The deficiency of vitamin K is responsible for this condition. Vitamin K deficiency in adults may be seen in patients with chronic small-intestinal diseases like celiac disease, Crohn’s disease, obstructed biliary tracts, and after small-bowel…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 77-year-old man presented with worsening hip and back pain. He also reports weight loss and loss of appetite. His PSA levels are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prostate cancer

Blastic lesions on X-Ray along with elevated PSA levels, loss of weight, and loss of appetite are suggestive of prostatic carcinoma with metastasis to bones.

Carcinoma of the prostate:

It is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years  They may range from indolent lesions that cause no harm to aggressive metastatic tumors. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements.

Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland.

Prostate carcinoma is a type of adenocarcinoma. Therefore, histopathology shows the malignant cells arranged in the form of glands. In contrast to benign glands, malignant glands have tightly packed cells and characteristically lack branching and papillary infoldings. The outer basal cell layer typical of benign glands is absent. The cells may show increased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, nuclear atypia, etc. α-methyl acyl-coenzyme A-racemase (AMACR) is positive and is upregulated in prostate cancer.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Advanced disease may produce ureteral obstruction. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in the decreasing order of frequency.

Management of Prostatic Carcinoma

Stage of cancer
Age>70 or Gleason score=6
Age<70 or Gleason score>6

Early prostate cancer: T1, T2A
Active surveillance
Radical prostatectomy

Locally advanced prostate cancer: T2B, T2C, T3, T4, N1
Brachytherapy + Androgen deprivation therapy
Brachytherapy + Radical prostatectomy

Metastatic prostate cancer

Androgen deprivation therapy

Chemotherapy and radiotherapy (hormone-resistant  tumor)

Radiopharmaceutical therapy (hormone-resistant bony metastasis)

Below image shows histopathology of Prostate carcinoma:

Pearl PF0895: Types of metastasis(osteoblastic or osteolytic) and their primary:

Predominantly osteoblastic:

* Prostate cancer

* Osteosarcoma

* Medullary carcinoma thyroid

Mixed osteoblastic and osteolytic:

* Breast cancer(preponderance toward osteolytic)

* Lymphoma

* Urothelial carcinoma

* Lung cancer

Predominantly osteolytic:

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Multiple myeloma

* Thyroid carcinoma(except medullary carcinoma thyroid)

* Gastrointestinal tract carcinoma

* Malignant melanoma
questions.learning: Prostate cancer Blastic lesions on X-Ray along with elevated PSA levels, loss of weight, and loss of appetite are suggestive of prostatic carcinoma with metastasis to bones.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is evaluated and found to have a refractive error of −2 diopters in the right eye and +1 diopter in the left eye. The fundus examination and visual acuity are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation: Anisometropia is defined as a significant difference in refractive power between the two eyes, regardless of whether the refractive error is myopia, hyperopia, or astigmatism. Clinically, a difference of ≥2 diopters (commonly ≥2–2.5 D) between the eyes is considered significant. In this child, the right eye has myopia (−2 D) and the left eye has hyperopia (+1 D). The interocular difference is 3 diopters, which clearly fulfills the diagnostic criteria for anisometropia. While the child does have myopia (Option A) in one eye and hyperopia (Option B) in the other, these terms describe individual refractive errors and do not explain the bilateral imbalance. Amblyopia (Option D) is a possible complication of untreated anisometropia due to unequal visual input to the brain, but it is not the diagnosis here, especially since the child currently has normal visual acuity and fundus findings. Therefore, the most accurate and comprehensive diagnosis explaining the refractive discrepancy is anisometropia
questions.learning: Anisometropia is defined as a significant difference in refractive power between the two eyes, regardless of whether the refractive error is myopia, hyperopia, or astigmatism.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The risk of Down syndrome is 100% in the offspring, if:
options: Mother only is the carrier of balanced translocation
Father only is the carrier of balanced translocation
Either parent is a carrier of translocation between two chromosome 21
Both parents are carriers of balanced translocation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Either parent is a carrier of translocation between two chromosome 21

Translocation Down syndrome most commonly results from a Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 21. The recurrence risk depends on the type of translocation and which parent is the carrier. A parent carrying a balanced Robertsonian translocation between two chromosome 21s [rob(21;21)] produces gametes that result in either trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) or monosomy 21 (non-viable). Therefore, all viable offspring will have Down syndrome (100% risk among live births).

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Mother only is the carrier of balanced translocation: The recurrence risk depends on the type of translocation; it is not 100% for common rob(14;21) carriers.
• B. Father only is the carrier of balanced translocation: The recurrence risk is lower than when the mother is the carrier and is not 100%.
• D. Both parents are carriers of balanced translocation: Simply stating that both parents are balanced translocation carriers does not imply a 100% risk; it depends on the chromosomes involved.
questions.learning: Either parent is a carrier of translocation between two chromosome 21 Translocation Down syndrome most commonly results from a Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 21.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the device
questions.explanation: The image displays a Lippes Loop, which is a classic first-generation, non-medicated (inert) intrauterine device (IUD). It is characterized by its distinctive double-S shaped plastic frame made of polyethylene, often impregnated with barium sulfate for radiopacity. Mirena (Option A) is a T-shaped hormonal IUD that releases levonorgestrel. Copper T (Option C) is a T-shaped device wrapped with copper wire, which is the most common medicated IUD used today. Progestasert (Option D) was an older T-shaped device that released progesterone. The Lippes Loop was once widely used globally but has largely been replaced in modern practice by more effective copper-bearing or hormone-releasing T-shaped devices. It worked primarily by causing a sterile inflammatory response in the endometrium that was toxic to sperm and prevented implantation. Identifying these historical devices is a common requirement in medical licensing examinations

Work sampling is a systematic observation and recording of activities of one or more individuals carried out at predetermined or random interval and thus it has to be used to evaulate the time that each doctor spends per patient.

It is a type of quantitative method of management. It helps in standardizing the methods of performing the jobs and determining the need for manpower.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Arrange the following events in the sequence in which they occur, after 'p wave' in ECG:

1. a wave in JVP
2. First heart sound
3. Rapid filling of ventricles
4. T wave in ECG
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-2-4-3

The correct sequence of events that occur after the p-wave is 1-2-4-3, ie:-

a wave in JVP → First heart sound  → T wave in ECG  → Rapid filling of ventricles.

The sequence of the events in this question can be better understood with the following diagram:

• The p wave in the ECG represents atrial depolarization, which causes contraction of the atria, represented by the 'a' wave in the JVP. Atrial contraction causes final filling of the ventricles (fourth phase of ventricular diastole)
• Atrial contraction is followed by the closure of the mitral valve, which causes the first-heart sound.
• This is followed by the isovolumetric contraction of the ventricle, which causes c wave in JVP, due to bulging of the tricuspid valve. This is followed by the rapid ejection phase of the ventricle.
• The T wave of ECG occurs during ventricular repolarization, which is followed by the opening of the mitral valve, followed by rapid filling phase of the ventricle (second  phase of ventricular diastole).

Note: Passive rapid filling occurs as the mitral valve opens just before atrial contraction occurs.
questions.learning: 1-2-4-3 The correct sequence of events that occur after the p-wave is 1-2-4-3, ie:- a wave in JVP → First heart sound → T wave in ECG → Rapid filling of ventricles.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As per the POCSO Act, who is defined as being entitled to protection under the law?
options: Girl child less than 16 years age
Girl child less than 18 years age
Any child less than 16 years age
Any child less than 18 years age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Any child less than 18 years age

Under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, a child is defined as any person below 18 years of age, irrespective of gender.

The Act provides gender-neutral protection against sexual offences and mandates child-friendly procedures during reporting, investigation, and trial.

This uniform age definition ensures comprehensive legal protection for all minors.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following hormone acts via this pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Leptin

The given image shows the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, which is associated with tyrosine kinase receptors. Among the given hormones leptin acts via this pathway.

Hormones that use receptor tyrosine kinase/ JAK-STAT signaling include the following:

• Growth hormone
• Fibroblast growth factor
• Hepatocyte growth factor
• Insulin
• Insulin-like growth factor-1
• Leptin
• Prolactin
• Vascular endothelial growth factor

Leptin is a hormone that is secreted by fat cells. The physiological effects of leptin are regulating appetite and energy balance. The leptin receptor acts via tyrosine kinase of the Janus kinase (JAK) family, JAK2. Leptin binds to the extracellular part of the leptin receptor, which causes phosphorylation (P) and activation of the intracellular JAK2. This causes phosphorylation of signal transducer and activation of transcription (STAT) proteins, which results in the transcription of target genes and the synthesis of proteins.

Phosphorylation of JAK2 also results in the activation of other intracellular enzyme pathways such as mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK) and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K).

Other options:

Hormones such as adrenal (Aldosterone)and gonadal steroid hormones, thyroid hormones, retinoid hormones, and vitamin D, bind with protein receptors inside the cell rather than on the cell surface. These hormones are lipid soluble and they readily cross the cell membrane and interact with receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus.

Vasopressin in the epithelial cells acts via V2 receptor. They use adenylyl cyclase as their second messenger system. Vasopressin in the vascular smooth muscles acts via V1 receptor that uses phospholipase C as the second messenger system.
questions.learning: Leptin — The given image shows the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, which is associated with tyrosine kinase receptors. Among the given hormones leptin acts via this pathway.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the sagittal section of the brain given below if the coloured area is affected, which of the following is not seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perianal anesthesia

Paracentral lobule (PCL) is the continuation of the precentral and postcentral gyri of the superolateral surface into the medial surface of cerebral hemisphere. It controls the motor and sensory innervations of the contralateral lower extremity. It is also responsible for cortical control of micturition and defecation.

The anterior two-thirds of PCL belong to Brodmann area 4, it reflects the primary motor cortex for the muscles of contralateral leg, foot, and perineum,it is functionally important in control of bladder and anal sphincters. Therefore, it's called the cortical center of defecation and micturition.

The posterior third of the PCL contains 3,2 and 1, it reflects the primary somatosensory representation of the leg and foot.

The A2 segment of the anterior cerebral artery supplies the paracentral lobule. Lesions in the paracentral lobule lead to:

• Weakness and loss of sensation in contralateral lower limb
• Urinary incontinence
• Fecal incontinence.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: An anesthetist used the airway device shown in the image given below on a patient. Which among the following statements is true regarding the adjunct?
options: It can cause damage to the teeth
It can be used in conscious patients
It can be safely used in facial trauma cases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It can be used in conscious patients

The image shows a nasopharyngeal airway and its insertion. The true statement is that it can be used in conscious patients.

A nasopharyngeal airway is used to provide artificial airway passage to the hypopharynx. To place a nasopharyngeal airway, the device should be lubricated and inserted into the nose with the bevel facing the nasal septum, at a 90-degree angle to the longitudinal axis of the body. It bypasses the gag reflex as they do not go through the mouth. Thus, it can be used in conscious patients or those who have been lightly anesthetized.

Care should be taken to avoid excessive force as damage to the nasal mucosa can result in epistaxis. The nasal approach should be avoided in conditions that put patients at higher risk for epistaxis. These conditions include but are not limited to coagulopathy, pregnancy, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, and uncontrolled hypertension. Absolute contraindications include basilar skull fractures, facial trauma, midface disruption, and injury to the roof of the mouth.

An oropharyngeal airway is used to maintain the airway in anesthetized patients. This adjunct prevents the tongue and epiglottis from falling back against the posterior pharynx and blocking the airway. They can cause coughing, retching, or laryngospasm in conscious patients.

To place an oropharyngeal airway, the device is inserted with the curved portion facing downwards. It is then rotated 180 degrees to be put in place. The below image shows the oropharyngeal airway:

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An elderly patient presents with watering, irritation, and foreign body sensation in the eye. On examination, the eyelid is as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Entropion

The lower eyelid is turned inward (inverted), causing the eyelashes to rub against the cornea and bulbar conjunctiva (trichiasis). The eye appears watery (epiphora) with conjunctival congestion due to chronic irritation. Long-standing entropion may produce corneal epithelial defects, abrasions, ulceration, vascularization, and corneal scarring, leading to visual impairment if untreated.

Key image findings

• Inward rolling (inversion) of the eyelid margin
• Eyelashes directed toward the globe
• Lashes touching the cornea/conjunctiva
• Excessive tearing (epiphora)
• Conjunctival hyperemia
• May show corneal haze, abrasion, ulcer, or scar in advanced cases

Clinical symptoms

• Foreign body sensation
• Watering
• Pain or irritation
• Photophobia
• Blurred vision (if cornea involved)

High-yield causes

• Involutional (senile) – most common; due to lid laxity
• Cicatricial – trachoma, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, chemical burns
• Congenital
• Spastic – secondary to blepharospasm

NEET PG Pearl

Differentiate entropion from ectropion:

| Entropion | Ectropion

| --------- | ---------

| Eyelid turns inward | Eyelid turns outward

| Lashes rub the cornea | Lashes point away from the eye

| Corneal irritation and ulceration are common | Exposure keratopathy and epiphora are common

| Trichiasis may be present | Punctum is everted, impairing tear drainage

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the condition known as when a gallstone becomes impacted in the cystic duct, causes dilation of the common hepatic duct, compresses the common bile duct, and leads to obstructive jaundice?
questions.explanation: The scenario describes Mirizzi's syndrome (Option D), a rare complication of chronic gallstone disease . It occurs when a large gallstone becomes impacted in the cystic duct or the neck of the gallbladder (Hartmann’s pouch). This impacted stone causes significant extrinsic compression or secondary inflammation of the adjacent common hepatic duct (CHD), leading to biliary obstruction and obstructive jaundice. Acute cholecystitis (Option A) involves inflammation of the gallbladder but does not typically cause dilation of the CHD or CBD unless a stone has migrated into the CBD (choledocholithiasis). Porcelain gallbladder (Option B) refers to calcification of the gallbladder wall. Cholesterolosis (Option C) is an accumulation of cholesterol within the gallbladder mucosa ("strawberry gallbladder"). Mirizzi's syndrome is a surgical challenge because the intense inflammation can lead to a cholecystobiliary fistula. Therefore, extrinsic compression of the bile duct by a cystic duct stone is the defining feature of Mirizzi's syndrome
