questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Myosin ceases to be in contact with actin filaments as a result of:
options: Cessation of calcium release from sarcoplasm
Attachment of ATP to myosin head
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Attachment of ATP to myosin head

Myosin ceases to be in contact with actin filaments as a result of the attachment of ATP to the myosin head.

Muscle contraction occurs by sliding of thin filament over thick filament. The sequence of events are as follows:

•  Troponin I is bound to actin and tropomyosin and covers the sites where actin interacts with myosin heads in a resting muscle. The myosin head contains tightly bound adenosine phosphate (ADP) and inorganic phosphate (Pi).
• Following an action potential, cytosolic Ca2+ is increased due to the Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.  Simultaneously Ca2+ influx happens through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels too.
• The free Ca2+ binds with troponin C. This binding will weaken the troponin I interaction with actin and exposes the actin-binding site for myosin.
• This results in the formation of myosin-actin cross-bridges.
• The cross-bridge between the head of the myosin and the active site of the actin causes a conformational change in the head and the power stroke occurs, moving the thin filament relative to the thick filament.
• Once the head of the cross-bridge tilts, the ADP and phosphate ion that were previously attached to the head are released and a new ATP molecule can bind in that place.
• The binding of the new ATP molecule to the free site on the myosin causes detachment of the head of the myosin from the actin.
• ATP is hydrolyzed and Pi released, causing a re-cocking of the myosin head and completing the cycle.
questions.learning: Attachment of ATP to myosin head Myosin ceases to be in contact with actin filaments as a result of the attachment of ATP to the myosin head. Muscle contraction occurs by sliding of thin filament over thick filament.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: At what time during the intrauterine life does talus ossification center appear?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6 months

The talus bone ossification center appears in the 6th month of intrauterine life.

Nearly all secondary centers commence ossification after birth, although a few develop in the last few weeks of intrauterine life. Secondary ossification centers that are already present when an infant is born include:

* Distal femur - 7th week

* Proximal tibia - 7th week

* Humerus - 8th week

* Calcaneus - 3 to 4th month

* Talus - 6th month

* Cuboid - 9th month

Forensic medicine textbooks like Knight's Forensic Pathology (4th edition page 456), The essentials of Forensic medicine and Toxicology
Dr. K.S. Narayan Reddy (34th edition page 75) states that the talus ossification begins at 7 months instead of 6th.

The answer is as per Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice (42nd Edition page 1436)
questions.learning: 6 months The talus bone ossification center appears in the 6th month of intrauterine life. Nearly all secondary centers commence ossification after birth, although a few develop in the last few weeks of intrauterine life.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient with a history of trauma one week back presents with confusion and ataxia. He is on treatment for alcohol dependence and his last intake was 2 weeks back. CT scan reveals the following finding. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subdural hemorrhage

The given clinical scenario and the plain CT scan showing a concavo-convex-shaped hematoma on the left side with a midline shift to the right is suggestive of subdural hematoma (SDH).

An acute SDH is the result of the accumulation of blood between the arachnoid membrane and the dura. It is usually due to the rupture of bridging veins running from the cerebral cortex to the dural sinuses. The level of consciousness is usually impaired at presentation and may deteriorate further as the hematoma expands. Elderly and alcoholic patients are at a higher risk of acute SDH formation after head trauma due to brain atrophy. On CT scan, acute SDH appears as a hyperdense, crescent-shaped (concavo-convex) lesion.

Open craniotomy for the evacuation of acute SDH is indicated for the following:

• Thickness >1 cm
• Midline shift >5 mm
• Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score drops by two or more points from the time of injury to hospitalization.

Chronic subdural hematoma results from a hematoma that expands over days or weeks by osmosis, ultimately producing symptoms of raised ICP or focal deficits. On a CT scan, diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface would be seen.
questions.learning: Subdural hemorrhage — The given clinical scenario and the plain CT scan showing a concavo-convex-shaped hematoma on the left side with a midline shift to the right is suggestive of subdural hematoma (SDH).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following do not represent the corrected refractive error?
questions.explanation: This question focuses on the nature of common visual impairments. Myopia (Option A), Hyperopia (Option B), and Astigmatism (Option D) are true ametropic refractive errors caused by a mismatch between the eye's axial length and its focusing power. Presbyopia, however, is not a refractive error in the traditional sense; it is an age-related loss of accommodative amplitude. It occurs because the natural lens loses its elasticity and the ciliary muscles weaken, making it difficult to focus on near objects. While it is corrected with glasses (like refractive errors), its underlying mechanism is physiological aging rather than a structural refractive mismatch. Myopia involves light focusing in front of the retina, while hyperopia involves light focusing behind it. Astigmatism occurs when the cornea or lens has an irregular curvature. Therefore, while all four impact vision, presbyopia is distinct as a progressive age-related condition of the lens's dynamic focusing ability rather than a static refractive state of the eye
questions.learning: This question focuses on the nature of common visual impairments. Myopia (Option A), Hyperopia (Option B), and Astigmatism (Option D) are true ametropic refractive errors caused by a mismatch between the eye's axial length and its focusing power.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which instrument is used to measure both the humidity of air and its dew point temperature?
questions.explanation: A sling psychrometer is a specialized instrument used to measure the relative humidity and dew point of the air. It consists of two thermometers: a "dry-bulb" that measures the actual air temperature and a "wet-bulb" covered in a water-saturated wick. By whirling the instrument in the air, evaporation cools the wet-bulb; the difference between the two temperatures (the psychrometric depression) is then used with standardized tables to determine humidity. A Kata thermometer (Option B) is primarily used to measure the cooling power of air and low air velocities. A Barometer (Option C) measures atmospheric pressure. A Dial thermometer (Option D) provides a simple reading of the current temperature but cannot measure humidity on its own. Accurate measurement of air humidity is critical in occupational health to assess heat stress and in hospitals to maintain appropriate environmental conditions for patient care and equipment longevity. Psychrometers are fundamental tools in environmental sanitation and meteorology
questions.learning: A sling psychrometer is a specialized instrument used to measure the relative humidity and dew point of the air. It consists of two thermometers: a "dry-bulb" that measures the actual air temperature and a "wet-bulb" covered in a water-saturated wick.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the function of IL-8?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chemotaxis

IL-8 is a potent neutrophil chemoattractant, guiding them toward sites of acute inflammation. It also activates neutrophils, enhancing their phagocytic function. Other options do not match its primary role—IL-1/IL-6 cause fever, IL-2 drives lymphocyte proliferation, and IL-12 promotes TH1 activation.

options: Angiotensin II on vascular smooth muscle and vasopressin acting via V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
Angiotensin II on vascular smooth muscle and vasopressin acting via V2 receptors on epithelial cells

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Pentavalent vaccine includes which of the following?
options: Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus , HBV, Injectable Polio
Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Haemophilus influenza B, Pneumococcal vaccine
Diphtheria, Tetanus, HBV, Haemophilus influenza B, Pertussis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diphtheria, Tetanus, HBV, Haemophilus influenza B, Pertussis

Pentavalent vaccine is a combination of five vaccines that provide protection against 5 life-threatening diseases such as diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B, and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). Administration of pentavalent vaccine reduces the number of pricks to a child.

It is given at 6, 10, and 14 weeks in the immunization program, and can replace the need for separate administration of Hepatitis B and DPT vaccines. However, the Hepatitis B birth dose and DPT booster doses should be continued. It is given 0.5ml intramuscularly in the anterolateral aspect of the mid-thigh.

Pentavalent vaccine is a freeze-sensitive vaccine and therefore should be stored and transported at 2- 8° C temperature. It is a very safe vaccine with a few mild side effects like pain, redness and swelling at the injection site, fever, vomiting, abnormal crying, and loss of appetite.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During assisted vaginal delivery, where is the vacuum device typically applied?
options: At 3 cm behind the anterior fontanelle
3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle
Between the anterior and posterior fontanelle
questions.explanation: In vacuum-assisted delivery, the cup must be placed over the flexion point. This point is located on the sagittal suture, approximately 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle. Placing the cup here ensures that traction results in maximum flexion of the fetal head, allowing the smallest possible diameter (suboccipitobregmatic) to present to the birth canal. Applying the cup behind the anterior fontanelle (Option A) would cause deflexion, increasing the presenting diameter and risk of failure. Placement directly on the posterior fontanelle (Option B) or generalized between the fontanelles (Option D) does not achieve optimal mechanical leverage for head flexion. Therefore, the specific 3 cm anterior position is critical for a safe and successful procedure
questions.learning: In vacuum-assisted delivery, the cup must be placed over the flexion point. This point is located on the sagittal suture, approximately 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: True statement about the action of enhancers of gene expression?
options: Work only when in close conjugation with promoter region
Work only when in upstream of promoter region
They are very specific to the gene
Recruit chromatin and modify regulatory mechanisms
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Recruit chromatin and modify regulatory mechanisms

The correct statement about the action of enhancers is that they recruit chromatin and modify regulatory mechanisms.

A promoter is a sequence on DNA where RNA polymerase binds and acts as the start signal for transcription. They are present upstream or downstream but close to the gene that is undergoing transcription.

Enhancers or repressors are proteins that regulate the expression of a gene by recruiting chromatin(DNA bound with histones) and modifying regulatory mechanisms and making it more or less accessible to transcription by RNA polymerase. They may be located upstream or downstream and can be present at any distance from the promoter region. These are not specific to any single gene and interact with many other proteins.
questions.learning: Recruit chromatin and modify regulatory mechanisms — The correct statement about the action of enhancers is that they recruit chromatin and modify regulatory mechanisms.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the usual method of collecting a sample of urine to detect UTI?
questions.explanation: In toilet-trained individuals, the "clean-catch" midstream urine sample is the preferred method for detecting a Urinary Tract Infection (UTI). This technique minimizes contamination from skin flora and urethral commensals. The patient is instructed to clean the area and discard the initial portion of the stream before collecting the sample. Early morning samples (Option A) are used to screen for proteinuria but are not specific for UTI. Suprapubic aspiration or catheterization (Option C) is the gold standard for accuracy but is invasive and usually reserved for infants or patients unable to provide a voided sample. Starting stream collection (Option D) is avoided because the first voided portion typically contains the highest concentration of contaminating urethral bacteria. Thus, midstream catch offers the best balance of diagnostic accuracy and ease of use
questions.learning: In toilet-trained individuals, the "clean-catch" midstream urine sample is the preferred method for detecting a Urinary Tract Infection (UTI). This technique minimizes contamination from skin flora and urethral commensals.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which vaccines are typically administered to newborns?
questions.explanation: The "birth dose" regimen in India’s National Immunization Schedule consists of exactly three vaccines administered immediately after birth. These are BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) to protect against severe forms of tuberculosis, OPV (zero dose of Oral Polio Vaccine), and Hepatitis B (birth dose). Pentavalent and Hib (Option A) are initiated at 6 weeks. MR (measles-rubella, Options A and B) is given at 9 months. IPV (inactivated polio vaccine, Option D) is administered at 6 and 14 weeks. This combination of three vaccines at birth provides foundational immunity against TB, Polio, and Hepatitis B before the infant leaves the hospital. Therefore, Option C represents the complete and accurate standard of care for neonatal immunization

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are advantages of state of haemodilution during pregnancy? 1. Optimum gaseous exchange between maternal and foetal circulation due to decreased blood viscosity. 2. Protection against adverse effect of supine and erect posture. 3. Protection against adverse effect of blood loss during delivery. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Hemodilution is a normal physiological adaptation during pregnancy resulting from a greater increase in plasma volume (40–50%) than in red cell mass (20–30%), leading to physiological anemia of pregnancy. This adaptation is beneficial for both the mother and the fetus.

• 1. Optimum gaseous exchange between maternal and foetal circulation due to decreased blood viscosity. ✓

• Reduced blood viscosity improves uteroplacental blood flow, facilitating efficient oxygen and nutrient transfer to the fetus.

• 2. Protection against adverse effect of supine and erect posture. ✓

• The expanded plasma volume helps maintain venous return and cardiac output, reducing the hemodynamic effects of postural changes during pregnancy.

• 3. Protection against adverse effect of blood loss during delivery. ✓

• Increased circulating blood volume provides a physiological reserve, allowing pregnant women to better tolerate the 500–1000 mL blood loss that normally occurs during childbirth.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Hemodilution is a normal physiological adaptation during pregnancy resulting from a greater increase in plasma volume (40–50%) than in red cell mass (20–30%), leading to physiological anemia of pregnancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the false statement regarding management of NSTEMI
options: Aspirin loading dose should be commenced immediately
ACC/ AHA guidelines call for either a P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel, prasugrel or ticagrelor) as a class I recommendation
Glycoprotein IIB/IIIA inhibitors are useful adjuncts
Fibrinolytic therapy is useful in acute coronary syndrome without ST-segment elevation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fibrinolytic therapy is useful in acute coronary syndrome without ST-segment elevation

A distinction in acute coronary syndrome between patients with and without ST-segment elevation at presentation is essential to determine the need for reperfusion therapy.

Fibrinolytic therapy is harmful in acute coronary syndrome without ST-segment elevation, unlike with ST-segment elevation, where acute reperfusion saves lives.

Antiplatelet and anticoagulation therapies and coronary intervention are mainstays of treatment.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman presents with decreased fetal movements, and her newborn shows respiratory distress. On examination, the neonate is cyanotic with increased work of breathing, and bowel sounds are auscultated in the left hemithorax. A chest X-ray is provided. Which congenital anomaly is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical finding of bowel sounds in the left hemithorax combined with severe neonatal respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen is diagnostic for Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH). The X-ray confirms this by showing multiple loops of air-filled bowel occupying the left chest and a contralateral shift of the mediastinum. CDH results from a failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close (Bochdalek hernia). The presence of abdominal contents in the chest prevents normal lung development, leading to life-threatening pulmonary hypoplasia and hypertension. Tetralogy of Fallot (Option B) and Transposition (Option C) are cyanotic heart diseases that would show normal lung fields and no bowel in the thorax. Tracheoesophageal fistula (Option D) typically presents with excessive salivation and choking during feeds. Management of CDH involves immediate stabilization with intubation (avoiding bag-mask to prevent bowel distension), gentle ventilation, and eventual surgical repair of the diaphragm once pulmonary pressures are controlled
questions.learning: The clinical finding of bowel sounds in the left hemithorax combined with severe neonatal respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen is diagnostic for Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following are properties of ventricular cardiac muscle?

1. All or none phenomenon
2. Length tension relationship
3. Long refractory period
4. Tetanus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1,2,3

All or none phenomenon, length tension relationship and long refractory period applies to cardiac muscles. Cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized due to long refractory period.

In cardiac myocytes, depolarization proceeds rapidly and an overshoot of the zero potential is present. This is followed by a plateau before the membrane potential reaches the RMP (-90mV). This plateau phase lasts for 200 msec or more. Repolarization is therefore not complete until contraction is 50% completed.

Phases of cardiac action potential

• 0→ Depolarisation and overshoot-Due to opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels
• 1→ Initial rapid repolarization-Due to closure of Na+ channels and opening up of K+ channels
• 2→ Plateau phase - Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels
• 3→ Late rapid repolarization
• 4→ Baseline (RMP)

Phases 3 and 4 are due closure of Ca2+ channels and a slow, delayed increase of K+ efflux through K+ channels.

During phases 0 to 2 and about half of phase 3 of cardiac action potential, cardiac muscle cannot be excited again, that is, it is in its absolute refractory period. It remains relatively refractory until phase 4. Thus, cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized.
questions.learning: 1,2,3 All or none phenomenon, length tension relationship and long refractory period applies to cardiac muscles. Cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized due to long refractory period.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Revised A 55 year old man with a history of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus came to OPD with following wound . What is the diagnosis based on the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carbuncle

The image below shows a case of a carbuncle on the back of the head which is a common location.

Carbuncle:

* A carbuncle is a deep infection of a group of contiguous follicles with S. aureus.

* Intense inflammatory changes in the surrounding and underlying connective tissues, including the subcutaneous fat.

* Larger than abscesses/boils as they represent a cluster of coalescing boils connected under the skin surface.

* Risk factors include diabetes, malnutrition, cardiac failure, drug addiction, obesity and prolonged steroid therapy.

* Smooth painful hard red lump, dome‐shaped and increases in size to reach a diameter of 3–10 cm or more.

* Suppuration begins after some 5–7 days, and pus is discharged from the multiple follicular orifices.

* Necrosis of the intervening skin leaves a yellow slough surmounting a crateriform nodule and can even develop into a deep ulcer with a purulent floor.

* Most commonly on the back of the neck, the shoulders or the hips and thighs.

* Constitutional symptoms like fever, malaise and prostration can be present if severe.

* In the frail and ill, death may occur from toxaemia or from metastatic infection while in favourable cases lesions they usually heal with scarring.

* Treatment includes antibiotics, incision and drainage or saucerization under local anaesthetic to help remove pus and necrotic tissue and expedite healing.

Option A: Botryomycosis presents as multiple indurated draining sinuses mimicking actinomycosis.

Option B: Ecthyma is a pyogenic infection of the skin characterized by the formation of adherent crusts, beneath which ulceration occurs. It most commonly results from mixed infection of group A streptococci > staphylococci and causes a deeper infection than impetigo. The buttocks, thighs, and legs are most commonly affected.

Option C: In erysipelas, well-defined raised margin erythematous lesions are seen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old nulliparous woman with primary infertility is found to have a 5–6 cm ovarian endometrioma on pelvic ultrasonography. She desires future fertility. Which of the following is the most appropriate fertility-preserving treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Laparoscopic cystectomy (cyst wall excision)

For women with ovarian endometrioma ≥4 cm who desire future fertility, the preferred fertility-preserving treatment is laparoscopic cystectomy (complete excision of the cyst wall).

Compared with drainage or ablation, laparoscopic cystectomy:

• Improves spontaneous pregnancy rates
• Reduces recurrence of endometrioma
• Provides tissue for histopathological examination
• Relieves pain more effectively

Why not the other options?

• A. Oophorectomy: Not appropriate in a young nulliparous woman as it reduces ovarian reserve and fertility.
• B. Cauterization (ablation) of the cyst wall: Higher recurrence rates and lower spontaneous pregnancy rates than cystectomy.
• C. Transvaginal cystectomy: Not the standard approach; laparoscopic surgery is preferred.
questions.learning: Laparoscopic cystectomy (cyst wall excision) For women with ovarian endometrioma ≥4 cm who desire future fertility, the preferred fertility-preserving treatment is laparoscopic cystectomy (complete excision of the cyst wall).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Thickest portion of sclera is -
questions.explanation: The sclera is the tough, fibrous outer coat of the eye that maintains its shape and protects internal structures. Its thickness varies significantly throughout the globe. The sclera is thickest at the posterior pole, near the optic nerve head, where it measures approximately 1.0 mm. Conversely, it is thinnest at the points just posterior to the insertions of the extraocular rectus muscles (Option B), where it can be as thin as 0.3 mm. This thinness makes the areas behind the muscle insertions particularly vulnerable to rupture during trauma or perforation during surgical procedures like strabismus surgery. The thickness anterior to the rectus insertions (Option A) is intermediate, roughly 0.6 mm. The "anterior pole" (Option D) refers to the center of the cornea; the sclera itself begins at the limbus. Understanding these anatomical variations is critical for surgeons to avoid accidental globe penetration and for clinicians assessing the severity of ocular injuries. Therefore, the posterior pole is the thickest region of the scleral shell
questions.learning: The sclera is the tough, fibrous outer coat of the eye that maintains its shape and protects internal structures. Its thickness varies significantly throughout the globe.

Correct answer: B. Orientia tsutsugamushi

The given image is of a Trombiculid mite and it transmits Orientia tsutsugamushi.

Orientia tsutsugamushi is an obligate, intracellular bacterium. It causes scrub typhus disease in humans.

Hard ticks are covered by a chitinous shield on their dorsal surface which is called scutum. They have a head or capitulum present at the anterior end, which is visible from above. Hard ticks transmit certain diseases like tick typhus, viral encephalitis, hemorrhagic fever, etc.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which condition is characterized by the presence of an empty delta sign on imaging?
questions.explanation: The "empty delta sign" is the pathognomonic radiological finding for Cerebral Venous (Sinus) Thrombosis on a contrast-enhanced CT scan. It refers to a triangular area of non-enhancement (the thrombus) surrounded by the enhancing wall of the superior sagittal sinus. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option A) presents with blood in the sulci and cisterns. Subdural hemorrhage (Option B) is a crescentic blood collection, and Intra parenchymal hemorrhage (Option D) is blood within the brain tissue. Cerebral venous thrombosis is a common cause of stroke in young adults, particularly women (associated with pregnancy, oral contraceptives, or dehydration). Patients typically present with headache, seizures, and focal deficits. While the empty delta sign is specific, the gold standard for diagnosis is MR venography (MRV). Prompt treatment with anticoagulation (even in the presence of venous hemorrhage) is essential to prevent venous infarction and improve neurological outcomes

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Kidney damage and Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) value between 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m² are found in which stage of Chronic Kidney Disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stage 4 (severe)

Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is defined as kidney damage and/or a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²) persisting for ≥3 months. CKD is classified into five stages based on the estimated GFR (eGFR) according to the KDIGO guidelines.

A patient with an eGFR of 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m² has Stage 4 CKD (Severe reduction in GFR).

Why not the other options?

• A. Stage 2 (Mild): GFR 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m² with evidence of kidney damage.
• B. Stage 3A (Mild to moderate): GFR 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m².
• D. Stage 5 (Kidney failure): GFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² or dialysis-dependent.

| Stage | eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²) | Description

| ----- | --------------------- | -----------

| G1 | ≥90 | Normal/high GFR (with evidence of kidney damage)

| G2 | 60–89 | Mild decrease

| G3a | 45–59 | Mild to moderate decrease

| G3b | 30–44 | Moderate to severe decrease

| G4 ⭐ | 15–29 | Severe decrease in GFR

| G5 | <15 | Kidney failure (ESKD)
questions.learning: Stage 4 (severe) Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is defined as kidney damage and/or a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²) persisting for ≥3 months.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All of the following statements are true regarding thiopentone except?
options: It is quickly concentrated in the brain after IV administration
It shows the phenomenon of redistribution
It has a short duration of action due to rapid renal excretion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It has a short duration of action due to rapid renal excretion

Thiopentone (Thiopental)- An ultra–short-acting barbiturate IV anesthetic used for induction of anesthesia.

Thiopentone is highly lipid soluble and rapidly enters the brain after IV injection. Its brief anesthetic effect is due to redistribution from brain to muscle and fat, not elimination.

Metabolism occurs mainly in the liver, not rapid renal excretion. Hence the short duration is redistribution-dependent, making option D false.
questions.learning: It has a short duration of action due to rapid renal excretion Thiopentone (Thiopental)- An ultra–short-acting barbiturate IV anesthetic used for induction of anesthesia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A young male patient was brought to the emergency department in an unconscious state after having suddenly collapsed at a railway station. As there was no pulse felt, cardiopulmonary resuscitation was started and the monitor showed ventricular fibrillation. Immediate defibrillation was performed. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Resume chest compressions

Chest compressions should be resumed immediately following shock delivery.

A pulse check and reanalysis of the cardiac rhythm is performed only after 2 minutes of chest compression and rescue breaths.

This is done because the defibrillator shock temporarily stuns the heart. Maintaining coronary perfusion during this period is aided by performing chest compressions.

Pearl PF1316: Adult Basic Life Support (BLS) Algorithm (Updated as per 2020 guidelines)

questions.text: What is the drug of choice for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Voriconazole

Voriconazole is the drug of choice in the treatment of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.

Voriconazole can also be used against Candida species (including glabrata and krusei), Scedosporium and Fusarium. The other options - itraconazole, posaconazole, lyophylised Amphotericin B - can be used as alternatives for the treatment of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis if voriconazole is unavailable.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Edmond Locard is most famous for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Theory of exchange

Edmond Locard is famous for his theory of exchange or Locard’s exchange principle.

This theory states that every contact leaves a trace. When two objects come into contact with one another, each will take something from the other object or leave something behind.

Locard is also renowned for his contribution to the improvement of dactylography, an area of study that deals with fingerprints. He developed the science of poroscopy, the study of fingerprint pores, and the impressions produced by these pores.
questions.learning: Theory of exchange Edmond Locard is famous for his theory of exchange or Locard’s exchange principle. This theory states that every contact leaves a trace.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident (RTA) presents with signs of seat belt abdominal trauma on the anterior abdominal wall. What should be the primary concern in terms of potential injuries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hollow viscus injury

The clinical scenario of a seat belt injury most likely indicates a hollow viscus injury. In cases of blunt abdominal trauma, particularly those involving seat belt injuries, there is a risk of sustaining injuries to the hollow viscera, which includes organs such as the stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and bladder.

Seat belt injuries can lead to compression forces against the abdomen, potentially causing shearing or tearing injuries to these structures.

Hollow viscus injuries can be challenging to diagnose clinically and may require imaging studies such as CT scans or exploratory surgery for confirmation.

Other Options:

Options A & B: While liver and spleen injuries are also common in blunt abdominal trauma, especially in cases of seat belt injuries, the question specifies signs of seat belt abdominal trauma on the anterior abdominal wall, which suggests a concern beyond these solid organs.

Option C: While the pancreas can be injured in cases of blunt abdominal trauma, the primary concern in this scenario, given the history of RTA and signs of seat belt abdominal trauma, should be focused on potential injuries to hollow viscera rather than the pancreas specifically.

questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following statements are true regarding overlap syndrome / mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) except:
options: Patients have overlapping clinical features of systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis
Both antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and rheumatoid factor (RF) are commonly positive
Presence of anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) antibodies is specific for MCTD
Prognosis is worse compared to individual connective tissue disorders
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prognosis is worse compared to individual connective tissue disorders

Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) is an overlap autoimmune disorder with features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis, and is strongly associated with anti-U1 RNP antibodies.

• Overlapping manifestations: Raynaud phenomenon, myositis, arthritis, sclerodactyly
• Anti-U1 RNP antibody: highly specific diagnostic marker
• ANA and RF are often positive
• Typically responds well to therapy

Prognosis of MCTD is generally better than many individual connective tissue diseases (especially systemic sclerosis and SLE), unless severe pulmonary hypertension develops. Thus, the statement that prognosis is worse is incorrect.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study is carried out among nursing staff to assess the amount of time spent on various patient care activities, including bed preparation, monitoring vital signs, attending doctors’ rounds, blood sample collection, and drug administration. Which management technique is most suitable for this type of work analysis?
questions.explanation: The study aims to estimate the proportion of time nursing staff spend on various activities throughout the day. Work Sampling is the most appropriate statistical technique for this purpose because it involves making observations at random intervals to determine how time is distributed across different tasks. This method is efficient for assessing workload and providing data for staffing without the need for constant, intrusive monitoring. In contrast, the Critical Path Method (Option A) is a project management tool used for scheduling dependent tasks, not for measuring time proportions. System Analysis (Option B) is a broader study of entire organizational processes. A Time and Motion Study (Option D) involves continuous observation and timing of every single step in a task; while it provides high detail, it is more intrusive and often unnecessary for a general analysis of nursing care time distribution. Therefore, Work Sampling is the standard choice for this healthcare analysis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In proximal transverse colon carcinoma, which of the following arteries are resected to prevent the spread of cancer?
options: Ileocolic, right colic and branch of middle colic
Ileocolic, left colic, and stem of middle colic
Ileocolic, right colic, and trunk of middle colic
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ileocolic, right colic, and trunk of middle colic

Transverse colonic carcinoma is treated with an extended right colectomy. The vessels to be ligated are ileocolic, right colic, and trunk of the middle colic vessels.

Procedures performed for tumors of the colon are summarized below:

Tumor location
Procedure of choice

Cecum/ Ascending colon

Right hemicolectomy

• Ligation and division of the ileocolic, right colic, and right branch of the middle colic vessels
• Resection of cecum + approx 10 cm of the terminal ileum with ileocecal junction + ascending colon + hepatic flexure

Hepatic flexure/Transverse colon

Extended right hemicolectomy

• Ligation and division of the ileocolic, right colic, and trunk of middle colic vessels
• Resection of the cecum + approx 10 cm of the terminal ileum with ileocecal junction + ascending colon + hepatic flexure + proximal transverse colon (distal transverse colon and splenic flexure are also sometimes removed)

Splenic flexure/ Descending colon

Left hemicolectomy

• Ligation and division of the left branch of the middle colic vessels, the left colic vessel, and the first branches of the sigmoid vessels
• Resection of the transverse colon (left MCA territory) + Splenic flexure + Descending colon up to the sigmoid colon

Sigmoid colon
Sigmoid colectomy, or LAR (Low anterior resection)

• Ligation and division of the sigmoid branches of the inferior mesenteric artery.
• Removal of the entire sigmoid colon and rectum

questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and exertional breathlessness. Physical examination reveals pallor. Laboratory investigations show microcytic, hypochromic red cells. Which is the most common type of anemia in India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iron deficiency anemia

The most common type of anaemia in a 65-year-old male is iron deficiency anemia(IDA). It is also the most common type of nutritional anemia in India.

IDA is an example of microcytic hypochromic anemia. The causes of IDA can be inadequate diet, impaired reabsorption, increased requirement, and increased blood loss.

The manifestations of IDA depend upon the underlying cause. In general, IDA presents with koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic changes in the tongue, gastric mucosa, malabsorption and pica (craving for consumption of non-edible materials)

Peripheral smears show small and pale red cells typically described as microcytic (reduced MCV) and hypochromic (enlarged zone of central pallor). Poikilocytosis can be seen in the form of elongated red cells, known as pencil cells. Target cells can be found in cases of severe IDA.

Diagnosis is mainly by laboratory studies. The typical findings are:

* Low hemoglobin and hematocrit

* Low serum iron and ferritin

* Increased Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC)

* Hepcidin is low (decreased stores of iron inhibit hepcidin synthesis)

IDA is treated by giving oral and parenteral preparations of iron or packed cell transfusion depending upon the severity of the anemia.

Other options:

Option A: In aplastic anemia, the bone marrow does not produce enough progenitor cells. It can be caused by autoimmune diseases, medications, and radiation. Aplastic anemia can lead to a decrease in all types of blood cells and is associated with a low MCV and a low hemoglobin level, not a high MCV.

Option B: Megaloblastic anemia can be caused by a deficiency of vitamin B12 or folate. Vegetarians are at increased risk of vitamin B12 deficiency because vitamin B12 is primarily found in animal products. Other conditions can also cause megaloblastic anemia, such as celiac disease, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis

Option D: Anemia of chronic disease is mediated by hepcidin, a positive acute-phase reactant (APR) that increases in chronic inflammatory states.It is seen in conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic infections, and malignancies.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the causes of fall in diastolic blood pressure is correct? 1. Loss of sympathetic outflow in the lumbar region 2. Antagonism of beta-1 adrenergic receptors 3. Blockade of alpha-1 adrenergic receptors 4. Antagonism of beta-2 adrenergic receptors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 3

Diastolic BP is mainly governed by Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR)

Not cardiac output.

Diastolic pressure mainly reflects peripheral vascular resistance. Loss of lumbar sympathetic outflow and alpha-1 blockade cause vasodilation and reduced resistance, lowering diastolic BP. Beta-1 antagonism primarily reduces heart rate and contractility, affecting systolic more than diastolic pressure. Beta-2 blockade causes vasoconstriction, which would increase diastolic pressure, not decrease it.

| Receptor | Action | Effect on DBP

| -------- | ------ | -------------

| α1 | Vasoconstriction | ↑ DBP

| β1 | ↑ CO | ↑ SBP mainly

| β2 | Vasodilation | ↓ DBP

| β2 blockade | Vasoconstriction | ↑ DBP
questions.learning: 1 and 3 Diastolic BP is mainly governed by Systemic Vascular Resistance (SVR) Not cardiac output. Diastolic pressure mainly reflects peripheral vascular resistance.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with elbow deformity and forearm shortening after a fall. An X-ray was done and given below. What is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Elbow dislocation

The given clinical history and X-ray are suggestive of elbow dislocation. X-ray shows posterior dislocation of the elbow joint.

Elbow dislocation is the most common dislocation in the pediatric age group and the second most common dislocation after the shoulder in adults.

Posterior dislocation is the commonest type of elbow dislocation. It frequently occurs due to a fall on the outstretched hands with the elbow slightly flexed. Other dislocations are postero-medial, postero-lateral, and divergent.

Anterior dislocation occurs when the elbow is flexed and there is a direct blow on the posterior aspect of the elbow joint.

Clinical features:

* The forearm appears shortened.

* Crepitus is absent.

* The three-point bony relationship is disrupted.

* Olecranon is above the intercondylar line

Elbow dislocation is an emergency and has to be reduced immediately. Closed reduction under general anaesthesia(GA) is attempted first. An above elbow POP slab is applied with 90º elbow flexion and mid-pronation for a period of 3 weeks after closed reduction under GA.

Stimson’s 2 step principles for closed reduction

* Step 1 - traction along the long axis of the humerus to counteract the contraction of biceps, triceps and brachialis

* Step 2 - traction along the long axis of the forearm to bring radius and ulna back into position
2 techniques in closed reduction

Prone technique - Grab the wrist of the injured arm. Apply traction and slight supination to the forearm. Using the other hand, apply pressure to the posterior aspect of the olecranon while the arm is pronated.

Supine technique - a helper stabilizes the humerus against the stretcher with both hands. Grasp the wrist, and apply slow, steady, inline traction, keeping the elbow slightly flexed and the wrist supinated

Complications:

* Early complications include neurovascular injury. Vascular injuries are rare and involve the brachial artery in open fractures associated with elbow dislocation.

* Late complications include myositis ossificans, recurrent dislocations, proximal radioulnar translocation, and ectopic calcifications
questions.learning: Elbow dislocation — The given clinical history and X-ray are suggestive of elbow dislocation. X-ray shows posterior dislocation of the elbow joint.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the best post-coital contraceptive method?
questions.explanation: Levonorgestrel (LNG) is considered the drug of choice (DOC) for post-coital (emergency) contraception. It is widely used, easily available (e.g., i-pill), and has a good safety profile with minimal side effects. It works mainly by inhibiting or delaying ovulation. Key points: 1. Effective if taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse 2. Can be given as a single 1.5 mg dose or two divided doses 3. Does not interfere significantly with the normal menstrual cycle Why other options are incorrect: (B) Estrogen: Used in older regimens; associated with more side effects (nausea, vomiting, thrombosis) (C) Norethisterone: Not used for emergency contraception; mainly for menstrual disorders (D) Ulipristal acetate: More effective pharmacologically, but LNG is the preferred DOC in Indian guidelines and exams Thus, as per exam standards, the best answer is Levonorgestrel
questions.learning: Levonorgestrel (LNG) is considered the drug of choice (DOC) for post-coital (emergency) contraception. It is widely used, easily available (e.g., i-pill), and has a good safety profile with minimal side effects.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old healthy man with a history of small streaks of blood in his stools is being sent for a colonoscopy to screen for colon cancer. This type of prevention is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Secondary

Colonoscopies for early detection/screening of colon cancer are an example of secondary prevention.

Early diagnosis (including screening) and treatment are the components of secondary prevention. Some examples of secondary prevention are as follows:

* Papanicolaou (Pap) smear for early detection of cervical cancer

* Mammography, for early detection of breast cancer

* Colonoscopies, for early detection of colon cancer

* Blood Pressure Screening

Secondary prevention measures focus on the sub-clinical stage and the early clinical stage, such as dysplasia in this case. These measures enable early detection and prompt effective intervention to correct departures from a state of health.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of these is seen in acute pancreatitis?
options: Lipase is more specific than amylase
Lipase requires 30 days to return to baseline
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lipase is more specific than amylase

✅ Lipase is more specific than amylase

• Lipase comes almost only from the pancreas, so elevations point to pancreatic injury.
• Amylase rises in many conditions (salivary gland disease, bowel perforation), so less specific.

❌ Lipase requires 30 days to return to baseline

• Lipase rises 4–8 h after onset, peaks at 24 h, and returns to baseline in 7–14 days.
• Lipase does not persist for a month;
• Prolonged elevation usually suggests ongoing pancreatic injury, chronic pancreatitis, or pseudocyst formation

❌ Lipase reflects severity of pancreatitis

• Level of lipase does not indicate how severe the pancreatitis is.
• Severity is assessed clinically (Ranson, BISAP, APACHE II).

❌ 75% cases have hypercalcemia on admission

• Actually, acute pancreatitis can cause hypocalcemia (from fat necrosis and saponification).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: On a chest X-ray, obliteration of the right cardiac border is observed. Which of the following structures is likely involved in this pathology?
questions.explanation: The "silhouette sign" is a fundamental concept in chest radiology where the loss of a normal anatomical interface indicates pathology in the adjacent lung tissue. The right cardiac border is anatomically adjacent to the "right middle lobe" (RML). Therefore, a consolidation or mass that "obliterates the right cardiac border" is located in the right middle lobe (Option C). Pathology in the right lower lobe (Option A) would obliterate the right diaphragmatic border but leave the cardiac silhouette sharp. The right ventricle (Option B) is not usually the border-forming structure on a PA chest X-ray, and the right atrium (Option D) is the border-forming structure, but its obliteration is caused by lung pathology sitting next to it. Understanding these relationships allows radiologists to localize lobar pneumonia or atelectasis on a single frontal projection. The RML is a common site for infection and its involvement is best confirmed on a lateral view showing an opacity between the major and minor fissures
questions.learning: The "silhouette sign" is a fundamental concept in chest radiology where the loss of a normal anatomical interface indicates pathology in the adjacent lung tissue.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Berry aneurysm occurs due to:
options: Endothelial injury of vessel due to HTN
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arterial internal elastic lamina defect

Berry aneurysm occurs due an arterial internal elastic lamina defect.

As an aneurysm develops, it typically forms a neck with a dome and the arterial internal elastic lamina disappears at the base of the neck. The media thins and connective tissue replaces the smooth-muscle cells. The site of rupture is most often the dome. Here the wall thins, and the tear that allows bleeding is usually ≤0.5 mm long.

Risk of aneurysm rupture is higher if:

• Aneurysm is >7 mm in diameter
• Aneurysm at the top of the basilar artery
• Aneurysm at the origin of the posterior communicating artery
questions.learning: Arterial internal elastic lamina defect Berry aneurysm occurs due an arterial internal elastic lamina defect. As an aneurysm develops, it typically forms a neck with a dome and the arterial internal elastic lamina disappears at the base of the neck.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old HIV-positive individual with a low CD4 count presents with fever, cough, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and characteristic findings on bone marrow biopsy. What is the mode of transmission of this disease?
options: Inhalation of bird or bat droppings
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inhalation of bird or bat droppings

The images show Histoplasma capsulatum:

• Mold phase with tuberculate macroconidia
• Small intracellular yeast forms within macrophages on bone marrow biopsy

Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus acquired by inhalation of microconidia from soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings. In immunocompromised patients (especially those with HIV/AIDS and CD4 <150 cells/µL), it can cause disseminated histoplasmosis, involving the lungs, bone marrow, liver, spleen, and reticuloendothelial system.

Why not the other options?

• B. Bite of infected rats: Associated with rat-bite fever (Streptobacillus moniliformis or Spirillum minus), not histoplasmosis.
• C. Ingestion of contaminated dairy products: Seen in brucellosis and Listeria infection.
• D. Skin inoculation: Typical for sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii), acquired via thorn pricks.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient with infertility presents with a combination of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Kartagener’s syndrome is a specific variant of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD) characterized by the classic triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. It results from a genetic defect in the axonemal dynein arms of motile cilia, leading to immotile or dyskinetic cilia. Because ciliary motion is essential for mucociliary clearance, affected individuals develop recurrent respiratory tract infections, chronic sinusitis, and progressive bronchiectasis. The same dynein arm defect also affects flagellar movement of sperm, resulting in male infertility due to immotile sperm. Cystic fibrosis (Option B)—also known as mucoviscidosis (Option C)—can cause bronchiectasis and infertility, but it does not cause situs inversus, which is the key distinguishing feature here. Klinefelter syndrome (Option D) leads to primary testicular failure and infertility but is not associated with respiratory disease or situs inversus. Thus, the presence of situs inversus (e.g., dextrocardia on imaging) is the crucial diagnostic clue confirming Kartagener’s syndrome
questions.learning: Kartagener’s syndrome is a specific variant of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD) characterized by the classic triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Type-2 necrotizing fasciitis is caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Group A Streptococcus

Classification of necrotizing fasciitis:

• Type I: Polymicrobial (mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms) – most common overall.
• Type II: Monomicrobial – Group A Streptococcus ± Staphylococcus aureus.
• Type III: Marine organisms (Vibrio vulnificus) or Clostridium species (gas gangrene variants in some classifications).

Why not the other options?

• B. Vibrio vulnificus: Causes Type III necrotizing fasciitis, usually after exposure to seawater or raw seafood.
• C. Clostridium septicum: Causes clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene) and spontaneous infections, often associated with colonic malignancy or neutropenia, not classic Type II necrotizing fasciitis.
• D. Staphylococcus aureus: May coexist with Group A Streptococcus in Type II disease but is not the classic primary causative organism.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with thick nasal discharge and headache. Examination reveals hypertrophy of the inferior turbinate with a mulberry appearance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypertrophic rhinitis

This clinical vignette is suggestive of hypertrophic rhinitis.

It is characterized by the thickening of the mucosa, submucosa, seromucous glands, periosteum, and bone.

Recurrent nasal infections, chronic sinusitis, chronic irritation of nasal mucosa due to smoking, prolonged use of nasal drops, vasomotor and allergic rhinitis, and industrial irritants are some of the causes of hypertrophic rhinitis.

Clinical features are thick and sticky nasal discharge, headache, and transient anosmia. Examination reveals hypertrophy of the turbinates with underlying fibrosis. Mulberry hypertrophy is seen in hypertrophic rhinitis. Maximum changes are seen in the inferior turbinate.

Treatment includes cryosurgery of turbinates, linear cauterisation, submucosal diathermy, partial or total turbinectomy and lasers.

Pearl PF1339: Clinical Features of Atrophic Rhinitis

* More common in females

* Usually starts at puberty

* It is a bilateral condition

* Symptoms:

* Foul smell from the nose

* Nasal obstruction in spite of roomy chambers due to large crusts filling nasal cavity

* Epistaxis on removing of the crusts

* Anosmia due to degeneration of nerve elements (merciful anosmia)

* Signs:

* Greenish or greyish black dry crusts covering the turbinates and septum

* After removal of crusts, nasal cavities appear roomy with atrophy of turbinates

* Nasal mucosa appears pale

Pearl PF1084: Antrochoanal Polyp

* Main etiological factors: Infection and allergy

* Usually affects children

* Site of origin: Mucosa of the maxillary antrum

* Clinical features:

* Usually single and unilateral

* Unilateral nasal obstruction which becomes bilateral when it grows posteriorly and obstructs opposite choana

* Mucoid nasal discharge

* Hyponasal voice

* Findings:

* Grows posteriorly and usually missed on anterior rhinoscopy

* Posterior rhinoscopy: Globular mass filling the choana or nasopharynx

* Investigation of choice: Nasal endoscopy. Shows nasal polyps that are pale, gelatinous and pedunculated

* Treatment of choice: FESS
questions.learning: Hypertrophic rhinitis — This clinical vignette is suggestive of hypertrophic rhinitis. It is characterized by the thickening of the mucosa, submucosa, seromucous glands, periosteum, and bone.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 6-month-old male infant presents with recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. He is diagnosed with severe combined immunodeficiency inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Which enzyme deficiency is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a group of rare disorders characterized by the absence of both T and B lymphocyte function. Approximately 15% of SCID cases are caused by a deficiency of the enzyme Adenosine deaminase (ADA), which is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. The lack of ADA leads to the toxic buildup of dATP in lymphocytes, which halts their development and function. ADA deficiency typically presents in infancy with the "classic SCID triad": recurrent infections, diarrhea, and failure to thrive. OTC deficiency (Option B) leads to hyperammonemia. HGPRT deficiency (Option C) results in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (gout/self-mutilation). Phosphomannose isomerase (Option A) is involved in protein glycosylation. ADA-SCID is a pediatric emergency because it is fatal without treatment; management options include hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, enzyme replacement therapy, or gene therapy

questions.text: A labourer's younger child is brought to the OPD with a swollen belly and dull face. He has been fed rice water (rice milk) in his diet mostly. On investigations, the child is found to have low serum protein and low albumin. What is the probable diagnosis?

A poor diet history (rice water) and a swollen belly are suggestive of Kwashiorkor.

Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) characterized by oedema and apathy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with bleeding due to factor IX deficiency. In which of the following conditions will you find an improvement after administering Vitamin K parenterally?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bile duct obstruction

Vitamin K–dependent factors

Without Vitamin K → these factors are produced but non-functional

Correct answer is B because vitamin K is required for hepatic synthesis of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X), and in bile duct obstruction fat-soluble vitamin absorption is impaired, leading to deficiency that improves with parenteral vitamin K.

Pernicious anemia is due to vitamin B12 deficiency. Hepatitis A causes hepatocellular injury where vitamin K response may be limited. Classical hemophilia (factor VIII deficiency) does not respond to vitamin K.

| Condition | Problem | Vitamin K effect

| --------- | ------- | ----------------

| Bile duct obstruction | ↓ absorption | ✅ Improves

| Vitamin K deficiency | ↓ activation | ✅ Improves

| Hemophilia | Factor absent | ❌ No effect

| Liver disease | ↓ synthesis | ❌ Limited

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A two-month-old infant presents with difficulty feeding, vomiting, and lethargy. Laboratory tests reveal hyperammonemia and high levels of orotic acid in the urine. Which of the following is the most probable enzyme deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency

The clinical scenario of a child with recurrent vomiting and failure to thrive, hyperammonemia and increased urinary excretion of orotic acid is indicative of Type 2 Hyperammonemia or ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency (OTC deficiency).

Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency leads to lethargy progressing to coma, protein aversion, intellectual disability, and hyperammonemia.

Type II hyperammonemia results from a deficiency of ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC). In the urea cycle, the enzyme ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyses the condensation of carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to the accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate, which is channelled to pyrimidine synthesis, leading to increased excretion of orotic acid.

Clinical symptoms include vomiting, irritability and severe mental retardation. Mild forms show episodes of hyperammonemia, manifested by vomiting and neurologic abnormalities (e.g., ataxia, mental confusion, agitation). These episodes usually occur after ingestion of a high-protein diet or as a result of a catabolic state such as infection.

The laboratory findings during the acute attack are hyperammonemia accompanied by marked elevations of plasma concentrations of glutamine and alanine with low levels of citrulline and arginine. The blood level of urea is usually low. There is a marked increase in the urinary excretion of orotic acid. Diagnosis is confirmed by gene analysis.

Management includes treatment of acute hyperammonemia attacks. For enteral use, citrulline is used in place of arginine in patients with OTC deficiency. Liver transplantation is a successful treatment for patients with severe OTC deficiency. Long-term treatment consists of a protein-restricted diet.

Other options:

Option A: In Type 1 Hyperammonemia (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency), the symptoms appear during the first few days or even hours of life, and the baby presents with the signs and symptoms of hyperammonemia (refusal to eat, vomiting, lethargy, convulsion, and coma). Increased intracranial pressure is frequent. The child will show low levels of citrulline and orotic acid in the blood.

Option C: Argininosuccinate lyase enzyme splits argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate. When deficient, argininosuccinate accumulates, leading to argininosuccinic aciduria, often presenting with brittle hair (trichorrhexis nodosa).

Option D: Orotic aciduria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in uridine monophosphate (UMP) synthase. This enzyme contains two activities, orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and orotidine decarboxylase. The lack of pyrimidines impairs nucleic acid synthesis needed for haematopoiesis, would result in megaloblastic anaemia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 55-year-old patient with colorectal cancer is receiving chemotherapy. Which drug acts primarily by inhibiting the availability of thymidylate during DNA synthesis?
questions.explanation: In the treatment of colorectal cancer, 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) is a fundamental antimetabolite drug. Its primary mechanism of action is the inhibition of thymidylate synthase, the enzyme responsible for converting dUMP to dTMP (thymidylate). By irreversibly binding to the enzyme along with a folate cofactor, 5-FU creates a "thymineless death" for rapidly dividing cancer cells by halting DNA synthesis. Methotrexate (Option D) also affects thymidylate but it works upstream by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase, thereby depleting the folate cofactor rather than primarily the enzyme itself. Cisplatin (Option B) is an alkylating-like agent that causes DNA cross-links. Rituximab (Option A) is a monoclonal antibody against CD20 used for lymphomas. 5-FU is often administered with leucovorin, which actually potentiates 5-FU's inhibition of thymidylate synthase by increasing the formation of the stable ternary complex. Clinically, 5-FU is associated with side effects like myelosuppression, diarrhea, and the characteristic hand-foot syndrome
questions.learning: In the treatment of colorectal cancer, 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) is a fundamental antimetabolite drug. Its primary mechanism of action is the inhibition of thymidylate synthase, the enzyme responsible for converting dUMP to dTMP (thymidylate).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The duodenum is derived embryologically from which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Foregut and midgut

The duodenum has a dual embryological origin:

• The proximal part (up to the opening of the bile duct) develops from the caudal foregut
• The distal part develops from the cranial midgut

Duodenum = Foregut + Midgut junction

• Foregut derivatives include: pharynx, esophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas
• Midgut derivatives include: distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, proximal 2/3 of transverse colon

The major duodenal papilla (bile duct opening) marks the transition between foregut and midgut.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was conducted in a school where information regarding vaccination status, gender of students, and their pain scale scores was collected. Mention the types of data taken in the same sequence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nominal, Nominal, Ordinal

The vaccination status and gender are classified as nominal data, since they represent categories without any order. The pain scale is an ordinal variable, because the numbers indicate ranking of severity but No size interval is defined.

Data always forms one of four scales of measurement – nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio scales (mnemonic: NOIR):

Nominal Scale Data

Ordinal Scale Data

Interval Scale Data

Ratio Scale Data

Example

Male/female; red/green; sub-urban/rural

Students ranked 1st/2nd/3rd in their class.

A customer feedback survey using terms like very good, good, poor and very poor or the Likert Scale.

Severity of a disease as mild, moderate, severe

Measurements on the celsius scale.

Pulse rate;

Notes

Have no quantitative value.

They have no order or ratio.

Arranged in a meaningful order.

No size interval is defined

Arranged in a meaningful order with a well defined size interval.

Example: Temperature in Celsius. If temperature in A is 40 deg Celsius and that in B is 20 deg Celsius, then A is 20 deg Celsius hotter than B (taking difference)

Does not have an absolute zero.

For example, Celsius scale has no such thing as “no temperature”. So the value cannot be zero.

Arranged in a meaningful order with a well defined size interval.

Eg: A pulse rate has well defined intervals and is meaningful in comparison. A 100/min pulse is exactly twice of 50 beats/min.

Has an absolute zero.

Eg: There can be a value of zero for pulse.

Type

Qualitative

Qualitative

Quantitative

Quantitative

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct order of the cardinal movements of labor? (NEET PG 2015)
options: Descent, engagement, internal rotation, flexion, external rotation
Descent, engagement, internal rotation, flexion, external rotation+
Engagement, Descent, Flexion, Internal, Rotation, Extension, External Rotation, Expulsion
Engagement, descent, external rotation, internal rotation, flexion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Engagement, Descent, Flexion, Internal, Rotation, Extension, External Rotation, Expulsion

The cardinal movements of normal labor describe the positional changes the fetus undergoes while passing through the birth canal.

Correct sequence:

1. Engagement
2. Descent
3. Flexion
4. Internal rotation
5. Extension
6. External rotation (restitution)
7. Expulsion

Key concepts:

• Engagement: Biparietal diameter passes pelvic inlet
• Flexion: Chin moves toward chest, presenting smaller diameter
• Internal rotation: Occiput rotates anteriorly toward symphysis pubis
• Extension: Head extends while passing under pubic symphysis
• External rotation: Head realigns with shoulders after delivery
• Expulsion: Delivery of shoulders and body
questions.learning: Engagement, Descent, Flexion, Internal, Rotation, Extension, External Rotation, Expulsion The cardinal movements of normal labor describe the positional changes the fetus undergoes while passing through the birth canal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What are the reasons for choosing coliform organisms as indicators of faecal pollution of water rather than the waterborne pathogens directly? I. They are present in great abundance in the human intestine and excreted in great numbers in faeces. II. They have lower resistance to forces of natural purification. III. They survive less than the pathogens. IV. They are easily detected by culture methods. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I and IV

The following statements are correct:

• I. They are present in great abundance in the human intestine and excreted in great numbers in feces: Coliforms, especially E. coli, are normal intestinal flora and are shed in large numbers, making them reliable indicators of fecal pollution.
• IV. They are easily detected by culture methods: Coliforms can be identified rapidly using simple and inexpensive methods such as the Most Probable Number (MPN) test and membrane filtration.

Why are II and III incorrect?

• II. They have lower resistance to forces of natural purification: An ideal indicator organism should have resistance similar to or greater than many pathogens, so that its absence suggests water safety.
• III. They survive less than the pathogens: Indicator organisms should survive at least as long as enteric pathogens, making this statement incorrect.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following statements correctly explains how ABO and Rh blood group incompatibility can result in erythroblastosis fetalis?
questions.explanation: Erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn) is the classic clinical example of a Type II hypersensitivity reaction, also known as a cytotoxic reaction . In this mechanism, specific antibodies (IgG) produced by the mother against fetal Rh or ABO antigens cross the placenta and bind to the surface of fetal red blood cells. This binding leads to the direct destruction of these cells through complement activation or opsonization and subsequent phagocytosis by splenic macrophages. Option B refers to Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity. Option C is a general term for all immune responses but lacks the specific pathological classification. Option D refers to Type III hypersensitivity involving circulating complexes. Because the pathology involves the direct, antibody-mediated destruction of target cells (erythrocytes), "cytotoxic" is the definitive descriptive term for this hypersensitivity mechanism. Recognizing this helps in understanding the rationale for using Rho(D) immune globulin as a preventative measure
questions.learning: Erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn) is the classic clinical example of a Type II hypersensitivity reaction, also known as a cytotoxic reaction .

questions.text: What is the diagnosis based on the CT image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. PUJO

Pelviureteric junction obstruction causes massive pelvis dilatation with parenchymal thinning. ADPKD shows multiple cysts, renal cyst is solitary, horseshoe kidney is fused poles.

• Dilated renal pelvis + calyces
• Abrupt narrowing at PUJ
• Normal ureter (key differentiator!)
• Kidney may appear enlarged

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 54-year-old female patient presents with abdominal pain and bilious vomiting. She had a history of abdominal hysterectomy 2 years back. On examination, abdomen auscultation revealed high-pitched bowel sounds. Investigations showed air within the biliary tree. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gallstone ileus

The given scenario shows abdominal pain with bilious vomiting and high-pitched bowel sounds which are suggestive of intestinal obstruction along with radiographic features of pneumobilia (air within the biliary tree) pointing to the diagnosis of gallstone ileus.

Gallstone ileus is a condition that occurs secondary to the erosion of the gallbladder wall, which results in a fistula to the duodenum. Through this, a large gallstone can pass from the gallbladder to the duodenum and usually gets impacted in the distal ileum (the most common site), where it may cause intestinal obstruction.

Rigler’s triad is a characteristic radiological feature seen in gallstone ileus and consists of:

1. Pneumobilia - air present in the intestine passes into the biliary tree through the fistula
2. Features of small bowel obstruction (abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, hyperechoic bowel sounds)
3. Ectopic gallstone - usually in the right iliac fossa

Plain X-rays show air-fluid levels consistent with a small bowel obstruction and pneumobilia can also be visualized on CT imaging.

Gallstone ileus is managed by an explorative laparotomy to relieve the bowel obstruction. The stone is milked away from the site of impacted and then crushed or removed.

Other complications of gallstones include biliary colic, acute and chronic cholecystitis, empyema of the gallbladder, mucocele, perforation, acute cholangitis, and acute pancreatitis.

Other options:

Option B: Adhesive intestinal obstruction is seen after any abdominal surgery or any cause for peritoneal irritation, the features are consistent with bowel obstruction (air-fluid levels, featureless distal ileum) but there is no pneumobilia.

Option C: Ischaemic colitis on contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen (CECT) shows bowel wall thickening, and signs of vascular insufficiency.

Option D: Diverticulitis on CT abdomen shows bright bowel outpouching, which may be complicated by infection and abscess formation.
