questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following publications is/are brought out by the World Health Organization? 1. CD Alert 2. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report 3. Weekly Epidemiological Record Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3 only

The World Health Organization (WHO) publishes several global health reports and surveillance bulletins. Among them, the Weekly Epidemiological Record (WER) is the official WHO publication that provides updates on outbreaks, vaccine-preventable diseases, and international public health events.

• 1. CD Alert ✗

• Published by the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), India, not WHO.

• 2. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) ✗

• Published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), USA.

• 3. Weekly Epidemiological Record (WER) ✓

• Official WHO weekly publication providing global surveillance data, disease outbreaks, immunization updates, and public health recommendations.
questions.learning: 3 only The World Health Organization (WHO) publishes several global health reports and surveillance bulletins. Among them, the Weekly Epidemiological Record (WER) is the official WHO publication that provides updates on outbreaks, vaccine-preventable…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old alcoholic with a history of binge drinking presents with an episode of vomiting bright red blood. His vitals are stable. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mallory Weiss Tear

The most probable diagnosis for the above-mentioned clinical presentation is Mallory Weiss tear .

Mallory Weiss Syndrome is due to a longitudinal tear in mucosa or submucosa of the gastroesophageal junction. It is a common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to the presence of longitudinal superficial mucosal lacerations (Mallory-Weiss tears). The left gastric artery is the most common vessel to bleed.

It mainly occurs in patients with repetitive forceful retching and vomiting and is associated with heavy alcohol intake. The presence of portal hypertension with oesophagal varices and hiatal hernia may aggravate the condition. The investigation of choice is endoscopy.

Management of Mallory Weiss tear is conservative, as it usually is self-limiting. Endoscopic electrocoagulation or sclerosant therapy is done in some cases. Angiographic embolization or high gastrotomy is necessary only in rare cases that don't respond to conservative management.

Boerhaave syndrome is characterized by a tear in the lower third of the oesophagus which occurs when a person vomits against a closed glottis, causing a leak into the mediastinum, pleural cavity and peritoneum. Here all layers are involved.

The patients initially present with severe chest pain, tachypnea, and shock. Clinical features include Mackler's triad

* Retching

* Chest pain

* Subcutaneous emphysema

This catastrophic event produces severe mediastinitis(deranged vitals tachypnea, tachycardia, fever, and hypotension) and generally requires surgical intervention.
questions.learning: Mallory Weiss Tear — The most probable diagnosis for the above-mentioned clinical presentation is Mallory Weiss tear . Mallory Weiss Syndrome is due to a longitudinal tear in mucosa or submucosa of the gastroesophageal junction.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What causes decrease in GFR?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decrease in glomerular coefficient

Decrease in glomerular coefficient causes decrease in GFR.

The glomerular filtration coefficient (Kf) is a measure of how efficiently the glomerulus filters blood into the kidney tubules. It depends on two key factors:

• Surface Area for Filtration: Greater surface area means higher filtration.
• Permeability of the Glomerular Membrane: Higher permeability leads to greater filtration.

Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the volume of fluid filtered from the renal glomerular capillaries into the Bowman's capsule per unit time.

The GFR is determined by the sum of the hydrostatic and colloid osmotic forces across the glomerular membrane, which gives the net filtration pressure. It is dependent on Glomerular Kf (glomerular ultrafiltration coefficient) also.

Mathematically, it can be expressed as follows:

GFR= Kf [PG + πB -PB- πG]

Forces favoring Filtration

• PG: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure (Option C)
• πB: Bowman’s capsule oncotic pressure

Forces opposing Filtration

• PB: Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure (Option D)
• πG: Glomerular capillary oncotic pressure (Option B)

The formula for glomerular filtration rate (GFR) incorporates Kf:

• A high Kf means efficient filtration (e.g., in healthy kidneys)-indicates high GFR
• A low Kf {occurs when the surface area is reduced (e.g., due to glomerular damage) or the membrane becomes less permeable (e.g., in diabetic nephropathy)}- indicates low GFR.

Kf is essential for maintaining proper kidney function, as it directly affects how well the kidneys filter blood to form urine.
questions.learning: Decrease in glomerular coefficient Decrease in glomerular coefficient causes decrease in GFR. The glomerular filtration coefficient (Kf) is a measure of how efficiently the glomerulus filters blood into the kidney tubules.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A motorcyclist sustains a metacarpal fracture in a road traffic accident and is found to have hypothenar atrophy. Which nerve is likely involved?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve provides the primary motor supply to the intrinsic muscles of the hand, including those of the hypothenar eminence (abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi, and opponens digiti minimi). Hypothenar atrophy is a classic sign of chronic ulnar nerve injury, often occurring at the wrist (Guyon's canal) or the elbow (cubital tunnel). In trauma, the nerve can be damaged during metacarpal fractures or carpal dislocations. The radial nerve (Option A) primarily supplies the extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers; its injury leads to "wrist drop." The median nerve (Option D) supplies the thenar muscles at the base of the thumb; its injury leads to "ape hand" deformity. The musculocutaneous nerve (Option C) supplies the biceps and brachialis in the upper arm and does not have intrinsic hand motor functions. Therefore, atrophy specifically affecting the hypothenar region confirms the involvement of the ulnar nerve
questions.learning: The ulnar nerve provides the primary motor supply to the intrinsic muscles of the hand, including those of the hypothenar eminence (abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi, and opponens digiti minimi).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young male who is a professional trumpet blower presented with a swelling on the left side of the neck. On examination, there is a gurgling sound while compressing the swelling. X-ray of the neck is seen below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Laryngocele

The given image along with the examination finding of Bryce's sign is suggestive of laryngocoele.

Laryngocele is an air-filled cystic swelling in the neck due to dilatation of the saccule. It is more commonly seen in trumpet players, glass-blowers, or weight lifters due to a raised transglottic air pressure in these people. It can be classified into internal, external, or combined types of laryngocele.

* Internal laryngocele is limited within the larynx and appears as a distension of the false cord and aryepiglottic fold.

* External laryngocele has a distended saccule that herniates through the thyrohyoid membrane and appears as a swelling in the neck.

* Combined or mixed laryngocele has both internal and external laryngoceles as its components where the air-filled sac extends both within the larynx and externally through the thyrohyoid membrane into the neck, and potentially into the mediastinum.

It presents with hoarseness of voice, cough, and airway obstruction (if large). External laryngocele presents as a reducible swelling in the neck that increases in size on coughing or performing the Valsalva maneuver. On pressing the neck swelling, a gurgling sound is heard, indicating a positive Bryce's sign. Adult laryngoceles can be associated with carcinoma.

Diagnosis is based on an indirect laryngoscopy and CT scan. Internal laryngocele is managed by marsupialization and external laryngocele is managed by a surgical excision through an external neck incision.

Other options:

Option A: The pharyngeal pouch(Zenker diverticulum) is a pulsion-pseudodiverticulum and results from herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the Killian triangle (or dehiscence of Killian). Killian's triangle is an area of muscular weakness between the transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus and the oblique fibres of the thyropharyngeus.

Option C: A tracheoesophageal fistula is an abnormal fistula communication between the oesophagus and the trachea. Type C lesion is associated with proximal oesophagal atresia and distal TEF, the proximal blind pouch ends approximately at the distance of one or two vertebral bodies from the distal TEF.

Option D: The tonsillar cyst is due to blockage of a tonsillar crypt and appears as a yellowish swelling over the tonsil. Very often it is symptomless. It can be easily drained.
questions.learning: Laryngocele — The given image along with the examination finding of Bryce's sign is suggestive of laryngocoele. Laryngocele is an air-filled cystic swelling in the neck due to dilatation of the saccule.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An intrauterine scan at the 13th week of pregnancy showed a fetus with multiple long bone fractures. What is commonly associated with this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Osteogenesis imperfecta

Osteogenesis imperfecta is commonly associated with this multiple long bone fractures.

Osteogenesis imperfecta is a connective tissue disorder that occurs due to abnormal type 1 collagen production. The main features are joints that are vulnerable to fracture, scleral alterations, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and deafness. Multiple bone fractures are a consequence of bone fragility. It is classified into four types based on scleral involvement, natural history, and mode of inheritance.

Protrusio acetabuli, wormian bones, and proximal femoral ‘shepherd’s crook’ deformities of the femurs are the common radiological findings that are observed. Management comprises the use of bisphosphonates, along with physiotherapy and walking aids.

The images below show blue sclera and wormian bones in osteogenesis imperfecta:

Other options:

Option A: Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant skeletal dysplasia with disproportionately short limbs, sleep apnea, and kyphoscoliosis. Facial features include button nose, frontal bossing, macrocephaly, etc.

The images below show the features of achondroplasia:

(a) Prominent forehead and body asymmetry, (b) a low nasal bridge, (c) trident hands, (d) scoliosis

Option C: Cretinism occurs due to iodine deficiency. Its clinical features are deaf-mutism, squint, mental retardation, and spastic or rigid neuromotor disorder.

Option D: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder. The affected persons will be tall with long limbs and digits. Spontaneous pneumothorax, aortic dissection, and lens dislocation are also seen. An early diastolic murmur is heard on auscultation.
questions.learning: Osteogenesis imperfecta Osteogenesis imperfecta is commonly associated with this multiple long bone fractures. Osteogenesis imperfecta is a connective tissue disorder that occurs due to abnormal type 1 collagen production.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which major histocompatibility complex (MHC) type is most likely associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation: The 26-year-old patient presents with acute unilateral anterior uveitis, characterized by blurred vision, photophobia, pain, and redness in one eye. The presence of concurrent joint pain suggests an underlying seronegative spondyloarthropathy, such as ankylosing spondylitis or reactive arthritis. This clinical constellation is strongly associated with the HLA-B27 antigen (Option A). HLA-B51 (Option B) is linked with Behçet’s disease, which typically causes bilateral uveitis and oral/genital ulcers. HLA-B47 (Option C) and HLA-B57 (Option D) have different associations (e.g., congenital adrenal hyperplasia or drug hypersensitivity) and are not classically linked with the combination of acute unilateral anterior uveitis and arthritis. Testing for HLA-B27 is a standard part of the systemic workup for recurring anterior uveitis. Therefore, given the classic inflammatory presentation in a young adult, HLA-B27 is the most likely associated major histocompatibility complex
questions.learning: The 26-year-old patient presents with acute unilateral anterior uveitis, characterized by blurred vision, photophobia, pain, and redness in one eye. The presence of concurrent joint pain suggests an underlying seronegative spondyloarthropathy, such as…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: After parotidectomy patients complains of loss of sensation while shaving. Which nerve is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Great auricular nerve

After parotid surgery, the nerve involved in the loss of sensation while shaving is the great auricular nerve.

The great auricular nerve (GAN) originates from the second and third nerve roots of the cervical plexus (C2-C3). It supplies the skin over the lower pinna, pre-auricular region, and angle of the mandible (image below). The main trunk passes over the sternocleidomastoid and into the anterosuperior portion of the parotid glands and branches into the anterior and posterior GAN. The anterior branch of GAN is often injured during parotid surgery during the initial elevation of the skin flap.

When GAN is injured, it can cause reduced sensations in the earlobe, pre-auricular skin, and the angle of the mandible that can interfere with habits such as shaving, wearing earrings, etc.

Other options:

Option A: The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve (V3 of trigeminal) supplies the posterior part of the temple, tragus, and adjoining auricle. It does not supply the area where a person is likely to shave. However, the injury to the auriculotemporal nerve resulting in aberrant regeneration would result in Frey's Syndrome (gustatory sweating).

Option C: Though the facial nerve is the most common nerve affected during parotidectomy, any damage would result in facial paralysis and not loss of sensation of the face.

Option D: The mandibular nerve is a branch of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) that supplies the skin over the mandible, lower lip, and cheek. However, they are not injured during parotidectomy.
questions.learning: Great auricular nerve After parotid surgery, the nerve involved in the loss of sensation while shaving is the great auricular nerve. The great auricular nerve (GAN) originates from the second and third nerve roots of the cervical plexus (C2-C3).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: You are posted as an intern in casualty when an MLC case is brought by the police with the following appearance. She was declared brought dead. What would you mark as the likely cause of death before sending the patient for postmortem?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Drowning

The given image shows frothing from nostrils and no clear signs of facial or conjunctival congestion. It is likely a case of drowning.

Frothing may also be seen in throttling or strangulation, but it might be associated with signs of conjunctival congestion, facial congestion, patterned bruise on neck etc. In the absence of these features, it is unlikely to be caused by strangulation.

Traumatic asphyxia is unlikely as the face of this patient is all whitened without signs of congestion or any obvious signs of trauma
questions.learning: Drowning — The given image shows frothing from nostrils and no clear signs of facial or conjunctival congestion. Frothing may also be seen in throttling or strangulation, but it might be associated with signs of conjunctival congestion, facial congestion,…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following disorders is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rett syndrome

Rett syndrome is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern.

Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder. It is caused due to mutation in the MECP-2 gene. The disorder is mostly seen in girls because affected boys usually die in infancy due to a defective single X chromosome.

Symptoms of Rett syndrome are microcephaly, developmental delay, autistic-like behavior, cognitive dysfunction, seizures, and repetitive motor actions.

Other options:

Option B: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is inherited in X linked recessive pattern. It occurs due to a mutation in the dystrophin gene. Typical features include calf muscle pseudohypertrophy and Gower's sign (using arms to lift themselves from a seated position). Laboratory investigations show elevated serum creatine kinase levels. Casimersen has been recently approved by the FDA for the treatment of DMD.

Option C: Huntington's disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It is a trinucleotide (CAG) repeat disorder and shows genetic anticipation (earlier onset of disease or increased severity in succeeding generations). Patients present with involuntary movements known as chorea. Tetrabenazine is used for treatment.

Option D: Tuberous sclerosis also known as Bournville disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It occurs due to mutation in TSC1 and TSC2 genes. It is characterized by subependymal nodules, angiomyolipomas, cafe au lait spots, shagreen patches, and cardiac rhabdomyomas.
questions.learning: Rett syndrome Rett syndrome is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern. Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A newborn presents with hypoplasia of the zygomatic bones, micrognathia, malformed external ears, and downward-slanting palpebral fissures. The condition results from abnormal development of which of the following pharyngeal arches?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. First and second pharyngeal arches

The clinical features described are characteristic of Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis), an autosomal dominant disorder caused most commonly by mutations in the TCOF1 gene, resulting in defective neural crest cell migration into the first and second pharyngeal arches. This leads to abnormal development of facial bones and external ears.

The patient has the classic features of Treacher Collins syndrome:

• Hypoplasia of the zygomatic bones
• Micrognathia (mandibular hypoplasia)
• Malformed external ears (microtia)
• Downward-slanting palpebral fissures

Why not the other options?

• A. First pharyngeal arch only: Although the mandible and zygoma are first arch derivatives, external ear abnormalities also involve the second arch.
• B. Second pharyngeal arch only: Does not explain the marked mandibular and zygomatic hypoplasia.
• D. Third and fourth pharyngeal arches: These primarily contribute to the hyoid bone, laryngeal cartilages, pharyngeal muscles, and cranial nerves IX and X, not the facial skeleton.
questions.learning: First and second pharyngeal arches — The clinical features described are characteristic of Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis), an autosomal dominant disorder caused most commonly by mutations in the TCOF1 gene, resulting in defective…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the incorrect statement regarding the marked structure.
options: It is the meeting point of frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones.
Blow to the lateral side of the skull injures the marked structure.
Accessory middle meningeal artery lies under this structure.
It corresponds to site of anterolateral fontanelle of fetal skull.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Accessory middle meningeal artery lies under this structure.

The structure marked in the image is the pterion. The incorrect statement is statement 3, which is the accessory middle meningeal artery lies under this structure.

The pterion is an H-shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull:

1. Frontal bone
2. Squamous part of the temporal bone
3. Greater wing of the sphenoid bone
4. Parietal bone

It is located approximately 4 cm above the midpoint of the zygomatic arch.

The pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery and the lateral fissure of the cerebral hemisphere. The bone in this area is thin, and any injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery, leading to extradural hematoma.

The pterion also corresponds to the site of the anterolateral (sphenoidal) fontanelle of the neonatal skull, which closes in the third month after birth.

The accessory meningeal artery may be a branch of the middle meningeal artery or might arise directly from the maxillary artery. It reaches the cranium via the foramen ovale and distributes principally in the extracranial region. It is distributed over the medial and lateral pterygoids, tensor veli palatini, greater wing and pterygoid processes of the sphenoid bone, mandibular nerve, and the otic ganglion. So, it supplies the trigeminal ganglion, dura mater and bone. But in some people, it may be replaced by small separate arteries.
questions.learning: Accessory middle meningeal artery lies under this structure. The structure marked in the image is the pterion.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling and severe pain in the right leg that has not subsided with analgesics. On examination, the pulse is feeble in the affected limb. Acute compartment syndrome is diagnosed, and intracompartmental pressure is 40 mmHg. On repeat examination, the pulse becomes absent. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fasciotomy

Acute compartment syndrome (ACS) is a limb-threatening surgical emergency caused by increased pressure within a closed fascial compartment, resulting in reduced tissue perfusion, muscle ischemia, and nerve injury. Urgent fasciotomy is the definitive treatment and should be performed without delay once the diagnosis is established.

• The patient has classic features of acute compartment syndrome:

• Severe pain out of proportion to the injury
• Pain not relieved by analgesics
• Feeble progressing to absent pulse
• Intracompartmental pressure of 90 mmHg (markedly elevated)

• These findings mandate emergency fasciotomy to decompress all involved compartments and restore tissue perfusion.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hot fomentation of the leg: Contraindicated; delays definitive treatment and may worsen edema.
• B. Cold fomentation of the leg: Does not relieve compartment pressure and delays life- and limb-saving surgery.
• D. Reassurance and send home: Dangerous and inappropriate; untreated ACS can lead to irreversible muscle necrosis, nerve damage, and limb loss.
questions.learning: Fasciotomy Acute compartment syndrome (ACS) is a limb-threatening surgical emergency caused by increased pressure within a closed fascial compartment, resulting in reduced tissue perfusion, muscle ischemia, and nerve injury.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In which chemical form is nitrogenous waste predominantly excreted from the human body?
questions.explanation: Humans are "ureotelic" organisms, meaning that the primary vehicle for the excretion of nitrogenous waste from protein metabolism is urea. Urea is synthesized in the liver through the urea cycle (ornithine cycle), which converts highly toxic ammonia into the less toxic, water-soluble urea. This urea is then transported through the blood to the kidneys, where it is eliminated in the urine. Nitric oxide (Option B) is a signaling molecule. Ammonia (Option C) is a toxic metabolic intermediate that is only eliminated in large quantities by aquatic animals (ammonotelic). Glutamine (Option D) acts as a safe carrier of ammonia in the blood but is not the final excretory product. The measurement of Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) is a standard clinical indicator of renal and hepatic function. Therefore, urea is the final, non-toxic form in which nitrogen is safely concentrated and eliminated from the human body

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A farmer presents to the emergency department with diarrhea, sweating, excessive lacrimation, and salivation. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the treatment of the condition?
options: Atropine is used as an antidote for OP poisoning
Pralidoxime has a role in reversing the enzyme in carbamate poisoning
Succinylcholine use is avoided in rapid sequence intubation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pralidoxime has a role in reversing the enzyme in carbamate poisoning

The clinical scenario is suggestive of organophosphate poisoning.

Oximes like pralidoxime are used to restore neuromuscular transmission in organophosphate antiChE poisoning. It attaches to the anionic site of the cholinesterase enzyme, which remains unoccupied in the presence of organophosphates. It binds and forms oxime-phosphonate which diffuses away, leaving the reactivated cholinesterase.

Pralidoxime is not an effective antidote to carbamates like carbaryl. This is because the anionic site of the cholinesterase enzyme is not free for attachment to pralidoxime. Hence, it does not reactivate the carbamylated enzyme. Carbamates spontaneously disassociate from AChE and recover in 24-48 hours.

Pralidoxime may potentiate the toxicity of carbaryl. Therefore, pralidoxime should be avoided in known single-agent carbaryl poisonings. However, pralidoxime is considered for use in mixed poisonings with an organophosphorus compound and a carbamate.

Atropine is useful in organophosphate poisoning because it is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine. An acetylcholinesterase enzyme has an active and anionic site. The organophosphates bind to the active site of AChEs (acetylcholine esterases) and deactivate it. This results in excessive Ach causing muscarinic activity. It has relatively insignificant action on nicotinic receptors.

Organophosphates and carbamates are powerful acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. Organophosphates are irreversible inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase (AChE). They form covalent bonds with the enzyme, leading to long-lasting inhibition, which is why they are used as pesticides and nerve agents.

Carbamates, on the other hand, are reversible inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase. They bind to AChE, but the enzyme is regenerated after a short period, usually within minutes to hours. This makes them less toxic and more controllable than organophosphates.

The predominant initial signs are of muscarinic excess, including: (DUMBBELSS)

* Diarrhea

* Urination

* Miosis

* Bronchospasm

* Bradycardia

* Emesis

* Lacrimation

* Salivation

* Sweating

Nicotinic manifestations include twitching of eyelids, tongue, and facial muscles which then leads to paralysis. CNS stimulation results in headache, tremors, ataxia, coma, and death.

Patients who present with organophosphate and carbamate poisoning require early endotracheal intubation to avoid respiratory depression, which is a common complication. Succinylcholine is avoided as it can exacerbate the neuromuscular blockade.

Pearl PF1113: Drugs used in Organophosphorus Poisoning

Drug

Symptoms for which it is used

Atropine

Muscarinic symptoms and CNS effects

Pralidoxime

Nicotinic symptoms

Diacetyl monoxime-specific cholinesterase reactivator

Nicotinic >muscarinic and CNS effects

IV diazepam

Convulsions

Oxygen, atropine, intubation, positive pressure ventilation

Pulmonary oedema, bronchospasm
questions.learning: Pralidoxime has a role in reversing the enzyme in carbamate poisoning The clinical scenario is suggestive of organophosphate poisoning. Oximes like pralidoxime are used to restore neuromuscular transmission in organophosphate antiChE poisoning.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A female patient presents with nausea, vomiting, and a sensation of objects moving around her. She is diagnosed with left vestibular neuritis. Her head impulse test is positive. What is the correct finding?
options: Right saccade with right side movement
Left saccade with right side movement
Right saccade with left side movement
Left saccade with left side movement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right saccade with left side movement

In the case of left vestibular neuritis, the correct finding on the head impulse test is a right saccade with left-side movement.

The head impulse test is to assess the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR). The abnormal head impulse test result is due to the VOR being impaired on the side of the vestibular lesion leading to saccades. Saccades are rapid, ballistic movements of the eyes that abruptly try to return to the point of fixation/ gaze.

The head impulse test is done by asking the patient to focus on a target. Then, the patient's head is quickly rotated to the left or right. If there is a deficiency in the VOR, the head movement will be followed by a catch-up saccade in the opposite direction. Thus, in left vestibular neuritis, a rightward saccade is seen following a left-side head rotation.

Vestibular neuritis is distinguished from central causes of vertigo by its characteristic findings: a positive head impulse test, absence of skew deviation, and spontaneous unidirectional nystagmus. Central vertigo, on the other hand, presents with a normal head impulse test, vertical skew deviation, bidirectional nystagmus, and additional neurological signs like diplopia, weakness, or dysarthria. In acute vestibular syndrome, especially in older patients with vascular risk factors, evaluation for a possible stroke is warranted.

Vestibular neuritis resolves spontaneously, but glucocorticoids can improve outcomes if administered within 3 days of symptom onset. Antiviral medications are only suggested for Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome). Vestibular suppressant medications can reduce acute symptoms. Patients should be encouraged to resume normal activity as soon as possible. Vestibular rehabilitation therapy can also be tried.
questions.learning: Right saccade with left side movement — In the case of left vestibular neuritis, the correct finding on the head impulse test is a right saccade with left-side movement.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient has undergone a gastrectomy (partial or total removal of the stomach) and is being monitored for postoperative complications and nutritional changes. Which condition is most likely to develop as a direct result of this surgery?
questions.explanation: A direct and major consequence of total or subtotal gastrectomy is the development of Vitamin B12 deficiency . The stomach’s parietal cells secrete Intrinsic Factor (IF), which is essential for the absorption of Vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum. Once the stomach or its secreting mucosa is removed, the patient can no longer absorb dietary B12, eventually leading to megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord if not supplemented. Folic acid (Option A) is absorbed primarily in the small intestine and is less specifically affected by the loss of the stomach. Gastric ulcers (Option C) are what the surgery often treats, and constipation (Option D) is not a specific metabolic consequence of gastrectomy compared to the profound risk of B12 malabsorption. Therefore, lifelong intramuscular Vitamin B12 injections are a mandatory component of postoperative care for gastrectomy patients. Recognition of this risk allows for the prevention of irreversible neurological damage
questions.learning: A direct and major consequence of total or subtotal gastrectomy is the development of Vitamin B12 deficiency . The stomach’s parietal cells secrete Intrinsic Factor (IF), which is essential for the absorption of Vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which one of the following is the myelinating cell of Central Nervous System?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oligodendrocyte

Oligodendrocytes are the myelinating cells of the central nervous system (CNS). They produce the myelin sheath around axons in the brain and spinal cord, allowing rapid saltatory conduction of nerve impulses between the nodes of Ranvier.

Why not the other options?

• A. Astrocyte: Provides structural and metabolic support, maintains the blood-brain barrier, regulates extracellular potassium, and participates in repair after CNS injury (gliosis). It does not produce myelin.
• B. Microglia: The resident macrophages of the CNS, responsible for phagocytosis and immune defense.
• C. Schwann cell: The myelinating cell of the peripheral nervous system (PNS). Each Schwann cell myelinates only one segment of a single axon.
questions.learning: Oligodendrocyte Oligodendrocytes are the myelinating cells of the central nervous system (CNS). They produce the myelin sheath around axons in the brain and spinal cord, allowing rapid saltatory conduction of nerve impulses between the nodes of Ranvier.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A neuron is receiving 400 inputs from 150 sensory neurons. This is an example of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Convergence

A single neuron receiving 400 inputs from 150 sensory neurons is an example of convergence.

Convergence means signals from multiple inputs uniting to excite a single neuron. It can be of 2 types:

• Convergence from a single source
• Convergence from multiple sources

The importance of convergence is that neurons are almost never excited by an action potential from a single input terminal. However, action potentials converging on the neuron from multiple terminals provide enough spatial summation to bring the neuron to the threshold required for discharge.
questions.learning: Convergence — A single neuron receiving 400 inputs from 150 sensory neurons is an example of convergence. Convergence means signals from multiple inputs uniting to excite a single neuron.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Inhibitory control by the hypothalamus is exerted on:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prolactin and growth hormone

Inhibitory control by the hypothalamus is exerted mainly on prolactin and growth hormone.

The major hypothalamic releasing hormones are:

• Thyrotropin releasing hormone (TRH)
• Corticotropin releasing hormone (CRH)
• Growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH)
• Gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH)

The major hypothalamic inhibitory hormones are:

• Prolactin inhibitory hormone or dopamine
• Growth hormone inhibitory hormone (GHIH), also called Somatostatin.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Calcium deposition is seen in which layer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. D

Calcium deposition occurs in the zone of calcified cartilage, where cartilage matrix becomes mineralized before being replaced by bone.

This zone lies between the zone of hypertrophy and the zone of ossification in the epiphyseal plate.

Zones A–C represent resting, proliferative, and hypertrophic cartilage, where growth occurs but no mineralization takes place.
questions.learning: D Calcium deposition occurs in the zone of calcified cartilage, where cartilage matrix becomes mineralized before being replaced by bone. This zone lies between the zone of hypertrophy and the zone of ossification in the epiphyseal plate.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 72-year-old man presents with a weak urinary stream and increased urinary frequency with small voided volumes. He experiences dizziness and hypotension while taking prazosin. Which α-blocker would be a more appropriate alternative in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient is suffering from Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) and experiencing orthostatic hypotension and dizziness, which are common side effects of non-subtype selective alpha-1 blockers like prazosin. Prazosin blocks alpha-1 receptors on both vascular smooth muscle and the prostatic urethra, leading to systemic vasodilation. Tamsulosin is a more suitable option because it is a selective alpha-1A receptor antagonist. The alpha-1A subtype is predominantly found in the prostate and bladder neck, while the alpha-1B subtype is found in the blood vessels. By selectively targeting the prostate, Tamsulosin relaxes the smooth muscle to improve urine flow with significantly less impact on systemic blood pressure compared to Prazosin, Terazosin (Option B), or Doxazosin (Option D). Alfuzosin (Option A) is also used for BPH but Tamsulosin remains the classic choice for minimizing "first-dose" syncope and dizziness in elderly patients. This uro-selectivity makes Tamsulosin the gold standard for medical management of BPH symptoms while maintaining cardiovascular stability
questions.learning: The patient is suffering from Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) and experiencing orthostatic hypotension and dizziness, which are common side effects of non-subtype selective alpha-1 blockers like prazosin.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following features is associated with vitamin A deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bitot spots

Bitot spots are triangular, pearly-white or yellowish, and foamy spots on the bulbar conjunctiva on either side of the cornea are associated with Vitamin A deficiency.

Option A: Pinguecula is a degenerative condition of the conjunctiva, characterized by the formation of a yellowish-white patch on the bulbar conjunctiva near the limbus. It usually presents as a triangular patch on the nasal side, with the triangle's apex commonly pointed away from the cornea.

Option C: Pterygium is a degenerative condition of the sub-conjunctival tissue. It is a connective tissue disorder and is never inflammatory.  It is made up of three parts: a "cap" (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge), a head, and a body. It occurs due to exposure to radiation: UV-B. The most common site is nasal.

Option D: Stocker's line - deposition of iron on the advancing edge is seen in Pterygium.

Pearl PF0046: WHO grading of Vitamin A deficiency

The term xerophthalmia is reserved to cover all the ocular manifestations of vitamin A deficiency.

Stage

The first symptom of xerophthalmia is nyctalopia.

The first sign of xerophthalmia is conjunctival xerosis.

The pathognomonic feature of xerophthalmia is the appearance of Bitot's spots.

Note:

Up to the level of Stage 2, the manifestations are reversible if treated with vitamin A supplements.

However, active conjunctival xerosis and Bitot’s spots begin to resolve within 2—5 days after supplementation. Most will disappear within 2 weeks, although a significant proportion of temporal lesions may persist in shrunken form and may therefore not be completely reversible.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A hospital wants to estimate the prevalence of diabetic nephropathy. Kidney biopsy samples are obtained from 500 adult patients with diabetes who receive care at the hospital. The samples are then interpreted by 10 different pathologists, 5 of whom work at the hospital and 5 of whom work at nearby institutions. A preliminary analysis shows that the pathologists who work for the hospital are 3 times more likely to interpret the biopsy samples as diabetic nephropathy compared to those who do not work for the hospital. Which of the following most likely explains this difference in interpretation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Observer bias

Hospital-employed pathologists are more likely to diagnose diabetic nephropathy, indicating observer bias. Observer bias occurs when the investigator’s expectations or affiliations influence interpretation of results. This is not confounding or selection bias, as the samples are the same; only interpretation differs.
questions.learning: Observer bias Hospital-employed pathologists are more likely to diagnose diabetic nephropathy, indicating observer bias. Observer bias occurs when the investigator’s expectations or affiliations influence interpretation of results.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 26-year-old female presents with dysphagia, weight loss, and halitosis. What is the most probable diagnosis based on the image provided?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Achalasia

The classic triad of dysphagia, weight loss, and regurgitation in a young patient, along with imaging showing smooth narrowing and gradual tapering, is highly suggestive of achalasia.

❌Option B: Ca  oesophagus

• Seen in lder age group
• Irregular narrowing, not smooth
• Dysphagia: solids first → then liquids

Option C : ❌Corrosive stricture

• History of acid/alkali ingestion
• Causes long, irregular strictures; Not typical smooth tapering on imaging

Option D : ❌Zenker’s diverticulum

• Seen in elderly
• Regurgitation of undigested food, Halitosis, gurgling
• Not typical smooth tapering on imaging

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old female presents with daytime sleepiness, impaired concentration, and impaired memory. On examination, her BMI is 43 kg/m2, blood pressure is 170/100 mm of Hg. Her awake arterial blood gas analysis shows bicarbonate - 33 mEq/L, PaCO2 - 53 mmHg, PaO2 - 70 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

The most probable diagnosis of this patient with awake high pCO2, low pO2, and BMI of 41 is obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS)/ Pickwickian syndrome is characterised by alveolar hypoventilation during wakefulness in obese people (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2), not explained by other causes of hypoventilation.

Patients with OHS are obese and have a history of daytime hypersomnolence, loud snoring, choking during sleep fatigue, impaired concentration and memory, a small oropharynx, and a thick neck.

OHS may be associated with the following findings:

* Elevated serum bicarbonate (>27 mEq/L)

* Hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg)

* Hypoxemia (PaO2 <70 mmHg)

* Polycythemia

Other options:

Option A: Central sleep apnea is characterized by a lack of respiratory effort during sleep, leading to recurrent pauses in breathing. It's less likely in this case due to the hypercapnia (elevated PaCO2) seen.

Option B: Narcolepsy involves excessive daytime sleepiness, sudden loss of muscle tone (cataplexy), sleep paralysis, and hallucinations during sleep onset. It doesn't typically cause elevated PaCO2.

Option D: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) involves repeated episodes of partial or complete upper airway obstruction during sleep. While obesity is a risk factor for OSA, the arterial blood gas analysis findings are more consistent with OHS.
questions.learning: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome — The most probable diagnosis of this patient with awake high pCO2, low pO2, and BMI of 41 is obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about Pompholyx is incorrect? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Most common site is soles

Pompholyx (Dyshidrotic eczema) is a recurrent vesicular eczema affecting the palms, fingers, and soles, characterized by intensely pruritic deep-seated vesicles.

• “Sago-grain” vesicles: Small, deep-seated, clear vesicles resembling tapioca pearls.
• Intense itching often precedes the eruption.
• Usually shows bilateral and symmetrical distribution.
• Commonly involves the lateral aspects of fingers and palms.

“Most common site is soles” is false.

• The palms and sides of the fingers are the most commonly affected sites.
• Soles may be involved, but they are not the predominant site.

Clinical Course

• Recurrent episodes of vesicles
• Followed by scaling, peeling, and fissuring
• Often aggravated by stress, sweating, or contact allergens

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the nerve being blocked in the local anesthesia procedure shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Greater palatine nerve

The image shows an intraoral injection directed toward the posterolateral hard palate near the greater palatine foramen. This is the site where the greater palatine nerve emerges.

The greater palatine nerve is a branch of the maxillary nerve (V2) and supplies:

• Posterior hard palate mucosa
• Palatal gingiva of posterior teeth

This nerve block is commonly used in dental and oral surgical procedures involving:

• Maxillary molars (palatal aspect)
• Palatal surgeries
• Extraction procedures requiring palatal anesthesia

Why other options are incorrect:

B. Maxillary nerve: This is a proximal nerve (V2) and is not directly blocked intraorally at the palate; requires deeper approaches like pterygopalatine fossa block.

C. Infraorbital nerve: Supplies upper lip, cheek, and anterior maxillary teeth region; blocked at infraorbital foramen, not palate.

D.Anterior ethmoidal nerve: Branch of ophthalmic division (V1); supplies anterior nasal cavity, not palate.
questions.learning: Greater palatine nerve — The image shows an intraoral injection directed toward the posterolateral hard palate near the greater palatine foramen. This is the site where the greater palatine nerve emerges.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 34-week newborn presents with breathing difficulty that improves with FiO₂ at 30%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyaline membrane disease

Hyaline membrane disease (neonatal respiratory distress syndrome) occurs due to surfactant deficiency (produced by type II pneumocytes), most commonly in  preterm infants, leading to alveolar collapse and impaired gas exchange.

• Seen in preterm or late preterm infants (like 34 weeks)
• Presents with respiratory distress soon after birth that improves with supplemental oxygen
• Chest X-ray shows diffuse reticulogranular (ground-glass) appearance with air bronchograms and reduced lung volumes
• Managed with oxygen, CPAP, and exogenous surfactant if needed
• Antenatal steroids reduce risk in preterm delivery

Differentiation:

• Transient tachypnea of newborn: hyperinflation, fluid in fissures, milder disease
• Meconium aspiration syndrome: patchy infiltrates, hyperinflation, term/post-term

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text:
Oculocephalic reflex assesses the integrity of which of the following cranial nerves?

A. III
B. IV
C. VI
D. VIII
E. VII
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A, C, and D

The oculocephalic reflex or doll's eye reflex is used to assess the integrity of the cranial nerves III, VI, and VIII.

It is a brainstem reflex examined by observing the the motion of eyes during the sudden rotation of the head of the patient by the examiner. It is done in both directions laterally, followed by flexion and extension. In a normal positive reflex, the eyes move conjugately in the opposite direction of the movement of the head to maintain their position in space.

The reflex has afferents in the vestibular nerve (VIII) that relay to the brainstem nuclei and bring about conjugate eye movements through the oculomotor nerve (III) and abducens nerve (VI).

A negative reflex occurs in any of the above cranial nerve palsies or brainstem injuries, where the eyes show no movement or movement in the same direction as head movement. This is used to assess brainstem reflexes in a comatose patient as a criterion of brain death.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Consider the following causes of visual loss: 1. Obstruction of the central retinal artery 2. Vitreous and retinal haemorrhage 3. Cataract 4. Retinal detachment Which of the above causes are associated with acute visual loss in a patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Acute visual loss is an ophthalmic emergency that requires prompt evaluation to prevent permanent blindness. Common causes include vascular occlusion, vitreous hemorrhage, and retinal detachment, whereas cataract typically causes gradual, progressive visual impairment.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Obstruction of the central retinal artery ✅

• Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) presents with sudden, painless, severe monocular vision loss and a characteristic cherry-red spot on fundus examination.

• 2. Vitreous and retinal haemorrhage ✅

• Sudden bleeding into the vitreous or retina causes acute painless visual loss or the sudden appearance of floaters and a curtain-like visual defect.

• 3. Cataract ❌

• Cataract causes gradual, painless, progressive diminution of vision, not acute visual loss.

• 4. Retinal detachment ✅

• Presents with sudden onset of flashes, floaters, and a curtain descending over the visual field, leading to acute painless visual loss.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 12-year-old child comes with cervical lymphadenopathy. Lymph node biopsy shows CD 10 + , CD 19 + , CD 20 +, CD 5 -, CD 23 -, and Tdt -. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Burkitt lymphoma

The clinical scenario of a child with cervical lymph node, which is positive for CD 10, 19, and 20 and negative for CD 5, 23, and tdt and the histopathology showing tumour cells showing a diffuse monotonous pattern with clumped and dispersed chromatin in the nuclei along with deeply basophilic cytoplasm containing lipid vacuoles points towards a diagnosis of Burkitt's lymphoma.

Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. It is characterized by the translocation of the c-Myc gene on chromosome 8. This leads to increased MYC protein levels. The translocation most commonly seen in Burkitt's lymphoma is t(8;14).

It can occur in 3 forms that have distinct clinical characteristics:

• African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma presents as a mass involving the mandible. It may also involve the abdominal viscera, particularly the kidneys, ovaries, and adrenal glands.
• Sporadic (non-endemic) is often seen as a mass involving the ileocecum and peritoneum.
• Aggressive lymphoma or acute leukaemia is seen in immunocompromised individuals

Histopathology shows tumour cells with round or oval nuclei, coarse chromatin, small nucleoli, minimal cytoplasm, and a high mitotic index. The phagocytes have abundant clear cytoplasm, creating a characteristic “starry sky” pattern. Bone marrow aspiration shows tumour cells with royal blue cytoplasm containing clear cytoplasmic vacuoles.

The tumour cells express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6, a phenotype consistent with a germinal centre B-cell origin.

Other options:

Option A: Diffuse large B cell lymphoma/ DLBCL is the most common type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma and is characteristic of large cell type and shows a diffuse pattern of growth.are positive for CD10, Cd23 and Bcl-6.

Option B: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) arises from immature B (pre-B) or T (pre-T) cells called lymphoblasts. Immunohistochemistry for terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is positive in pre-B and pre-T lymphoblasts.

Peripheral smear shows lymphoblasts that have condensed chromatin, less conspicuous nucleoli, and smaller amounts of cytoplasm which lacks granules as shown below.

Option C: Mantle cell lymphoma is a lymphoid neoplasm in which tumour cells closely resemble the normal mantle zone B cells surrounding the germinal centre. Mantle cell lymphomas express high levels of cyclin D1. These cells are positive for CD19, CD20, CD5, and surface immunoglobulins (Ig). They are negative for CD23. In cases, where cyclin D1 is negative, SOX11 marker can be used to identify this lymphoma.

Lymph node biopsy shows medium-sized lymphoma cells with irregular nuclear outlines, scanty cytoplasm, and condensed chromatin in mantle cell lymphoma.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presents with leg pain. She had fever and cough 3 days prior. Currently, there is pain on palpation of the calf muscles. Reflexes and other clinical examinations are normal. Lab test reveals CK levels of 2000 IU. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Viral Myositis

The clinical picture showing pain in the calves occuring within a week of an upper respiratory tract infection (URI), with elevated creatine kinase levels suggests the diagnosis of viral myositis. The specific history of URI suggests influenza myositis.

Infectious myositis has a male predominance and is typically seen in young adults. Childhood form presents with fever, malaise, and rhinorrhea and is usually followed by severe pain, especially in the calves. The muscle pain is usually worse with movement and the symptoms last for about a week. In children, toe walking and wide-based gait may be seen because of the involvement of the gastrocnemius-soleus muscles.

Other viral causes of myositis include HIV-1 (one of the most common causes of myositis), group B coxsackievirus (epidemic myalgia), HTLV-1 (Human T-lymphotropic virus), and cytomegalovirus (CMV).

Lab features of influenza myositis include elevated CK which may be as high as 500 times normal the value. Urine myoglobin is usually positive. Detection of the virus with PCR testing of nasopharyngeal specimens can be carried out but is not of much clinical significance. The histopathological examination would reveal muscle fiber necrosis without much inflammatory change.

Treatment includes bed rest, IV fluids, and symptomatic management with analgesics and antipyretics. Amantadine and other antiviral agents may be considered in adults. Complications include myocarditis and respiratory dysfunction. Rhabdomyolysis is an uncommon complication.
questions.learning: Viral Myositis — The clinical picture showing pain in the calves occuring within a week of an upper respiratory tract infection (URI), with elevated creatine kinase levels suggests the diagnosis of viral myositis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A child is rescued from a major train accident. During triage, the child is found to be stable and can walk, but he has a large laceration on the leg with severe inflammation around the wound. What is the most appropriate triage category for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Yellow

A child with a large laceration on the thigh which is inflamed but is stable, will be classified under the yellow category.

The yellow (medium priority) category includes patients who need resuscitation or surgery within 24 hours and have a good chance of survival with prompt treatment. Spinal injuries, along with moderate head injuries, compound fractures, and pelvic fractures, typically fall under this category due to the potential for delayed complications.

Triage includes rapid classification of the injured based on their injuries and the chances of survival with prompt medical intervention into four categories- red (high priority), yellow (medium priority), green (low priority) and black (least priority). It provides maximum benefit to the greatest number of injured in a disaster situation. It lessens the burden on medical facilities.

Pearl PF2180: Triage Colour Coding

Triage system consists of four colour codes:

Color code
Type of patients
Examples

Red (High priority)

Need for immediate resuscitation or surgery in the next 6 hours or transfer.

May survive if timely medical intervention can be given

• Tension pneumothorax
• Airway obstruction
• Hemothorax
• Cardiac tamponade
• Acute circulatory arrest
• Major intra-abdominal bleed etc.

Yellow (Medium priority)

Possible resuscitation or surgery in the next 24 hours.

Likely to survive if prompt treatment is given.

• Compound fractures
• Degloving injuries
• Pelvic fracture
• Spinal injuries
• Moderate head injury

Green (Low priority)

Ambulatory patients or minor illnesses.

Likely to survive if treatment is slightly delayed.

• Simple fractures
• Minor lacerations etc.

Black (Least priority)

Dead or moribund patients.

• Severe brain injury
• Major damage / disruption to chest wall and abdominal structures

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient presents to the emergency department. The arterial blood gas report is as follows: pH, 7.2; pCO2, 81mm Hg; and HCO3, 40 meq/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Respiratory acidosis

The arterial blood gas values suggest a likely diagnosis of respiratory acidosis.

The various buffering systems present in the body maintain the systemic arterial pH between 7.35-7.45. The most common acid-base disorders are metabolic acidosis or alkalosis and respiratory acidosis or alkalosis.

Normal values in an arterial blood gas are as follows:

• pH: 7.35-7.45
•

PaCO2: 35-45 mmHg

•

HCO3: 22-26 mEq/L

•

PaO2: 75-100 mmHg

Respiratory changes (changes in PCO2) promote a corresponding change in metabolic response (changes in HCO3-) and vice versa as a compensatory mechanism. In general, PCO2 and HCO3- move in the same direction for compensation in metabolic and respiratory acid-base disorders respectively. A change in the two parameters in opposite directions points to a mixed acid-base disturbance.

Respiratory acidosis can be secondary to severe pulmonary disease, respiratory muscle fatigue, or ventilatory control abnormalities. It is marked by an increase in PaCO2 and a decrease in pH. A compensatory rise of HCO3- can also be seen.

A rapid rise in PCO2 (acute hypercapnia) can present with dyspnea, confusion, and psychosis. It can be seen in severe asthma secondary to bronchospasm, anaphylaxis, or inhalational burns. Chronic hypercapnia causes sleep disorders, memory loss, and daytime somnolence. It is commonly seen in end-stage obstructive lung disease.

Acute respiratory acidosis may need tracheal intubation and assisted mechanical ventilation. Rapid correction of hypercapnia should be avoided as it can trigger cardiac arrhythmias and seizures. Chronic respiratory acidosis is difficult to manage and improvement in lung function is the primary aim.

Other options:

Option A: Respiratory alkalosis arises due to alveolar hyperventilation and can be due to salicylates, high altitude states, cardiac failure, and anemia.

Option B: Metabolic acidosis arises due to an accumulation of endogenous acids. Examples include lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis, and starvation. It can also be seen in renal failure.

Option D: Metabolic alkalosis can be seen in Liddle's syndrome, hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, massive blood transfusion, and cystic fibrosis. It is marked by elevated pH and HCO3- values. A rise in PaCO2 indicates a compensatory respiratory response.
questions.learning: Respiratory acidosis — The arterial blood gas values suggest a likely diagnosis of respiratory acidosis. The various buffering systems present in the body maintain the systemic arterial pH between 7.35-7.45.
